posts.title: The Living Ocean
posts.desc: A fish with a transparent head, a shrimp that strikes twice, and animals filmed more than two miles down. Thirty-three photographs, with a short caption and research links for each.
posts.keywords: sea marine deep sea photography fish coral water nature octopus reef

sections.text: Barreleye · Macropinna microstoma The green spheres inside its head are its eyes. They look upward through a transparent dome, then rotate forward when the fish feeds. The two dark spots above its mouth are smell organs. Research · Photo: MBARI

sections.head: Sunlit water
sections.text: Neptune grass · Posidonia oceanica This meadow is near Marseille, France. Seagrass spreads by growing new shoots from underground stems. The leaves come and go, but some Mediterranean clones have persisted for thousands of years. Research · Photo: Karim saari Ochre sea stars · Pisaster ochraceus Robert Paine removed these sea stars from a stretch of Washington shore. Mussels took over, crowding out other species. The experiment helped establish the idea of a keystone species: an animal with an effect far larger than its numbers suggest. Research · Photo: Collin Smith / USGS Lined chiton · Tonicella lineata Chitons scrape food off rocks with a ribbon of teeth called a radula. The working tooth tips are hardened with magnetite, an iron oxide. They grow replacements as the old teeth wear down. Research · Photo: Jerry Kirkhart Great Barrier Reef · Flynn Reef, Australia · More than 2,900 reefs The Great Barrier Reef contains more than 2,900 separate reefs. Each coral colony is made of small animals called polyps, which build the limestone skeleton beneath them. The branching and plate-shaped colonies here share one outcrop. Research · Photo: Toby Hudson Mandarinfish · Synchiropus splendidus Many blue fish get their color from microscopic structures that reflect light. Mandarinfish also have cells containing blue pigment, called cyanophores. Researchers found them in this fish and its close relative, the psychedelic mandarinfish. Research · Photo: Diego Delso Ribbon eel · Rhinomuraena quaesita The yellow flaps on its snout are expanded nostrils. Young ribbon eels are black with a yellow dorsal fin; adult males are blue and yellow. They usually live in burrows in sand or rubble beside coral reefs. Research · Photo: Rickard Zerpe Mimic octopus · Thaumoctopus mimicus It can flatten itself into the shape of a flatfish or trail two banded arms like a sea snake. Researchers saw it use the snake-like display when harassed by damselfish. The disguise changes with the situation. Research · Photo: Rickard Zerpe Coconut octopus · Amphioctopus marginatus Researchers filmed these octopuses carrying coconut-shell halves across the seabed, then assembling them into shelters. Carrying the shells makes walking awkward. The payoff comes later, when the octopus needs somewhere to hide. Research · Photo: Rickard Zerpe Blue-ringed octopus · Hapalochlaena sp. Its bite can deliver tetrodotoxin, which blocks nerve signals and can paralyze breathing muscles. The blue markings become conspicuous when it's disturbed. Research · Photo: Shaymary Peacock mantis shrimp · Odontodactylus scyllarus Its strike produces two impacts: the club hits, then a vapor bubble collapses against the target. The bubble forms because the fast-moving club drops the water pressure, a process called cavitation. Both impacts help break a shell. Research · Photo: Cédric Péneau Variable neon slug · Nembrotha kubaryana This sea slug eats sea squirts. Chemists isolated a blue pigment from its body that had already been found in sea squirts, suggesting it came from the slug's food. Research · Photo: Diego Delso Porcelain crab · Neopetrolisthes maculatus The anemone provides shelter among its stinging tentacles. The crab feeds by sweeping feathery mouthparts through the water and collecting suspended food. The large claws are separate from these feeding fans. Research · Photo: Diego Delso

sections.head: In open water
sections.text: Portuguese man o' war · Physalia physalis A man o' war is a colony of connected, genetically identical parts called zooids. They specialize in feeding, catching prey, and reproduction. The gas-filled float carries the colony along with the wind and current. Research · Photo: Andrespuche Blue dragons · Glaucus spp. These slugs drift at the surface and feed on bluebottles and other floating stinging animals. They store some of their prey's stinging capsules at the tips of their finger-like branches, where the capsules can still fire. Research · Photo: Doug Beckers Leopard seal · Hydrurga leptonyx Photographer Paul Nicklen describes a leopard seal bringing him live penguins, then dead ones, during an Antarctic assignment. He interpreted it as an attempt to feed him. What the seal intended is harder to establish. Research · Photo: Gilad Rom Sperm whales · Physeter macrocephalus These two are swimming, but sperm whales also rest upright just below the surface. Researchers recorded whales drifting almost motionless and failing to react to a passing boat, suggesting they were asleep. Those dives occupied about 7% of the study's recording time. Research · Photo: Gabriel Barathieu Giant manta ray · Mobula birostris Two captive mantas made unusual repeated movements in front of a mirror, including exposing parts of their bodies to it. Researchers suggested they might be inspecting themselves. That small study didn't establish that mantas pass the standard mirror self-recognition test. Research · Photo: Arturo de Frias Marques Great white shark · Carcharodon carcharias A tagged white shark named Nicole traveled from South Africa to Australia, about 6,900 miles in 99 days. She was identified back at the original South African tagging site less than nine months after departure. The outward trip was tracked; the return was confirmed by her markings. Research · Photo: Andrew Shiva Green sea turtle · Chelonia mydas Green turtles nesting on Ascension Island feed along the Brazilian coast, more than 1,400 miles away. Satellite tags have followed females across that stretch of open Atlantic, often along remarkably straight routes. Research · Photo: Charles J. Sharp

sections.head: Under the microscope
sections.text: Radiolarian · Stylosphaera coronata laevis This perforated skeleton belonged to a single cell. Many radiolarians build their skeletons from silica, the main ingredient in glass. Their remains settle to the seafloor and become part of the sediment. Research · Photo: Picturepest Diatoms · Light micrograph · About 20% of global carbon fixation Diatoms are estimated to carry out about a fifth of the planet's photosynthetic carbon fixation, turning carbon dioxide into organic matter using sunlight. Each cell in this chain does that work inside a silica shell. Research · Photo: John R. Dolan, NOAA Diatom shell · Stephanopyxis grunowii A single-celled alga made this patterned silica wall. In other diatom species, researchers have measured how regular pore arrangements guide and filter light, much like manufactured photonic materials. Research · Photo: Anatoly Mikhaltsov

sections.head: Below the sunlight
sections.text: Submersible lamps reveal the colors in these deep-sea photographs. The water around the animals is dark. Siphonophore · Marrus orthocanna The transparent bells propel a colony of connected zooids, each specialized for a job. Feeding structures trail below them. The colony grows by budding new parts from one fertilized egg. Research · Photo: Kevin Raskoff, Monterey Peninsula College Giant phantom jelly · Stygiomedusa gigantea Its bell can grow more than three feet across, and its four mouth-arms can exceed 33 feet. MBARI has filmed small fish swimming among those arms. Open water offers few hiding places; a jelly can provide one. Research · Photo: MBARI Sully hydrothermal vent · Northeast Pacific The dark plume carries mineral particles, not smoke from a fire. Around vents, microbes use energy from chemical reactions to make food, a process called chemosynthesis. They support animal communities where sunlight can't reach. Research · Photo: NOAA Pompeii worm · Alvinella pompejana It lives in tubes on hydrothermal chimneys, where hot vent fluid meets cold seawater. In a pressurized aquarium, most survived a heat test that reached 108 F. Two hours at 122 to 131 F killed them. Research · Photo: Olivier Dugornay

sections.head: Recently described
sections.text: Described 2024 Mystery mollusc · Bathydevius caudactylus MBARI researchers first saw this swimming sea slug in 2000 and described it in 2024. Its broad hood traps small crustaceans. It can also release a glowing finger from its tail, apparently as a decoy, then grow a replacement. Research · Photo: MBARI Described 2024 Tailspot wrasse · Halichoeres sanchezi A diver photographed an unfamiliar wrasse in 2013. Researchers collected it near San Benedicto Island, Mexico, during a 2022 survey and confirmed it as a new species. These are two females; the larger males have a different color pattern. Research · Photo: Allison and Carlos Estape Described 2022 Rose-veiled fairy wrasse · Cirrhilabrus finifenmaa Scientists had mistaken this Maldivian fish for an adult of another species. Ahmed Najeeb helped describe it as a separate species, the first fish formally described by a Maldivian researcher. Finifenmaa means rose in Dhivehi. Research · Photo: Luiz A. Rocha Described 2020 Duobrachium comb jelly · Duobrachium sparksae NOAA scientists described this comb jelly from video alone, without collecting a specimen. Three sightings came from one dive near Puerto Rico, about 2.4 miles down. Its tentacles appeared to touch the seabed while its body hovered above. Research · Photo: NOAA Ocean Exploration Described 2020 E.T. sponge · Advhena magnifica The holes that look like eyes are openings in a glass sponge. Water moving through its body brings food particles. Its shape suggested the name Advhena magnifica, magnificent alien; anatomical study established the new genus. Research · Photo: NOAA Ocean Exploration Described 2018 Aphrodite anthias · Tosanoides aphrodite Divers collected this fish about 390 feet down at St. Paul's Rocks in the Atlantic. Genetic analysis placed it in a genus previously known only from the Pacific. The species name honors Aphrodite, the Greek goddess of beauty. Research · Photo: Luiz A. Rocha

posts.title: The Brain Behind the Warehouse
posts.desc: Stock on a shelf may already belong to another order. Warehouse software tracks what's available and directs each move, from receiving a delivery to putting a parcel on a truck.
posts.keywords: warehouse WMS operations inventory fulfillment supply chain logistics software

sections.text: Home

sections.head: The Brain Behind the Warehouse
sections.text: A warehouse needs to know which stock is available, where it is, and what should move next. Its software turns those answers into work someone can carry out on the floor. 12 min read You can have 500 shirts in a warehouse and still be unable to fill an order for 100. If 300 are reserved for other orders and 120 more are held for inspection, only 80 are available for the new order. A warehouse management system , or WMS, tracks those differences and turns orders into work: which stock to use, where to find it, and what to move next. 01

sections.head: What the system records
sections.text: The WMS connects three records. The item master describes the product: its dimensions, weight, packaging, and any lot or serial tracking. The location master describes the places it can occupy. The inventory record says how much of that item is in a particular location, who owns it, and whether it can be used. A SKU, stock keeping unit, identifies a distinct item. A medium blue shirt and a large blue shirt have different SKUs. A lot identifies a batch; a serial number identifies an individual unit. Those distinctions let a business recall one production batch without pulling every unit of the product. Quantities need units. Twelve cases are not twelve shirts. If each case holds ten shirts, the WMS needs that conversion to receive cases and pick individual units correctly. A wrong case quantity can make every scan look valid while every count is wrong. 02

sections.head: How a move becomes a record
sections.text: A directed picking task might read: go to A-12-03, scan the location, scan the shirt, put two units in tote T-17. The system chooses the task using the order, the stock, and the warehouse's rules. The scans check identifiers against the task. Confirmation records the quantity moved from the shelf to the tote, with a time and user. The shirts are still in the building; their recorded location has changed. A barcode doesn't count the contents of a box. Someone can scan the right label and enter the wrong quantity, or move stock without recording it. Voice systems, sensors, and automation can also confirm work. What matters is that physical movement gets a matching transaction, and exceptions can be traced. Receiving to shipping Select a stage or use the arrows. Item movement: receive, put away, store, transfer, pick, pack, stage, ship. 03

sections.head: Receiving
sections.text: A supplier may send an advance ship notice, or ASN, before the truck arrives. It describes what is coming. At the dock, the receiver checks the delivery against that notice and the purchase order, records the quantities actually received, and logs shortages, extras, or damage. A pallet or tote can have a license plate number, or LPN: an identifier attached to a container and its recorded contents. Scanning it retrieves that record. It doesn't prove the contents match, so the receiving process still needs rules for inspection and discrepancy handling. Dock-to-stock time measures how long receiving takes to make goods available for use. A pallet waiting for inspection can be physically present without being available to an order. With cross-docking, goods needed for an outbound shipment go toward shipping without a trip through storage. 04

sections.head: Choosing a location
sections.text: Putaway moves received stock into storage. The WMS chooses a destination using location rules : suitable temperature, enough capacity, permitted item types, and other constraints. Slotting decides where products should live to make picking easier. Frequently picked items benefit from accessible locations and shorter routes. Weight, dimensions, congestion, and items often ordered together also matter. A single popularity ranking won't settle all of those tradeoffs. Full pallets may sit in reserve storage while individual units sit in a smaller forward pick location. Replenishment moves stock from reserve to that pick location, either when it falls below a threshold or when upcoming work needs more. An empty pick location can stop a task even when there is plenty of stock elsewhere. 05

sections.head: Present, available, and counted
sections.text: On hand is the quantity recorded in the warehouse. Allocated stock is reserved for demand. A hold blocks stock from use, perhaps pending inspection or because it is damaged. Reservations and holds are separate controls, even when a screen groups them together. The recorded quantity also needs a physical check. Cycle counting audits selected locations throughout the year. A discrepancy goes through review, recount, or adjustment according to the operation's rules. Repeated misses in one location are a reason to investigate the process there. For dated stock, FIFO means first in, first out. FEFO means first expiring, first out: use the stock with the earliest eligible expiration date. A customer may also require enough shelf life remaining at delivery, so the oldest lot isn't always suitable. 06

sections.head: Why an order isn't being picked
sections.text: An order arrives from the business's sales or order system with items, quantities, a destination, and a deadline. Allocation reserves eligible inventory for it. The WMS may reserve a quantity first and choose the exact stock later, or assign specific locations, lots, or containers. Release authorizes work to proceed. The operation must fit that work around people, equipment, pack stations, and carrier cutoffs. A wave groups orders for processing; a waveless operation feeds work more continuously. The sequence varies by product. In Oracle WMS , for example, running a wave can create the allocations. Checks for a stuck order 01 Received? Did the order reach the WMS? 02 Eligible? Is the stock usable for this order? 03 Reserved? Has enough inventory been assigned? 04 Released? Has work been authorized? 05 Created? Did processing create the task? 06 Reachable? Can this worker see and execute it? These are diagnostic checks, not a processing sequence shared by every WMS. 07

sections.head: Picking without wasting the trip
sections.text: In discrete picking, a worker picks one order at a time. Batch picking combines demand from several orders, then sorts the items afterward. Cluster picking keeps those orders separate during the trip, often in different totes on one cart. Zone picking gives workers parts of the floor, with the order moving between zones or being consolidated later. Those choices solve different problems. Batching saves repeated visits to a popular item but adds sorting work. Clusters avoid that later sort but limit how many orders fit on the cart. Zones reduce travel within each area but need a reliable handoff. Workers can follow scanners, spoken instructions, or lights at the bins. In goods-to-person systems, conveyors, cranes, shuttles, or robots bring stock to a station. The WMS still tracks inventory and demand; equipment software controls the movement. Less walking can leave packing or station capacity as the next constraint. 08

sections.head: Packing and shipping
sections.text: At packing, the items are checked against the order and assigned to containers. Cartonization uses item and container data to propose how to pack them, subject to weight, fit, and packing rules. It may happen before picking rather than at the pack bench. Box size affects the bill. Parcel carriers can charge by dimensional weight , calculated from package volume, when it exceeds actual weight. Carrier selection and label printing may belong to the WMS, a shipping application, or a transportation management system (TMS). Contents Packing slip Lists shipped items and quantities so the receiver can check them. Freight Bill of lading Records the freight shipment and carriage details. It can be electronic. To the buyer Outbound ASN Describes the shipment before arrival. In an X12 EDI exchange, this is the 856. To the business system Ship confirmation Reports what actually shipped so other systems can update their records. With a GS1 logistics label , the container's identifier is the SSCC, or Serial Shipping Container Code, commonly carried in a GS1-128 barcode. The ASN associates that identifier with the contents. The number on the label and the number in the message must agree. A truck can leave while the business system still shows an open order. Check whether the WMS created the ship confirmation, whether it was delivered, and whether the receiving system accepted it. Inventory posting and invoicing depend on that business's setup; printing a label alone doesn't settle either. Inventory maintenance Select a stage or use the arrows. Inventory maintenance: replenish pick locations, count stock, block unsuitable inventory, inspect returns. 09

sections.head: Returns and quarantine
sections.text: A returned shirt needs an identity, a condition assessment, and a decision. It might be restocked, repaired, returned to the supplier, or scrapped. A disposition code records that decision. The physical return and the customer's credit are related events, but one does not prove the other happened. Stock awaiting a decision can be held in the software and separated physically. A software hold prevents normal allocation when the rules are enforced. It cannot stop someone taking the item off a shelf. Quarantine needs both a recorded restriction and a floor process that respects it. Parts to finished goods Select a stage or use the arrows. Production supply: receive parts, store, release a work order, kit, assemble, receive finished goods. 10

sections.head: Supplying a factory
sections.text: A bill of materials, or BOM, lists the components required for a product. A work order specifies what to build and how many. The warehouse supplies those parts and receives finished goods. The production system manages the build. Example bill of materials one finished unit 1× Steel frame 1× Motor 1× Control board 6× Fasteners 1× Trim kit = 1 finished product Kitting gathers parts for a build. Line replenishment keeps components available at the production station; a kanban is a signal to supply more, such as an empty bin or an electronic request. Partly completed production is work in process, or WIP. Component consumption can be recorded directly or inferred. With backflushing , a reported production event deducts the expected components. In the example, reporting 200 finished units could consume 1,200 fasteners. If the line actually used 1,230, the extra 30 need recording too. A correct BOM cannot account for unreported scrap. A line can stop for want of one component while every other component is abundant. Some plants need parts delivered just in sequence, in the order production will use them. Total warehouse stock is a poor measure of whether the next build can begin. 11

sections.head: The other systems involved
sections.text: A WMS shares work with other software. These names describe responsibilities; they don't guarantee a separate product for each one. Common responsibilities ERP: enterprise resource planning Purchasing, production planning, financial records, and other business processes. OMS: order management system Customer orders and fulfillment decisions across locations or channels. WMS: warehouse management system Warehouse inventory, locations, and work. MES: manufacturing execution system Production execution, progress, and quality records. WES / WCS: warehouse execution / control systems Coordinate work across resources and control material-handling equipment. MHI's software definitions and WES integration overview . Product boundaries overlap. Electronic data interchange, or EDI, exchanges standardized business documents. X12's 940 requests warehouse shipping work; the 945 reports the shipment. The buyer's 856 serves a different recipient and purpose. Systems also exchange data through application programming interfaces (APIs) and files. An integration needs to handle delays, rejections, and duplicates. If a shipment was posted but its acknowledgment was lost, resending the message must not deduct the inventory again. Message IDs, processing logs, and reconciliation are what let teams distinguish a missing event from an event processed twice. 12

sections.head: Measuring the result
sections.text: A perfect order arrives on time, complete, undamaged, and with accurate documentation. For a direct measurement, count orders meeting all four conditions and divide by the total orders. Four separate success rates don't show whether the failures hit the same orders. APQC's measure multiplies the four rates and calls the result an approximation. Four rates of 97 percent produce an estimate of 88.5 percent. As a probability calculation, that assumes independent failures. The demo lets you change that assumption. What counts as a perfect order? Change the success rates, then change which orders fail. 88.5% perfect orders in this model Each button switches between 97% and 99.5%. These are example rates. On time Use 99.5% delivered by the date you promised In full Use 99.5% the complete order, no missing items or short counts Undamaged Use 99.5% arrives in sellable condition, nothing broken Documented correctly Use 99.5% the required documents are accurate Independent failures Same orders fail Different orders fail With independent failures, 0.97 × 0.97 × 0.97 × 0.97 = 88.5%. Change the overlap to see why the four rates alone cannot tell you how many orders were perfect. Example probabilities, not warehouse benchmarks. The overlap settings hold the individual rates constant. For 1,000 orders, a 97 percent rate means 30 failures on each measure. If the same 30 orders fail all four, 970 are perfect. If four separate groups of 30 fail, only 880 are. Both operations report 97 percent on every individual measure. Other measures answer narrower questions: receiving time, pick accuracy, units per labor hour, or cost per order. Compare like work over a consistent period. A full-pallet pick and a single-item pick are different jobs, even if a dashboard calls both one pick. 13

sections.head: What changes between warehouses
sections.text: Third-party logistics (3PL) Stores and ships goods for other businesses. Separate each client's stock, apply their rules, and record billable work. E-commerce Small orders across many products. Handle individual-unit picking, carrier cutoffs, and returns. Food Shelf life and storage conditions limit what can ship. Track lots and dates, enforce eligibility, and locate affected stock for recalls. Pharmaceuticals Product identity and traceability require careful records. Preserve required lot or serial history and control release from inspection. Apparel Styles split into sizes and colors. Keep variants distinct and support the operation's handling and return processes. Manufacturing Production needs particular components at particular times. Supply the line in the required quantity and sequence. 14

sections.head: What a labor saving means
sections.text: A labor management system compares recorded work with planned or engineered task times . Those comparisons need to account for travel, load size, equipment, and delays outside the worker's control. Otherwise, a slow replenishment looks like a slow picker. Suppose a change saves 20 seconds on each of 10,000 daily tasks. That is about 56 labor hours. At an assumed fully loaded cost of $25 an hour, it represents roughly $1,389 of daily capacity. These are example inputs, not an industry payback estimate. That capacity becomes a cash saving only if the business can reduce paid hours or avoid adding them. It may instead absorb growth or ease a backlog. Software, equipment, maintenance, and new work elsewhere in the process still belong in the calculation. 15

sections.head: Choosing and changing the system
sections.text: A WMS can be a standalone product or part of an ERP. ERP warehouse modules can support directed work and real-time inventory; the label on the product doesn't tell you how capable it is. Evaluate the actual operation: owners, lots, automation, shipping requirements, peak volume, and integrations. Configuration sets rules the product supports. Customization adds behavior through code. Either can cause failures and need testing after an upgrade. Supported extensions may be reasonable; a heavily modified process carries a larger maintenance burden. Implementation means mapping the work, cleaning and migrating data, connecting systems, testing, training, and cutting over. Before that cutover, run real examples through receiving to shipment. Include a short delivery, a held lot, a partial pick, a rejected message, and a retry. A happy-path demonstration leaves those questions unanswered. If a pick location runs empty ten minutes before the carrier cutoff, who gets the replenishment task, can they complete it, and what happens to the order if they can't? A trial on the floor can establish that. A feature list can't. © 2026 Ethan Willingham

posts.title: All In: Managing Professionals
posts.desc: People can meet every requirement and still hold back their best work. Managing professionals means making room for judgment while staying clear about responsibility and the problems you need solved.
posts.keywords: management managing professionals leadership people work trust teams responsibility

sections.text: Home Leading a team

sections.head: All In: Managing Professionals
sections.text: You can require someone to do the job. Earning their best work takes more: clear expectations, useful feedback, and enough trust for them to use the judgment you hired them for. scroll Being good at a job doesn't tell you how to manage the people doing it. An engineer can design a system and struggle to coach another engineer. A good analyst can become the bottleneck for an entire team by checking every decision. The work changes when you become a manager. You choose priorities, help people improve, and take responsibility for what the team delivers. Much of that depends on expertise you don't have. These sections draw on management research and a few useful books, with a development guide at the end. Four terms used here 1

sections.head: Professional (knowledge worker)
sections.text: Someone whose work depends on specialized knowledge and judgment: an engineer, analyst, designer, or customer success manager. Peter Drucker called them knowledge workers. 2

sections.head: Engagement
sections.text: How involved someone feels in their work and how much they care about doing it well. 3

sections.head: Discretionary effort
sections.text: The extra attention and initiative someone chooses to put into a job beyond its requirements. 4

sections.head: All in
sections.text: A person who wants the work to succeed and takes responsibility for helping it succeed. Act I Two kinds of worker 01

sections.head: The man with the stopwatch
sections.text: A useful method for a task with a known answer. At Bethlehem Steel, Frederick Taylor studied how laborers loaded pig iron. He prescribed when to lift and when to rest, selected workers suited to the task, and paid more for meeting the target. His account reported a large increase in output. 47 tons The daily pig-iron target in Taylor's account, up from an average of 12.5 tons. The result depended on worker selection, prescribed rest, and higher pay. Taylor, The Principles of Scientific Management , 1911 That approach fits work whose steps can be observed and repeated. It also gives the manager a particular role: work out the method, then make sure people follow it. The trouble starts when you carry that role into a job where finding the method is part of the work. The manager's move Before prescribing a method, ask whether the task has a known answer or needs someone to work one out. 02

sections.head: The worker who owns the factory
sections.text: Expertise changes what a manager needs to provide. An experienced engineer may understand a technical problem better than their manager. The manager still needs to set expectations and judge the result, but prescribing each step can waste the expertise they hired. Drucker described the difference this way: Knowledge workers own the means of production. It is the knowledge between their ears, and it is a totally portable and enormous capital asset. Peter Drucker Give people the outcome, the constraints, and the information they need to make decisions. Keep fixed procedures where consistency matters, such as lockout rules, hazardous-material handling, and critical handoffs. People can follow those rules and still have room to diagnose a problem or improve a process. The manager's move For each assignment, make clear which boundaries are fixed and which decisions belong to the person doing it. 03

sections.head: What you expect from people
sections.text: Your assumptions shape the work you give them. Douglas McGregor described two views of workers in The Human Side of Enterprise . Theory X assumes people avoid work and need close control. Theory Y assumes people can direct their own effort toward goals they accept. These assumptions affect how you manage. If you make every decision and give someone only routine tasks, you leave them little opportunity to show initiative. Their dependence on you may be a result of the arrangement. The manager's move When someone seems passive, check what they are actually allowed to decide. Act II The thing you cannot command 04

sections.head: The gap
sections.text: Meeting the requirements leaves plenty of judgment unaccounted for. An engineer can complete the assigned fix or also investigate why the problem keeps returning. A customer success manager can answer the ticket or notice that several customers are struggling with the same setup. That extra attention is discretionary effort. What you can require, and what you cannot What authority can compel the floor What a professional could give the ceiling discretionary effort The bars illustrate a distinction, not measured amounts. Job requirements cover part of the work; people choose how much additional attention and initiative to give. 70 % of the variation in engagement scores across business units is attributed to managers in Gallup's estimate. This describes differences among teams, not a manager's share of one person's motivation. Gallup, State of the American Manager A committed team can still work on the wrong priorities or deliver poor results. Engagement helps people do the work; the manager also has to choose the work, set a quality standard, and address misses. The manager's move Ask what makes it hard to do good work on your team. Start with the obstacles you can change. 05

sections.head: Pay and the work itself
sections.text: Fixing a bad working condition may leave the job just as dull. Frederick Herzberg's account of motivation separates the things people complained about from the things they found satisfying. Pay, policies, and working conditions appeared in one group. Achievement, responsibility, and growth appeared in the other. Herzberg's two groups Hygiene factors Salary and benefits Company policy Working conditions Job security A reasonable boss Motivators Achievement The work itself Responsibility Recognition Growth and advancement Herzberg called the first group hygiene factors and the second motivators. This is a useful distinction to consider when improving a job, not a rule that pay can never motivate. In an AT&T example Herzberg described, shareholder-correspondence clerks gained authority to sign their own letters and handle more of each inquiry. Pay stayed the same. The reported service index rose from the 20s to the 90s . The change gave them more responsibility for a complete piece of work. I can charge a man's battery, and recharge it, and recharge it again. But it is only when he has his own generator that we can talk about motivation. Frederick Herzberg The manager's move Check whether people have a problem they can own from start to finish. Keep fair pay and decent conditions part of the job. 06

sections.head: Autonomy, mastery, purpose
sections.text: A reward can change how someone approaches a problem. In Sam Glucksberg's 1962 experiment , a cash incentive slowed people solving a puzzle that required them to rethink an object's use. When the setup made the solution more obvious, the incentive helped. A later review of 128 studies found that some expected, tangible rewards reduced intrinsic motivation, the desire to do an activity for its own sake. Daniel Pink organized his account around autonomy, control over how you work; mastery, getting better at the work; and purpose, understanding why it matters. These are useful questions about a job. The research doesn't establish that every bonus harms creative work. Does a cash bonus help? An illustration of the two puzzle conditions in Glucksberg's experiment. illustrated performance Routine work the solution is easier to see no bonus yet Creative work the solution needs a new use for an object no bonus yet Offer a cash bonus on both Toggle the bonus to compare the two conditions. The bar lengths are illustrative. Illustration based on Sam Glucksberg's 1962 reward experiment . The manager's move Before adding an incentive, ask what behavior it will reward. A target for speed can discourage the investigation you need. 07

sections.head: Small wins
sections.text: People notice whether their effort leads anywhere. Teresa Amabile and Steven Kramer examined nearly 12,000 workday diary entries . Progress on meaningful work was closely associated with better days. A small step forward could matter; blocked progress and setbacks could spoil the day. An experiment by Dan Ariely, Emir Kamenica, and Dražen Prelec tested something more basic: whether anyone acknowledged the work. 15¢ vs 27.5¢ Average pay at which participants stopped doing a repetitive task. Those whose pages were acknowledged continued to 15¢; those whose pages were ignored stopped at 27.5¢. The group whose work was shredded stopped at 29¢. Ariely, Kamenica & Prelec, 2008 The manager's move Use a one-on-one to ask what is stuck and look at what was finished. Acknowledgment is more useful when you have actually read the work. Act III The craft 08

sections.head: Match the support to the task
sections.text: An expert can be a beginner on a new assignment. Andy Grove called this task-relevant maturity : how much experience and confidence someone has with the particular work in front of them. A senior engineer may need little direction on a design and close support when managing people for the first time. Four ways to support the work new Direct Eager, unskilled. Give clear, specific instruction. learning Coach Skill rising, confidence dipping. Explain, support, encourage. capable Support Able but cautious. Ask questions and help them decide. owner Delegate Skilled and committed. Set the goal, then trust and clear the path. Too much direction limits an experienced person. Too little can leave a beginner stuck. Treat these stages as a guide to the conversation. The four styles come from Hersey and Blanchard's Situational Leadership model. Grove's related idea appears in High Output Management . The one-on-one gives you a place to find out what support is needed. Let the person bring their agenda. Ask about decisions, obstacles, and work you would otherwise miss. Grove made the case for the time this takes: Ninety minutes of your time can enhance the quality of your subordinate's work for two weeks, or for some eighty-plus hours. Andy Grove, High Output Management The manager's move Agree on check-ins when you assign new work. Adjust them as the person gains experience. 09

sections.head: Ask before giving advice
sections.text: Find out how the person understands the problem. In Google's original Project Oxygen findings, coaching ranked first among the behaviors of its best managers; technical expertise ranked last. Google reported that median manager-favorability scores rose from 83% to 88% between 2010 and 2012 as it put the findings to use. Michael Bungay Stanier calls the urge to supply an answer the "advice monster." His questions, "What's on your mind?" and "And what else?", give the other person time to explain. Ask what they have tried and where they want help. Offer an answer when it is useful, especially when they lack information you have. Coaching is no longer a specialty. You cannot be a good manager without being a good coach. The leadership handbook of Bill Campbell The manager's move Before solving the problem, ask what the person thinks the next step should be. 10

sections.head: Care personally, challenge directly
sections.text: Useful feedback names something the person can change. Kim Scott's Radical Candor puts care for the person alongside direct feedback about their work. Her term ruinous empathy describes a familiar failure: avoiding a clear message because it might hurt. The person then keeps making a mistake you could have helped them correct. Scott's feedback model Ruinous empathy Care without direct feedback. The problem goes unaddressed. Radical candor Care for the person and give clear feedback. Manipulative insincerity Little care and little honest feedback. Obnoxious aggression Direct criticism without care for the person. ← doesn't challenge challenges directly → Make praise specific too. Tell someone what they did and why it helped. Buckingham and Goodall's case for noticing strengths is useful here. It doesn't remove the need to correct errors or enforce standards. The manager's move Describe the behavior, its effect, and what needs to change. Give the person a chance to explain what happened. 11

sections.head: Leave room for other people to think
sections.text: Helping can become taking over. Liz Wiseman calls leaders Multipliers when they make use of other people's capabilities, and Diminishers when their own interventions limit them. A manager can do the latter while trying to help: answer every question, rescue every project, or propose more ideas than the team can pursue. 2× The difference in capability people said their leaders used in Wiseman's study. This was participants' assessment of their capacity, not a measured doubling of team output. Wiseman, Multipliers It isn't how much you know that matters. What matters is how much access you have to what other people know. Liz Wiseman The manager's move In your next meeting, ask for other people's assessment before giving yours. Notice whether you leave them a decision to make. Act IV The conditions you build 12

sections.head: Make it safe to report a problem
sections.text: Reported errors depend on whether people feel able to report them. In her hospital research, Amy Edmondson found that teams judged to work well together sometimes reported more medication errors. Better reporting could explain the apparent contradiction: people felt able to admit mistakes. A low reported error rate can also mean problems stay hidden. Psychological safety is the shared belief that speaking up won't bring punishment or humiliation. Google's team study also identified it as an important factor. It matters when someone has to question a plan, flag a risk, or ask for help. 85 % of respondents in one exploratory study said they had stayed silent about a work concern at least once. Fear of being labeled negatively was the most common reason. Milliken, Morrison & Hewlin, 2003 The manager's move When someone brings bad news, start by understanding it. Admit your own mistakes and make sure reported problems lead to action. 13

sections.head: Give people the context to decide
sections.text: Delegation needs a named owner and enough information. Netflix's culture memo calls this context, not control . Explain the strategy, the constraints, and the risks so the person closest to the work can make an informed decision. Then say who owns the decision and when it needs to be escalated. Removing an approval step helps only if the person has authority to act. Keep review where the risk requires it, and explain why it is there. If you dummy-proof the system, only dummies will want to work there. Reed Hastings, Netflix The manager's move Choose a recurring decision you currently approve. Decide what information and authority would let someone else own it. 14

sections.head: Specific goals
sections.text: Agree on what a good result looks like. In Gary Latham and James Baldes's logging study , trucks were loaded to about 60% of the legal weight limit. The company replaced "do your best" with a goal of 94%, agreed with drivers and their union. Loads rose to around 90%. The company estimated savings of $250,000 in trucks it no longer needed to buy. Locke and Latham's review of goal-setting research describes why specific, challenging goals often help: they direct attention and make progress easier to assess. People also need the skills, feedback, and commitment to pursue them. 46 % of U.S. employees strongly agreed they knew what was expected of them at work in Gallup's August 2024 measure, down from 56 percent in January 2020. Gallup, 2024 Choose the measure carefully. A speed target can sacrifice quality. For unfamiliar work, a learning goal may be more useful: test the plausible approaches and explain which one should proceed. Agree on what must be learned before setting an output quota. The manager's move Ask each person what result they are working toward and when it is due. Resolve any disagreement about what counts as success. 15

sections.head: Company examples
sections.text: These practices exist outside research studies. Four approaches in practice SAS Institute SAS describes an employee model with a 35-hour week and benefits including on-site healthcare and childcare. On that page, SAS reports historical turnover of about 4% , against an industry average of 15% . Semco The Brazilian manufacturer gave workers control over hours and, in some roles, salaries, supported by access to company financial information. A Harvard Business School case records the workforce growing from 90 to 2,500 and annual revenue from $4M to $160M by 2001. 3M 3M describes its practice of allowing employees 15% of their time for independent projects. An adhesive with a weak bond became useful on removable notes. That became the Post-it Note , one of the products 3M traces to its culture of employee experimentation. Microsoft Satya Nadella promoted a culture of "learn-it-alls," encouraging people to question what they knew and learn from one another. Over the following decade, Microsoft became a much larger cloud business. Its 2014 filing and later results show the turnaround, though they cannot isolate culture as the cause. The figures are historical accounts and company reports. They do not establish that the management practices caused the results. Company histories cannot isolate the effects of culture from products, markets, or other decisions. They do show different ways to give employees authority. Before copying one, identify the decision you would actually let someone make. The manager's move Choose a practice that changes the work itself. A new title or office layout does little on its own. Act V The hard part 16

sections.head: When someone is falling short
sections.text: Address the problem while there is still time to improve. A missed standard needs a conversation. Describe the gap and ask what is causing it. The answer might be skill, workload, unclear expectations, or a poor fit for the role. You need to know which before choosing a remedy. Working conditions can change performance substantially. Toyota rehired about 85% of the former workforce when it reopened GM's troubled Fremont plant as NUMMI. The same people worked differently in a different system. Check the system you have given someone before concluding they cannot do the job. Three questions before deciding the seat Wrong role? Would a different role make better use of their skills? the mirror Did I cause this? Were the expectations clear? Did they have the support and resources to meet them? the call Wrong person? If the mismatch remains after a fair effort, decide what happens next. Use the answers to choose between support, a change of role, and ending the arrangement. Set a review date when you choose an improvement plan. If improvement is possible, agree on the required change, the support you will provide, and a date to review it. If the role is a poor fit, address that directly. Waiting without a plan leaves the person uncertain and the team carrying unfinished work. Judge the effect on the team as well as individual output. Housman and Minor's study of toxic workers found substantial costs from serious misconduct, even among productive employees. A sales total or delivery count can miss the damage someone does to colleagues. >2× Estimated savings from avoiding a toxic worker compared with hiring a top-1% performer in Housman and Minor's study: $12,489 in avoided turnover costs versus $5,303 from additional output. The comparison applies to their data and cost assumptions. Housman & Minor, Toxic Workers , 2015 This calls for a decision about the person and the job. A forced ranking that requires dismissing a fixed share of the team cannot tell you whether any particular person has failed a reasonable standard. The manager's move For the performance issue you keep postponing, write down the gap, the next action, and the review date. Then have the conversation. Act VI The job changes again 17

sections.head: Managing through other managers
sections.text: Several teams need decisions that one team cannot make alone. A director cannot inspect every decision or coach every person. Doing so creates a queue and leaves the team's managers unsure of their authority. The job includes choosing priorities across teams and helping their managers lead. Three responsibilities at this level direction Choose what matters Choose outcomes and make the tradeoffs between teams clear. system Make work visible Agree on ownership, measures, and regular reviews of progress and risk. leaders Build the bench Coach managers and prepare people who can take on critical roles. Watch whether the managers you lead can make good decisions without waiting for you. This transition is the manager-of-managers passage in The Leadership Pipeline . It extends Andy Grove's definition of managerial output in High Output Management . Agree with each manager on the outcomes, resources, and decisions they own. Review how their team is doing and how they are developing people. Use skip-level conversations to understand the work; avoid giving instructions that create a second chain of command. A broad goal such as "improve retention" needs choices. Which customers need attention? What work will stop? Where will quality take precedence over speed? Put people and budget behind those choices. Warn executives about risks early and explain changes to the teams affected. Cross-team disagreements need a shared outcome and someone responsible for resolving the decision. Bring the evidence and explain the tradeoff. Escalate when the people involved cannot resolve it, with the disagreement clear enough for someone else to decide. Check who can cover critical roles. If one person's week away stops decisions, give someone else practice making those decisions while there is still help available. The director's move Review the decisions waiting for you. Delegate the ones a team can own and spend time on the choices that require several teams. Act VII · The Playbook

sections.head: For Your Improvement
sections.text: A manager needs practice too. It helps to name the skill you're working on and find a way to use it in your current job. FYI: For Your Improvement is a reference book built for that process. The wheel and reader below let you explore its competency framework and plan an assignment. FYI: For Your Improvement comes from the work of Michael Lombardo and Robert Eichinger and is published by Korn Ferry. It is organized for reference: each chapter covers a competency, describes what different levels of skill look like, and suggests ways to practice. Start with feedback about your work, find the relevant chapter, and choose an assignment. You can return to the same chapter as the job changes, or use it to help someone else plan their development. The book describes leadership in terms of competencies , skills expressed through observable behavior. That gives you something specific to work on. "Become a better manager" is hard to practice. "Give clear feedback when a commitment is missed" is an action you can try, review, and improve. People differ in how easily they learn a skill, and some jobs fit them better than others. The framework helps identify which behavior needs attention and what practice might be useful. The Map The competency framework, on one wheel The book uses the Korn Ferry Leadership Architect framework: 38 competencies grouped into 12 clusters and 4 factors . The inner ring shows factors, the middle ring clusters, and the outer ring competencies. Hover or tap a segment to see its description and where it belongs. The chapter reader below has its own navigation, so you can browse the framework here and read a chapter independently. Much of the advice in this essay falls under People and Self . People has the widest wedge because it contains the most competencies. Each competency has four descriptions: less skilled , skilled , talented , and overused . The overused description is especially useful when something you normally do well is causing trouble. Careful planning, for example, can delay action if you keep revising the plan. A related skill can help you balance that tendency; the book calls it a compensator . If a skill is difficult to develop directly, another competency may partly substitute for it. These connections give you more than one way to address a problem, and they are included in the reader. A chapter also asks why someone might struggle with the skill. Open "How to build it" to see possible causes, practice tips, an assignment, and related competencies. Use the causes as questions to investigate, rather than assuming every item describes you. The Chapter Choose a chapter Pick a factor or cluster to see what it covers and browse its entries. Choose a competency for the complete chapter here: four skill descriptions, possible causes of difficulty, tips, an assignment to try in your job, and the related skills that may substitute or compensate for it. The level buttons show one description at a time. The previous and next buttons take you through all 38 competencies; the navigation rows let you choose directly. Hover over a related-skill button, or focus it with the keyboard, to preview its tips without leaving the chapter. Click it when you want to read that skill. The assignments connect the book to a broader approach to development: learning through work, with feedback and formal study to help. The Center for Creative Leadership describes this in its 70-20-10 framework , drawn from research in which executives looked back on the experiences that helped them learn. It groups those experiences into…

sections.head: Quick reference
sections.text: A prompt for each section. Follow a link to return to the discussion. The stopwatch Check whether the task has a known method. The portable factory Agree on boundaries and decision ownership. Theory X, Theory Y Check whether people have room to show initiative. The gap Ask what prevents good work. Pay and the work Fix conditions; give people complete problems to own. Autonomy, mastery, purpose Check what behavior the incentive rewards. Small wins Remove an obstacle and read the finished work. Support for the task Match check-ins to experience with this assignment. Coaching Ask how they would approach the problem. Feedback Describe the behavior and the change needed. Multipliers Hear other assessments before giving yours. Psychological safety Respond usefully when someone reports a problem. Context and decisions Give the owner information and authority. Goals Agree on the result, measure, and date. Company examples Identify the decision a practice would delegate. Performance problems Name the gap, next action, and review date. Managing managers Resolve the choices that require several teams. Use the competency reader to plan practice in your current role.

sections.head: The evidence has limits.
sections.text: These sources include controlled experiments, workplace studies, company histories, and advice from practitioners. They answer different questions. No one study establishes a complete way to manage a team, and a useful practice still has to work for the people and the job in front of you.

sections.head: The Optional Body
sections.text: How much of yourself can you lose, and go on living? Scroll to find out, and watch the weight. scroll to descend 100.00% 154.0 lb Now, the least a person can be. No legs, no hips, the pelvis cut away and the skin drawn shut beneath. No shoulders, no arms. The face cleared off, no eyes, no ears, no nose, no tongue. A head and half a trunk. Inside it: a heart that is a pump, lungs worked by a machine, kidneys swapped for a filter, a pancreas down to a drip. Four of the organs are machines now. Only two are still the body's own, the only two no machine can replace, the liver and the brain. And yet, the person remains as conscious and aware as you or I.

sections.head: Then a line is drawn. The saying goes: nobody is home. But if nobody is home, where are we?
sections.text: Whatever we are has no weight. Schrödinger thought consciousness was single, that we are all one mind . If we have no body or remembered experience to set us apart, why not? Every engraving is public domain, from Wikimedia Commons : the whole figure is Andreas Vesalius, De Humani Corporis Fabrica (1543); most organs are Henry Vandyke Carter's plates for Gray's Anatomy (1918), with a few from Johannes Sobotta's Atlas of Human Anatomy (1906). Part weights are approximate, from standard anatomical references; the running percentage is computed from them. © 2026 Ethan Willingham

posts.title: The Old Masters
posts.desc: Fourteen paintings, with short notes on the artists and a closer look at each image.
posts.keywords: art painting museum masters classic gallery oil landscape

sections.text: Plate I · 1597

sections.head: The Musicians
sections.text: Michelangelo Merisi da Caravaggio Click to zoom Medium Oil on canvas Size 92.1 × 118.4 cm (about 36 × 47 in.) Held at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York . Rogers Fund, 1952. Caravaggio killed a man in a fight in Rome in 1606 and fled the city. He spent the rest of his life painting in Naples, Malta, and Sicily while seeking a papal pardon. He died in 1610 before he could return to Rome. Plate II · probably after 1827

sections.head: Landscape with a Plowed Field and a Village
sections.text: Georges Michel Click to zoom Medium Oil on paper, mounted on canvas Size 51.1 × 70.2 cm (about 20 × 28 in.) Held at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York Michel worked as a restorer at the Louvre, where he studied Dutch landscapes by Ruisdael, Van Goyen, and Rembrandt. This village is invented. He painted on paper mounted on canvas, a cheaper way to get the smooth surface of the wood panels those painters used. Plate III · 1871

sections.head: Breton Brother and Sister
sections.text: William-Adolphe Bouguereau Click to zoom Medium Oil on canvas Size 129.2 × 89.2 cm (about 51 × 35 in.) Held at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York . Catharine Lorillard Wolfe Bequest, 1887. Bouguereau based this painting on sketches he made in Brittany in the late 1860s, then completed it in his studio. The children are posed in traditional Breton clothing. American collectors bought many of these rural scenes; this one came to the Met through Catharine Lorillard Wolfe's bequest. Plate IV · 1899

sections.head: Girl Holding Lemons
sections.text: William-Adolphe Bouguereau Click to zoom Medium Oil on canvas Size 65.9 × 49.8 cm (about 26 × 20 in.) Held at The Israel Museum, Jerusalem . Gift in memory of Goldie Weisbord. In the year he painted this, Bouguereau took his son Paul to Menton on the French Riviera. Paul had tuberculosis, and his doctors recommended sea air. During the stay, Bouguereau found a room in their hotel where he could paint . Plate V · 1888

sections.head: By the Stream ( Au Bord du Ruisseau )
sections.text: William-Adolphe Bouguereau Click to zoom Medium Oil on canvas Painted 1888 Provenance Bought from the artist by Joseph Barrigan of Providence on May 30, 1888. M.S. Rau catalog . The girl's red stockings lie beside her on the bank. Bouguereau painted the skin, cloth, and plants with almost no visible brushwork. His reputation declined after his death , as tastes shifted toward modern painting. Exhibitions in the late twentieth century brought renewed interest in his work. Plate VI · 1865

sections.head: The Veteran in a New Field
sections.text: Winslow Homer Click to zoom Medium Oil on canvas Size 61.3 × 96.8 cm (about 24 × 38 in.) Held at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York . Adelaide Milton de Groot Bequest, 1967. Painted Summer 1865, after Lee's surrender at Appomattox and Lincoln's assassination. Homer first painted a scythe with a wooden cradle, a set of spokes that caught the cut wheat. He painted the spokes out , though they now show through the aging paint. The simpler blade resembles the Grim Reaper's scythe. The man's Union Army jacket and canteen lie in the lower right corner. Plate VII · 1772

sections.head: The Shipwreck
sections.text: Claude-Joseph Vernet Click to zoom Medium Oil on canvas Size 113.5 × 162.9 cm (about 45 × 64 in.) Held at National Gallery of Art, Washington, D.C. Acquired in 2000. Commissioned November 1771, by Henry, 8th Lord Arundell of Wardour. Lord Arundell commissioned this with a companion painting, Moonlight , for his house in Wiltshire. The pair put a shipwreck beside a calm harbor. They stayed in the family until 1952 and were separated after that sale. Plate VIII · 1820

sections.head: Salisbury Cathedral from Lower Marsh Close
sections.text: John Constable Click to zoom Medium Oil on canvas Held at National Gallery of Art, Washington, D.C. Andrew W. Mellon Collection, 1937. Provenance Unsold in Constable's lifetime. Sold at his studio auction in 1838. In 1821 and 1822, Constable painted cloud studies on Hampstead Heath, often recording the date, time, wind direction, and weather on the back. These were small oil paintings made outdoors. This view of Salisbury dates from just before that period. Plate IX · 1839

sections.head: The Rape of Proserpine
sections.text: Joseph Mallord William Turner Click to zoom Medium Oil on canvas Size 92 × 122.2 cm (about 36 × 48 in.) Held at National Gallery of Art, Washington, D.C. Gift of Mrs. Watson B. Dickerman, 1951. First shown Royal Academy of Arts, London, 1839. Turner showed this at the Royal Academy in 1839, with a passage from Ovid's Metamorphoses in the exhibition catalog. The subject is Pluto's abduction of Proserpine. The figures are small enough that you can take in the whole landscape before noticing what's happening at the lower left. Plate X · 1834

sections.head: Venice: The Dogana and San Giorgio Maggiore
sections.text: Joseph Mallord William Turner Click to zoom Medium Oil on canvas Size 91.5 × 122 cm (about 36 × 48 in.) Held at National Gallery of Art, Washington, D.C. Widener Collection. First shown Royal Academy Summer Exhibition, 1834. Commissioned by Henry McConnel, a Manchester cotton manufacturer. Henry McConnel commissioned this view of Venice, then ordered Keelmen Heaving in Coals by Moonlight to hang beside it. The second painting shows men loading coal at night in Newcastle. He sold both to John Naylor in 1849. When he tried to buy one back in 1861, Naylor refused. Plate XI · c. 1804

sections.head: Boats Carrying Out Anchors and Cables to the Dutch Men of War
sections.text: Joseph Mallord William Turner Click to zoom Medium Oil on canvas Size 101.6 × 130.8 cm (about 40 × 51 in.) Held at National Gallery of Art, Washington, D.C. Corcoran Collection (William A. Clark). Seven men work the small boat in the foreground, with warships farther out. Four are rowing. The boat sits low between the waves, and another follows behind it. Turner gives most of the canvas to the sea and sky. Plate XII · 1754

sections.head: Intérieur du Port de Marseille
sections.text: Claude-Joseph Vernet , from the Ports of France series. Click to zoom Medium Oil on canvas Size 165 × 263 cm (about 5 ft 5 in. × 8 ft 8 in.) Held at Musée national de la Marine, Paris , on deposit from the Louvre. Commissioned by King Louis XV of France in 1753, for the Ports of France series. Vernet included himself, his wife Virginie, and their son Livio among the people on the quay. Louis XV's commission required him to show the work of each port in detail. Here that means cargo in jars and bales, grain piled on the quay, and ships from around the Mediterranean. Plate XIII · 1850

sections.head: The Ninth Wave
sections.text: Ivan Aivazovsky (Hovhannes Aivazian). Click to zoom Medium Oil on canvas Size 221 × 332 cm (about 7 ft 3 in. × 10 ft 11 in.) Held at The State Russian Museum, St. Petersburg . Transferred from the Hermitage in 1897. The title comes from a sailors' belief that the ninth wave is the largest and most dangerous. The survivors cling to a broken mast as daylight reaches the water. Aivazovsky painted his seascapes from memory in his studio ; he said a breaking wave moved too quickly to paint from life. Plate XIV · c. 1852

sections.head: The Hamlet of Optevoz
sections.text: Charles-François Daubigny Click to zoom Medium Oil on canvas Held at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York . Robert Graham Dun Bequest, 1900. Setting Optevoz, a village in southeastern France. Daubigny based this painting on drawings he made at Optevoz in 1852. He'd first visited the village in 1849. One of the preparatory sketches is also at the Met; a later painting in Philadelphia shows the same view from farther back, in different light.

sections.head: Ways to set up the swarm
sections.text: With 15 colors, the force grid and six flow patterns give you about this many different setups: 4, 510, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000, 000 How this is counted Mirrored cells change together, leaving 15 × 16 ÷ 2 = 120 independent values. Five choices for each value and six patterns give 6 × 5 120 , rounded above to three significant digits. This counts settings with the palette and physics held fixed. Randomized force values and starting positions add more. In Particle Life , each particle reacts to nearby colors. The force matrix sets which colors attract or repel; a short-range repulsion also pushes them apart. Different settings produce clusters, chains, or scattered particles. A starling murmuration near Gretna. Photo by Walter Baxter , CC BY-SA 2.0 . Flow field

sections.head: Steering the particles
sections.text: The "ghost" is an extra force I added to the simulation. Its direction depends on position in the frame. It nudges passing particles along paths that form spirals and rings. Turn the field off to see the color-based interactions alone. Choose a pattern from the menu to hold it, or check Cycle automatically to let the shapes blend into one another. Density layers applies a second pattern to tightly packed particles. Drag a finger or mouse through the swarm to push particles aside. A quick swipe sends them flying. Hold Shift while dragging with a mouse to stir them instead. Unlock raises the desktop limit from 40,000 to 100,000. On phones, it raises the limit from 8,000 to 40,000. This builds on Ventrella's Clusters , Tom Mohr's Particle Life , and lisyarus's WebGPU implementation . The simulation and added flow field are in particle-life.js .
