The leg moves farther; the drawing does not measure muscle length or stiffness. Range, tolerance and muscle structure need separate measurements.

sections.head: Injury prevention needs its own evidence
sections.text: Lauersen's review of 25 trials and 26,610 participants found no clear injury reduction from stretching programs. Strength-based prevention programs performed better. These were different sets of trials, not one head-to-head contest between stretching and lifting. Lauersen 2014 good Sports-injury prevention programs Stretching 0.96 risk ratio, 95% interval 0.85 to 1.10 Strength training 0.32 risk ratio, 95% interval 0.21 to 0.48 Each estimate compares its program with control. A ratio of 1 means no difference. The strength estimate concerns specific prevention programs, not a promise that any gym routine cuts injuries by two thirds. Lauersen 2014

sections.head: Soreness and the warm-up
sections.text: A Cochrane review found no clinically important reduction in delayed muscle soreness from stretching before or after exercise. Stretch if you want more range or like how it feels; soreness prevention is a poor reason to add it. Herbert 2011 good Long static holds immediately before a maximal effort can temporarily reduce performance. The effect is smaller with brief holds, especially when followed by an active warm-up. For lifting, prepare with lighter practice sets and do prolonged flexibility work afterward or separately. Behm 2016 good Foam rolling can give a small, short-term increase in range and may reduce perceived soreness. The mechanism remains uncertain. Evidence for these effects does not establish the popular claim that a roller breaks up adhesions or permanently releases fascia. Wiewelhove 2019 mixed

sections.head: Flexibility and survival
sections.text: The sitting-rising test and the Flexindex study both associated better test scores with lower mortality. These were cohort studies, not stretching interventions. Getting up from the floor involves balance and strength as well as range; flexibility scores can also reflect existing health. Statistical adjustment does not show that increasing flexibility through stretching extends life. Brito 2014 Araujo 2024 mixed Using the range

sections.head: Strength work can help too
sections.text: Strength training can improve range of motion. Afonso's review of 11 trials, involving 452 people, found no clear difference between strength training and stretching in their range gains. The programs and participants varied considerably, so it does not establish that any lift replaces every stretch. Afonso 2021 good A controlled squat lets you practice the hip and ankle range used in that squat. It does not automatically give you the shoulder range for overhead work. Use a load and range you can control comfortably. Mike Powell in flight. A long jump calls for strength and coordination through a large range of motion; a flexibility test measures only part of that. Mike Powell at full extension in the long jump, 1986. Photo by Lori Shepler / Los Angeles Times, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

sections.head: Stretch a restriction you can name
sections.text: If an ankle restriction keeps your heel from staying down in a squat, targeted stretching is a reasonable experiment. Recheck the squat after working on ankle range. Avoid forcing a joint through pain. The ACSM flexibility recommendation is about 60 seconds total per exercise on at least two days a week. You can divide that time across shorter holds. Treat it as a starting dose, rather than a requirement to hold every position for a full minute. Garber 2011

sections.head: Prevention programs do more than stretch
sections.text: The FIFA 11+ combines running, strength, balance and jumping exercises. In Soligard's trial in teenage female soccer players, it reduced injuries overall, though the primary lower-extremity injury result was uncertain. That supports the program in its tested setting; it does not give a few leg swings the same effect. Soligard 2008 good Nordic hamstring curls have a promising but contested prevention record. A 2019 review estimated roughly half as many hamstring injuries in programs including them. A later reanalysis restricted to randomized trials found the evidence inconclusive. They can be part of hamstring training, without treating the headline reduction as guaranteed. van Dyk 2019 Impellizzeri 2021 mixed You can also do yoga because you enjoy it. For chronic non-specific low back pain, a Cochrane review found small average improvements compared with no exercise, generally below its threshold for clinical importance. Stretching alone and a whole yoga program are different interventions. Wieland 2022 mixed The plan

sections.head: A week you can count
sections.text: This example fits around three lifting days and totals 150 moderate-equivalent minutes. Adapt it to your current fitness. Day Lifting Aerobic work Count Mon Full body Brisk walk, 15 min 15 Tue Off Moderate cycling, 30 min 30 Wed Full body Brisk walk, 15 min 15 Thu Off Vigorous exercise, 15 min total, or moderate work, 30 min 30 Fri Full body Brisk walk, 15 min 15 Sat Off Moderate walk or ride, 45 min 45 Sun Rest Optional easy movement 0 counted Moderate-equivalent minutes 150 Warm up before lifting with easier movement and practice sets. Add flexibility work where it serves a specific need. Thursday's vigorous minutes can be broken into intervals; easy recovery minutes count only if they reach moderate intensity. If you use the 4x4 instead, its four work bouts give 16 vigorous minutes, with warm-up and recovery time added separately. You do not have to begin with this whole week. An inactive person can start with short comfortable walks and increase duration or frequency gradually. Hard intervals are optional. Walking steps and walking minutes describe the same activity in different ways, so do not add them twice when counting your week. U.S. guidelines The limit of this guide. This is general information from an enthusiast, not a personal medical prescription. New chest pain, fainting or unusual breathlessness needs medical attention. An existing condition or medication may change appropriate intensity. The heart-rate calculator cannot measure your actual maximum or training thresholds. The evidence

sections.head: Sources and their limits
sections.text: Cohorts can show who tends to live longer. Trials can test whether training changes fitness or range. The evidence labels apply to the stated claim, not to every possible interpretation of the paper. posts.title: What You're Supposed to Eat
posts.desc: In a controlled feeding trial, people ate more from the ultra-processed menu. Compare that result with diet trials, protein and fiber targets, and the evidence for supplements.

sections.text: Adriaen van Utrecht, Banquet Still Life , 1644, Rijksmuseum. Public domain. Eight parts Start here Two questions The diet wars Ultra-processed What to add Supplements Why it fails The plan Start here

sections.head: The short version
sections.text: In a trial of 160 adults, Atkins, the Zone, Weight Watchers, and Ornish produced similar average weight loss after a year. The results ranged from about 5 to 7 pounds, with no statistically significant difference between diets. Adherence was much more closely associated with weight loss than the assigned diet. Dansinger 2005 good This is the food companion to Big Enough , on muscle, and Still Moving , on movement. The comparisons below show what different menus changed in actual studies. The calculator gives rough planning estimates. The whole thing, on one card Six decisions that account for much of the practical advice below. 1 · Weight is energy For weight loss, sustain a calorie deficit. Choose a pattern you can keep. 2 · Protein About 0.7 g per pound is a useful target for someone lifting regularly. 3 · Fiber 25 to 38 g a day for ages 19 to 50, with lower targets for older adults. 4 · Food quality Build meals from varied foods. Frozen vegetables and canned beans count. 5 · Sugary drinks Replace some soda and sweetened coffee with water or unsweetened drinks. 6 · Supplements Name the need before buying. Benefits differ by product and person. The protein figure comes from resistance-training studies. The fiber figures are age-based adequate-intake targets. Both are explained below. The map

sections.head: Weight and health
sections.text: Losing weight and reducing disease risk are related goals. A calorie deficit can lower weight; changing the foods within that calorie budget can also affect cholesterol, blood pressure, and appetite.

sections.head: Energy balance
sections.text: Over time, taking in less usable energy than you expend reduces the body's energy stores. But neither side of that equation stays fixed: hunger, movement, metabolism, and body size all change. Short-term scale changes also include water and the food in your gut. Energy balance is an accounting rule, not an explanation of why weight loss is easy or hard. Hall 2012 good Protein takes more energy to process than fat or carbohydrate. A commonly cited estimate is 20 to 30 percent of protein's calories, compared with 0 to 3 percent for fat. Westerterp 2004 good Protein and resistance training can also help preserve lean tissue during weight loss. In one four-week trial of 40 young men on a large calorie deficit and an intensive exercise program, the higher-protein group gained more lean mass and lost more fat. The result came from high protein together with a demanding training program. Longland 2016 good

sections.head: What counting can miss
sections.text: Food records can miss a great deal. In a 1992 study, ten people with obesity who reported difficulty losing weight underreported their calorie intake by an average of 47 percent and overreported physical activity by 51 percent. Those figures describe a small, selected group, not the average person. Lichtman 1992 mixed A record of food intake is a measurement with error. Exercise contributes to weight loss, though the result is often smaller than a simple calories-burned calculation predicts. The Hadza study found similar daily expenditure to Western comparison groups after accounting for body size; it did not show that adding exercise to an individual's life burns nothing. Pontzer 2012 mixed A review of randomized aerobic-exercise trials found reductions in weight and body fat as weekly exercise increased. Jayedi 2024 strong

sections.head: Health beyond the scale
sections.text: PREDIMED tested heart health rather than weight loss. It assigned 7,447 older adults at high cardiovascular risk to a Mediterranean diet supplemented with olive oil or nuts, or advice to reduce dietary fat. The rate of major cardiovascular events was about 30 percent lower in the Mediterranean groups over nearly five years. The original report was retracted after randomization problems were found; the revised analysis still supported the benefit. Estruch 2018 good The result concerns a whole eating pattern in older people at high cardiovascular risk. Comparisons

sections.head: Why diet comparisons often end close
sections.text: Low-carb and low-fat diets can both produce weight loss. Large comparisons usually find modest differences in their average results. Stanford's DIETFITS trial assigned 609 adults without diabetes to healthy low-fat or healthy low-carb diets for twelve months. Average losses were about 12 and 13 pounds, respectively, without a statistically significant difference. The particular genotype pattern and insulin measurement the researchers tested did not identify which diet would work better. Gardner 2018 good Four diets after a year Average loss in one trial with 40 people assigned to each diet. The differences were not statistically significant; the bars are group averages, not predictions for an individual. A review of 48 trials involving 7,286 participants found small differences between named diets. Its roughly 16-pound estimates for low-carb and low-fat at a year were differences from a no-diet comparison, not the average loss in this four-diet trial. Johnston 2014 strong POUNDS LOST assigned 811 people to four calorie-reduced diets with different proportions of fat, protein, and carbohydrate. After two years, average weight losses were similar. Attendance at counseling sessions was strongly associated with the result. Sacks 2009 good Hall compared equal-calorie cuts to fat or carbohydrate under controlled feeding for six days. In that experiment, cutting fat produced more measured body-fat loss than cutting carbohydrate, despite the larger insulin reduction with carbohydrate restriction. Hall 2015 good Six days cannot settle which diet someone will maintain for years. It does test the claim that lowering insulin necessarily produces more fat loss. Restricting eating hours is another way to reduce intake. In a twelve-month trial, adding an eight-hour eating window to calorie restriction did not significantly improve weight loss compared with calorie restriction alone. Liu 2022 good A 2025 review found broadly similar results across fasting and continuous calorie restriction, with a small short-term advantage for alternate-day fasting. Semnani-Azad 2025 strong

sections.head: Diets for medical conditions
sections.text: A diet chosen for a medical condition needs a different comparison. Low-carbohydrate diets can improve blood-sugar control in type 2 diabetes. In a review, 57 percent versus 31 percent met a blood-sugar threshold at six months, but that definition allowed medication use; the advantage was smaller when remission required stopping medication and uncertain by twelve months. Goldenberg 2021 good DASH lowers blood pressure. Appel 1997 good A medically supervised ketogenic diet can reduce seizures in drug-resistant epilepsy, and a low-FODMAP diet, which temporarily limits certain fermentable carbohydrates, can reduce IBS symptoms. Neal 2008 good Halmos 2014 good Food processing

sections.head: A menu that changed intake
sections.text: Twenty adults ate more on an ultra-processed menu than on an unprocessed menu while living in an NIH research ward. They were allowed to eat freely. Changing the menu changed the average intake by about 500 calories a day. Each person received both menus, in random order, for two weeks each. Intake was 508 calories a day higher on the ultra-processed diet. Participants gained about 2 pounds during that phase and lost about 2 during the unprocessed phase. Hall 2019 good The offered meals were designed to match calories and several nutrients. They were not identical foods with processing switched on or off: texture, the energy density of solid food, and other properties differed. Two menus, different intake Average weight change during each two-week menu phase. The same participants ate 508 more calories a day on the ultra-processed menu. This short trial establishes a difference between these two menus. Its weight changes should not be projected at the same rate for a year. NOVA classifies foods by the purpose and extent of processing. Its ultra-processed category includes industrial formulations containing ingredients or additives rarely used in home cooking, such as some packaged snacks, soft drinks, and reconstituted meat products. Monteiro 2019 mixed Freezing vegetables or canning beans does not automatically put them in that category. Neither a wrapper nor a long ingredient list is a reliable health verdict by itself. The meat stall occupies the foreground; the Holy Family gives alms in the distance. Aertsen painted the contrast in 1551. Pieter Aertsen, A Meat Stall with the Holy Family Giving Alms (1551), North Carolina Museum of Art. Public domain. The trial did not isolate one cause of the extra intake. Participants ate the ultra-processed meals faster, and the solid food was more calorie-dense. The diets also differed in protein proportion and fiber type. The study could not tell which of those differences accounted for the extra intake.

sections.head: Long-term health evidence
sections.text: A 2024 review of published meta-analyses included data from nearly 10 million participants. Higher ultra-processed intake was associated with more cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and earlier death. The pooled relative risks were about 1.50 for cardiovascular mortality and 1.21 for all-cause mortality, though those estimates came from different analyses and exposure definitions. Lane 2024 mixed These were observational studies; the authors rated certainty for the cardiovascular-mortality estimate very low. Smoking, income, activity, and the rest of the diet can complicate the comparison. The broad category also combines foods with very different nutritional value. A useful substitution. Replace some ready-to-eat snacks and sugary drinks with meals built from beans, vegetables, whole grains, fruit, and a protein source. Frozen vegetables, canned beans, and packaged whole-grain bread can make that practical. The two levers

sections.head: Protein and fiber
sections.text: Protein and fiber are worth considering separately. Protein supports lean tissue, especially with resistance training. Fiber-rich foods are associated with lower disease risk and can improve several risk factors. Neither removes the need to consider the rest of the diet. Cheese, bread, fruit, and nuts on a table painted around 1615. Cheese and bread are processed foods too; processing alone is a poor way to judge the whole meal. Floris van Dijck, Still Life with Cheese (c. 1615), Rijksmuseum. Public domain.

sections.head: Protein and fullness
sections.text: In a small study of 19 adults, raising protein from 15 to 30 percent of calories was followed by an average reduction of about 440 calories a day during a free-eating phase. Weigle 2005 mixed Everyone followed the diet phases in the same order, so this is suggestive evidence rather than a large randomized comparison. It supports trying more protein when meals leave you hungry, not a guarantee that your intake will fall by that amount. For someone lifting regularly, about 0.7 grams per pound of bodyweight is a reasonable target. A training meta-analysis estimated that average gains in fat-free mass, which includes muscle and other non-fat tissue, stopped increasing near that intake, with substantial uncertainty around the cutoff. Morton 2018 strong That estimated training target does not establish a ceiling for every person or purpose. Choose protein from foods you like and can afford, including fish, eggs, dairy, beans, lentils, or soy.

sections.head: Fiber and disease risk
sections.text: The longstanding adequate-intake targets are 25 grams of fiber for women and 38 for men aged 19 to 50; after 50 they are 21 and 30 grams. They come from a reference of 14 grams per 1,000 calories. Dietary Reference Intakes good A WHO-commissioned review included 185 prospective studies and 58 trials. Higher-fiber diets were associated with roughly 15 to 30 percent lower risks across several outcomes, including mortality, heart disease, diabetes, and colorectal cancer. Mortality was measured in the observational studies. Trials supported benefits for weight, blood pressure, and cholesterol. Reynolds 2019 good Higher-fiber diets and lower risk Higher fiber intake is associated with lower disease risk. This is a schematic illustration of the direction, not a fitted mortality curve or a prediction of your risk. The review found substantial benefit around 25 to 29 grams a day and suggested that higher intakes could help further. It did not establish unlimited benefit. Beans, lentils, whole grains, fruit, vegetables, and nuts supply fiber along with other nutrients. The large review excluded isolated-fiber supplement trials, so it cannot answer whether powders work. Separate trials show that psyllium can lower LDL cholesterol. Jovanovski 2018 strong Add fiber gradually so your body can adjust. NIDDK fiber guidance Three planning estimates interactive Bodyweight 170 lb lb kg Activity Mostly sitting Active Very active Goal Lose Maintain Build Calories a day 2,210 illustrative estimate Protein 123 grams a day Fiber 31 grams a day The calorie estimate multiplies bodyweight by a rough activity factor and omits age, height, sex, and medical history. Protein uses the training target of 1.6 g/kg (about 0.7 g per pound); fiber uses 14 g per 1,000 estimated maintenance calories. These examples are for adults, outside pregnancy or breastfeeding. For a more detailed model, see the NIDDK Body Weight Planner . The aisle

sections.head: What supplements have evidence for
sections.text: A supplement is easiest to assess when you name the job: correcting a deficiency, preventing a particular birth defect, improving training, or preventing disease. Evidence for one job does not establish the others. Routine multivitamins have not shown a clear benefit for preventing cardiovascular disease or extending life in generally healthy adults. In the Physicians' Health Study II, 14,641 male doctors were followed for about eleven years, with no statistically significant reduction in major cardiovascular events. Sesso 2012 good A 2024 observational analysis of 390,124 adults also found no mortality benefit. Loftfield 2024 mixed The USPSTF judged the evidence insufficient to recommend multivitamins for cardiovascular or cancer prevention. O'Connor 2022 good

sections.head: When supplementation causes harm
sections.text: Beta-carotene is a clearer warning. In a large trial of male smokers, supplementation increased lung-cancer incidence by 18 percent relative to the comparison group. A second trial of beta-carotene plus vitamin A in smokers and asbestos-exposed workers was stopped early after harmful results. ATBC 1994 strong CARET 1996 strong A 2007 review found no significant mortality effect when all antioxidant trials were pooled, but an increased risk in the lower-bias subset, particularly for beta-carotene, vitamin A, and vitamin E. Bjelakovic 2007 good These trials tested pills, rather than diets rich in vegetables. Antioxidant trials: mortality Relative risks of all-cause mortality from the lower-bias antioxidant trials, excluding selenium trials. Lines show 95 percent confidence intervals; 1.00 is no difference. Vitamin E: 1.04 (1.01 to 1.07); beta-carotene: 1.07 (1.02 to 1.11); vitamin A: 1.16 (1.10 to 1.24). Supplements were sometimes given in combination. The full pool of trials was statistically inconclusive. Bjelakovic 2007 good

sections.head: What the broad verdict misses
sections.text: The multivitamin evidence has exceptions too. The same physicians' trial found an 8 percent relative reduction in total cancer incidence, without a demonstrated reduction in cancer mortality. Gaziano 2012 good COSMOS cognitive studies found small improvements in test scores among older adults. Those results do not establish that multivitamins prevent dementia. Vyas 2024 good Targeted supplements have clearer uses. Folic acid around conception reduced recurrent neural-tube defects by 72 percent in a trial of women with a previous affected pregnancy. MRC 1991 strong General prevention guidance recommends 400 to 800 micrograms daily for people planning to or who could become pregnant, starting before conception. People with a previous affected pregnancy need individual advice. USPSTF 2023 strong B12 is important for vegans and people who cannot absorb enough; iron treats iron deficiency, not every cause of anemia. NIH B12 good NIH iron good Ask what the supplement is for. Creatine can improve resistance-training results. Kreider 2017 strong Vitamin D treats established deficiency, but routine extra dosing did not prevent cancer or major cardiovascular events in VITAL. Recommendations differ for groups such as older adults and pregnancy. Manson 2019 good The Endocrine Society's guidance addresses those differences. Prescription icosapent ethyl reduced cardiovascular events in selected statin-treated, high-risk patients with elevated triglycerides. That result does not apply to every fish-oil capsule. Bhatt 2019 good The hard part

sections.head: Why weight returns, and what medicines change
sections.text: Weight regain has physiological causes. Losing weight can increase hunger and reduce the energy your body expends. In a small study, hunger and several appetite-hormone changes persisted a year after substantial diet-induced weight loss. Sumithran 2011 good Those changes make maintaining the loss harder. A controlled study found that maintaining a weight at least 10 percent below the starting weight reduced energy expenditure beyond the change expected from body size. Leibel 1995 good The more extreme example is The Biggest Loser : fourteen former contestants had regained much of their lost weight six years later, while their resting expenditure averaged about 500 calories a day below the researchers' prediction. Fothergill 2016 mixed That small, unusual cohort does not tell every dieter what will happen to their metabolism. Long-term results vary. A review of older US weight-loss programs found that participants retained about a quarter of their initial loss after several years; it was not a finding that a fixed percentage of all dieters fail. Anderson 2001 good The National Weight Control Registry documents people who have maintained substantial losses for years, but they volunteered after succeeding. It cannot estimate how often that happens in the population. Thomas 2014 mixed

sections.head: Medicines that reduce appetite
sections.text: Semaglutide mimics a gut-hormone signal involved in appetite and blood-sugar control, GLP-1. Tirzepatide acts on both GLP-1 and a second hormone signal, GIP. In trials of adults with obesity or overweight and a related complication, without diabetes, semaglutide produced an average 14.9 percent weight loss over 68 weeks, versus 2.4 percent with placebo. Tirzepatide's highest studied dose produced 20.9 percent over 72 weeks, versus 3.1 percent. Both trials included lifestyle support. Wilding 2021 strong Jastreboff 2022 strong Weight after semaglutide withdrawal The semaglutide group in the STEP 1 extension lost an average 17.3 percent by week 68, then regained 11.6 percentage points over the following year. Lines connect the reported means; intervening values are not shown. Participants regained about two-thirds of the loss on average. Semaglutide and the trial's lifestyle intervention both stopped at week 68; several cardiometabolic improvements also moved back toward baseline. Semaglutide also has evidence beyond weight. SELECT enrolled 17,604 people with established cardiovascular disease and overweight or obesity, without diabetes. Heart attack, stroke, or cardiovascular death occurred in 6.5 percent on semaglutide versus 8.0 percent on placebo over about 40 months of follow-up. The time-to-event analysis estimated a 20 percent relative reduction, a hazard ratio of 0.80, in that composite outcome. It did not establish a separate 20 percent reduction in each component. Lincoff 2023 strong Plan for ongoing treatment. In the extension study, substantial weight returned after treatment stopped. Wilding 2022 good These medicines also commonly cause nausea, diarrhea, or constipation and require a clinician to check suitability and risks. Some lost weight is lean tissue. In a tirzepatide body-composition substudy, about a quarter of the loss was lean mass, which includes more than skeletal muscle. Look 2025 good The plan

sections.head: Meals you can repeat
sections.text: Start with meals you can repeat, then change the part that is causing a problem. A filling lunch, fewer sugary drinks, or a reliable source of B12 may matter more than adopting an entire named diet. Make a few filling meals repeatable. Combine a protein source with vegetables or fruit, and include beans, whole grains, nuts, or other foods that fit the meal. Use the numbers for their purpose. The protein target here comes from training studies. Fiber targets depend on age and energy needs. They can help plan food without tracking every nutrient. Change the menu where it helps. Try replacing some packaged snacks with a meal or a more filling snack. Convenience foods such as frozen vegetables and canned beans can help. Check sugary drinks. Replacing some soda or sweetened coffee can reduce calorie intake. Trials and cohort studies support a connection between these drinks and weight gain. Malik 2013 Choose a sustainable weight plan. Weight loss needs an energy deficit. A named diet is useful when its food and rules help you maintain that change. Give supplements a specific job. B12, folic acid, iron, vitamin D, and creatine have different indications. A broad promise of better health is harder to substantiate. Get help with repeated regain. A clinician can assess causes, support, and whether medication is appropriate. Reducing sodium lowered blood pressure in the controlled DASH-Sodium trial. Sacks 2001 good Some observational studies reported higher risk at very low intake, but measurement error and illness can create that pattern. Research using repeated 24-hour urine samples found a rising cardiovascular risk with higher sodium, rather than a clear protective middle. Ma 2022 good Current US guidance is less than 2,300 milligrams of sodium daily for most people aged fourteen and older, with needs differing when sweat losses are high. Dietary Guidelines 2025-2030 good That is sodium, not the weight of table salt. Evidence sketches interactive Protein Fiber Walking Salt Vitamin pills Protein and training. Average fat-free-mass gains showed diminishing returns near 0.7 g per pound. The estimated cutoff is uncertain. This curve is schematic, not a fitted result. Peeters painted her own face in the pewter lid of the jug, a small self-portrait among the cheeses and costly tableware. Clara Peeters, Still Life with Cheeses, Almonds and Pretzels (c. 1615), Mauritshuis. Public domain. A limit of this guide. I am not a doctor. This guide cannot account for your medical history, medications, pregnancy, or eating-disorder history. Its numbers describe study groups and rough planning estimates, not an individual prescription. A clinician or registered dietitian can help when those circumstances change what is appropriate. The fine print

sections.head: Sources, and how to read them
sections.text: Sources are linked beside the claims they support. Trials can test causation under their study conditions; cohorts can find associations over longer periods. A review is only as reliable as the evidence it pools. The grades are editorial shorthand for that distinction and the important limitations, not formal GRADE ratings. posts.title: The Other Hours
posts.desc: Blood pressure can be high without symptoms. Read about sleep, smoking, screening, and the limits of popular recovery treatments, then use the checklist to choose a place to start.

sections.text: Vilhelm Hammershoi, Dust Motes Dancing in the Sunlight , 1900. Public domain. Start here Sleep Relationships Exposure Preventive care Light Heat Stress Cold Products Follow-up 01 / Start here

sections.head: What the evidence can tell you
sections.text: Only about one in five US adults with high blood pressure has it controlled. The national survey found that many didn't know they had it. Blood pressure can be high without symptoms, which makes measuring it useful. CDC NCHS 2024 The three other guides in Staying Alive cover strength , movement , and food . A trial of blood-pressure treatment answers a different question from a study linking friendships with survival. Neither supplies a personal health ranking.

sections.head: Clinical outcomes
sections.text: Did an intervention reduce illness or death? Check the population and the absolute difference.

sections.head: Observed associations
sections.text: Did people with a habit fare better? Illness, income, and other habits may explain some of the difference.

sections.head: Short-term measurements
sections.text: Did a treatment change blood chemistry, soreness, or mood? That can be useful without proving disease prevention. 02 / Sleep

sections.head: Enough sleep, and help when it fails
Enough sleep, with a regular schedule
sections.text: Adults aged 18 to 60 should regularly sleep seven or more hours, according to the sleep-medicine consensus. If you need more to function well, a mortality graph isn't a reason to set an earlier alarm. AASM and Sleep Research Society 2015 Observational studies link both short and long sleep with higher mortality. Illness and depression can lengthen sleep, so the direction of cause is uncertain. Cutting a healthy nine-hour sleeper down to seven has not been shown to extend life. Cappuccio et al. 2010 A study of about 61,000 people with wrist trackers linked consistent sleep timing with lower mortality. Work schedules and health may contribute to the association. Try a steady wake time, provided it leaves enough time to sleep. Windred et al. 2024 Vincent van Gogh, "The Siesta" (after Millet), 1890, Musee d'Orsay. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

sections.head: When the problem needs treatment
sections.text: Loud snoring, witnessed pauses in breathing, gasping awake, or persistent daytime sleepiness are reasons to ask about sleep apnea, repeated obstruction of the airway during sleep. CPAP keeps the airway open with pressurized air. In SAVE it improved sleepiness and quality of life but did not reduce cardiovascular events in patients with established cardiovascular disease. Average use was 3.3 hours a night; we cannot assume low adherence explains the null result. McEvoy et al. 2016 For chronic insomnia, the American College of Physicians recommends cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia, or CBT-I, as the initial treatment. It addresses the habits and thoughts that keep insomnia going. Persistent insomnia deserves treatment beyond changes to the bedroom. Qaseem et al. 2016

sections.head: Alcohol, caffeine, and sleep products
sections.text: Alcohol can shorten the time it takes to fall asleep while disrupting sleep later in the night. Using it as a sleep aid trades one problem for another. Ebrahim et al. 2013 Caffeine depends on dose and timing. A 2023 meta-analysis found an average reduction of about 45 minutes in total sleep across its experiments, not a fixed cost per cup. In a later crossover trial of 23 male moderate caffeine users, 100 mg had no statistically significant sleep effect at the tested intervals of four, eight, or twelve hours before bed. A 400 mg dose disrupted some sleep measures even twelve hours before bed. The sample was small and excluded women. Gardiner et al. 2023 ; Gardiner et al. 2025

sections.head: Try an earlier caffeine cutoff
sections.text: This is clock arithmetic for an experiment you choose. It does not estimate your metabolism or a safe dose. Target bedtime Hours without caffeine before bed 8 hours 10 hours 12 hours With the selected interval, stop at 12:30 pm, same day These example intervals aren't validated personal cutoffs. Dose still matters. Compare your sleep after reducing caffeine or moving it earlier; the tool cannot promise an unaffected night. Blue-light-filtering glasses have inconclusive sleep evidence: the small trials in a Cochrane review disagreed. Melatonin has uses in sleep timing, but the label is a separate problem. A 2023 analysis found 22 of 25 US gummy products inaccurately labeled, including one with no detectable melatonin; an earlier supplement analysis also found wide variation. The findings concern the products sampled. Singh et al. 2023 ; Cohen et al. 2023 ; Erland and Saxena 2017 03 / Relationships

sections.head: The people around you
sections.text: In a meta-analysis of 148 studies, stronger social relationships were associated with 50 percent higher odds of survival during follow-up. That is an odds ratio. It predicts neither extra years of life nor the effect of adding a weekly dinner. Holt-Lunstad et al. 2010 A later analysis separated loneliness, the feeling of being disconnected, from social isolation, having few contacts, and living alone. Their adjusted mortality odds ratios were 1.26, 1.29, and 1.32 respectively. A ratio of 1.26 means 26 percent higher odds, which is different from a 26 percent higher risk. Living alone doesn't necessarily mean being lonely; a crowded household can be lonely too. Holt-Lunstad et al. 2015 Pierre-Auguste Renoir, "Luncheon of the Boating Party" (1880 to 1881), The Phillips Collection. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons. Poor health can make social life harder; income and neighborhood conditions can affect both health and connection. Adjusting for those differences can't remove every shared cause. The association doesn't establish the mortality benefit of a particular social routine. Choose contact you can repeat: a standing meal, a walk with someone, a group built around work you care about. If you feel isolated despite seeing people often, more appointments may miss the problem. A sense of purpose tracks with survival in older adults. The study cannot separate having a reason to get up from being well enough to pursue it. Alimujiang et al. 2019 04 / Exposure

sections.head: The air, the drink, the smoke
Smoking
sections.text: Current smokers in a large US study lost more than a decade of life expectancy compared with people who had never smoked. Quitting before age 40 avoided about 90 percent of the excess mortality associated with continuing. Quitting later still helped. Jha et al. 2013 For nonpregnant adults who smoke, the USPSTF recommends behavioral support and approved medications, including nicotine replacement, varenicline, or bupropion. Pregnancy changes the medication discussion. USPSTF 2021 Nicotine e-cigarettes help more people stop smoking than nicotine replacement in the trials pooled by Cochrane. The review does not establish their long-term safety. A smoker's decision about replacing cigarettes is different from a nonsmoker's decision to start vaping; continuing to smoke while vaping also leaves the cigarette exposure in place. Lindson et al. 2025

sections.head: Alcohol
sections.text: The old finding that light drinkers outlive abstainers is vulnerable to who gets counted as an abstainer. Some people stop drinking because they are sick. A 2023 analysis that addressed this and other biases found no statistically significant mortality advantage for low-volume drinking. Genetic evidence from China also links higher alcohol consumption with higher blood pressure and stroke risk. Zhao et al. 2023 ; Millwood et al. 2019 Alcohol causes several cancers. Its Group 1 carcinogen classification means the evidence that it causes cancer is established; it does not mean a glass of wine carries the same risk as smoking. Lower intake reduces exposure. There is no reason to start drinking for heart health. NCI If you drink heavily and regularly, get medical help with stopping. Alcohol withdrawal can be dangerous. NIAAA

sections.head: Air at home
sections.text: Fine particles from combustion, traffic, and wildfire smoke are associated with premature death. In a large Medicare cohort, the association persisted even at concentrations below the US standards in force at the time. Exposure isn't entirely a personal choice; housing and local air policy matter. Di et al. 2017 Test for radon, a radioactive gas that can enter from the soil and raises lung-cancer risk. If the result is high, arrange mitigation. For smoke or other indoor particles, a properly sized particle filter can reduce exposure in the room where you use it. It doesn't remove every gas, replace ventilation when outdoor air is clean, or fix a source of pollution. EPA ; EPA 05 / Preventive care

sections.head: The numbers and checks worth knowing
Blood pressure
sections.text: In SPRINT, high-risk adults without diabetes were assigned to systolic targets below 120 or below 140 mm Hg. Intensive treatment reduced major cardiovascular events by 25 percent and deaths by 27 percent relative to standard treatment during the trial. Annual cardiovascular event rates were 1.65 percent with intensive treatment and 2.19 percent with standard treatment. It also increased some adverse events, including hypotension and acute kidney injury. A clinician should interpret the target alongside your risks and how pressure is measured. SPRINT Research Group 2015 ; AHA/ACC 2025 Different denominators, different questions 47.7% Of all US adults had hypertension. 59.2% Of adults with hypertension knew they had it. 20.7% Of adults with hypertension had it controlled below 130/80. NHANES, August 2021 to August 2023. Awareness and control use adults with hypertension as their denominator. CDC NCHS 2024 For home measurements, use a validated upper-arm monitor and a cuff that fits. Avoid smoking, caffeine, and exercise for 30 minutes beforehand. Rest quietly for five minutes, sit with your back supported and feet flat, and support the bare arm at heart level. Take two readings a minute apart and keep a record. Bring the monitor and the readings to your clinician; a single reading doesn't establish the usual pressure. American Heart Association 2025

sections.head: Cholesterol and glucose
sections.text: LDL cholesterol contributes causally to atherosclerosis, the buildup of plaque in arteries. Exposure over time matters. A lipid panel helps assess risk, and ApoB, a measure of the number of certain cholesterol-carrying particles, can be useful in selected situations. Treatment decisions also use age, smoking, blood pressure, diabetes, and family history. Ference et al. 2017 Diabetes screening is also a question of eligibility. The USPSTF recommends screening adults aged 35 to 70 who have overweight or obesity, with earlier consideration for some higher-risk groups. A1c, which reflects blood sugar over the past few months, or fasting glucose can be used. USPSTF 2021

sections.head: Screening with a reason
sections.text: Screening means testing people without relevant symptoms. Symptoms need evaluation on their own schedule. A test can prevent deaths while also producing false alarms, unnecessary treatment, or complications. The following are US recommendations for the populations described, not a complete preventive-care plan. Colorectal cancer: screening from 45 to 75 for asymptomatic adults at average risk; selective decisions from 76 to 85. Options include an annual fecal immunochemical test, or FIT, and colonoscopy at ten-year intervals when results and history permit. A positive stool test needs follow-up colonoscopy. USPSTF 2021 Lung cancer: annual low-dose CT for adults aged 50 to 80 with at least 20 pack-years who currently smoke or quit within 15 years, provided health and willingness permit curative treatment. Twenty pack-years means one pack a day for twenty years, or an equivalent exposure. USPSTF 2021 Breast cancer: the USPSTF recommends mammography every two years from 40 to 74 for its average-risk population, including women and other people assigned female at birth. Prior breast cancer, certain genetic risks, or young-age chest radiation require a different plan. Evidence is insufficient for a general recommendation from 75 onward. USPSTF 2024 NordICC randomized invitations to colonoscopy; 42 percent of invitees attended. At ten years, colorectal cancer occurred in 0.98 percent of the invited group versus 1.20 percent of usual care; the mortality difference was not statistically significant. Low uptake complicates interpretation without establishing why mortality didn't significantly differ. Estimates among attendees require additional assumptions. Bretthauer et al. 2022

sections.head: Vaccines, teeth, and hearing
sections.text: A meta-analysis of randomized trials of influenza vaccination found fewer major cardiovascular events, with the clearest signal in patients with recent acute coronary syndrome. Udell et al. 2013 A 2025 Welsh natural experiment used a birth-date cutoff for eligibility for Zostavax, the older live shingles vaccine. It estimated 3.5 percentage points fewer new dementia diagnoses over seven years among vaccine recipients, corresponding to a 20 percent relative reduction. The estimate applies to that older population and vaccine. It does not establish the same dementia effect for Shingrix, the vaccine now used in the US. Its established reason for use is preventing shingles and its complications. Eyting et al. 2025 ; CDC Interdental cleaning has low-certainty evidence for reducing gingivitis, inflamed gums, alongside brushing. The review did not assess heart attacks or dementia. Dental pain, infection, and losing teeth are enough reason to seek dental care. Worthington et al. 2019 In ACHIEVE, hearing aids and audiological counseling did not slow three-year cognitive decline in the whole trial. A prespecified analysis suggested benefit in the older, higher-risk subgroup. Treating hearing loss helps communication; dementia prevention remains a more qualified claim. Lin et al. 2023 06 / Daylight

sections.head: Daylight and the body clock
sections.text: Light reaching your eyes helps set the timing of sleep and wakefulness. Outdoor daylight is often a convenient source of bright daytime light, while dimmer evenings and a dark bedroom support the day-night contrast. Timing matters: the best schedule for a night-shift worker may differ from a daytime worker's. Brown et al. 2022 The light consensus measures melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance at the eye, accounting for the spectrum's effect on the body clock. Ordinary lux alone doesn't capture it. A window or appropriate indoor lighting can contribute. Weather, latitude, time of day, and the light's direction all change the exposure, so there is no universal ten-minute outdoor dose in that recommendation.

sections.head: Vitamin D
sections.text: VITAL tested 2,000 IU of vitamin D a day in about 26,000 midlife and older adults who weren't selected for deficiency. It did not reduce the primary outcomes of invasive cancer or major cardiovascular events. Its fracture analysis also found no reduction. These findings do not answer whether a diagnosed deficiency should be treated. Manson et al. 2019 ; LeBoff et al. 2022 During the original trial, vitamin D was associated with a 22 percent relative reduction in confirmed autoimmune disease. After two additional years off the randomized treatment, the seven-year hazard ratio, comparing event rates during follow-up, was 0.98, with a confidence interval spanning benefit and harm. Newly confirmed cases also revised the original on-treatment estimate to 0.85, which was no longer statistically significant. Hahn et al. 2022 ; Costenbader et al. 2024 For generally healthy adults under 75, the 2024 Endocrine Society guideline advises the usual recommended intake and suggests against routine extra doses or vitamin D testing. It gives different advice for selected groups, including adults 75 and older, pregnancy, and high-risk prediabetes. Established medical reasons for testing or treatment are a separate matter. Endocrine Society 2024

sections.head: Visible light and ultraviolet are different
sections.text: A Swedish cohort linked avoiding sun exposure with higher mortality in women. It cannot establish that ultraviolet exposure prolongs life: sun habits travel with other differences in health and lifestyle. The sunscreen trial offers a different kind of evidence, with fewer invasive melanomas after assignment to daily sunscreen, although the event counts were small. Lindqvist et al. 2016 ; Green et al. 2011 Get daytime light while protecting your skin. Shade, clothing, and sunscreen let you spend time outside with less ultraviolet exposure. Seeing daylight does not require tanning or burning, and you should never stare at the sun. FDA 07 / Heat

sections.head: What the sauna findings show
sections.text: The sauna mortality study followed 2,315 Finnish men. Those reporting four to seven sessions a week had a 40 percent lower adjusted rate of death from any cause than those reporting one session a week. That comparison does not show what would happen if everyone in the once-a-week group began going daily. Laukkanen et al. 2015 Health and the circumstances that permit frequent sauna use may contribute to the association. Adjustment cannot remove all those differences. The findings have limited reach beyond the men and sauna practice studied. In a small controlled study with 20 young sedentary adults who completed it, eight weeks of hot-water heat therapy improved blood-vessel measures and blood pressure. Investigators assigned matched groups; it was not randomized. It tested immersion, not sauna use, and did not measure disease prevention or lifespan. Brunt et al. 2016 Use a sauna if you enjoy it, without treating the cohort percentage as a promised benefit. Avoid alcohol with heat, leave if you feel faint or unwell, and ask about suitability if illness or medication affects your response to heat or blood pressure. Laukkanen et al. 2018 08 / Stress

sections.head: Breathing and meditation
sections.text: Workers reporting job strain, high demands with little control, had a higher rate of coronary heart disease in a large pooled analysis. This was observational evidence. The problem may include working conditions that a breathing exercise cannot change. Kivimaki et al. 2012 Meditation programs produced modest improvements in anxiety, depression, and pain in a review of randomized trials. The review did not establish superiority over active alternatives such as exercise or other behavioral treatments. Goyal et al. 2014 Slow breathing is a simple way to try settling yourself. Sit comfortably and breathe gently at a pace that feels easy, without forcing deep breaths or long holds. Stop if you become dizzy. Blood-pressure trials are inconsistent, so use it as an optional calming practice, not a way to replace prescribed treatment. de Freitas Goncalves et al. 2022 A small Wim Hof experiment found that a combined training program changed adrenaline and inflammatory responses to an injected bacterial component in 24 healthy men. The experiment didn't test infections, autoimmune treatment, or lifespan. Kox et al. 2014 09 / Cold

sections.head: The plunge and its tradeoffs
sections.text: Repeated cold-water immersion immediately after lifting can interfere with the adaptation you're training for. In a small twelve-week trial, the cold-water group gained less muscle and some measures of strength than the active-recovery group. It doesn't establish an exact waiting interval after lifting. Roberts et al. 2015 Cold can reduce the soreness people report after exercise. That may be useful when short-term comfort matters, but less soreness doesn't establish better muscle growth or faster recovery of every aspect of performance. Hohenauer et al. 2015 The dopamine figure comes from ten men immersed for an hour in water around 57 F. The researchers measured blood dopamine, which rose about 250 percent. They did not measure a lasting increase in brain dopamine or test a two-minute home plunge. Sramek et al. 2000 In a randomized cold-shower trial, participants reported 29 percent less sickness absence from work, while reported illness days did not differ. The trial doesn't establish why they missed less work, or show that cold prevented illness. Buijze et al. 2016 The immediate cold-shock response can affect breathing and heart rhythm. Avoid hyperventilating or holding your breath in or near water. A heart condition or history of fainting is a reason to discuss cold immersion before trying it. No trial cited here establishes a longevity benefit. Shattock and Tipton 2012 10 / Products

sections.head: Supplements and health claims
sections.text: Ask what outcome a product changed, in whom, and against what comparison. A supplement that raises a blood marker may still have no demonstrated effect on illness. Evidence for one medical use also doesn't validate every claim on a consumer panel.

sections.head: Multivitamins
sections.text: In three cohorts totaling about 390,000 adults, use was not associated with lower mortality. That is observational evidence, not proof that vitamins are never useful. Deficiency and pregnancy involve different needs. Loftfield et al. 2024

sections.head: Fish oil
sections.text: Ordinary omega-3 supplements did not reduce VITAL's primary major cardiovascular outcome. Prescription icosapent ethyl reduced cardiovascular events in a selected, high-risk group already taking statins. Manson et al. 2019 ; Bhatt et al. 2019

sections.head: High-dose antioxidants
sections.text: In the ATBC trial, beta-carotene supplementation increased lung-cancer incidence in male smokers. ATBC Study Group 1994

sections.head: Detoxes and cleanses
sections.text: NCCIH finds no convincing research supporting these programs for removing toxins or improving health. Restriction, laxatives, or supplements can create problems of their own. NCCIH

posts.title: The Same Chance
posts.desc: I believe everyone gets exactly the same chance at contentment, even people who die young. What that chance looks like, and how pain turned me around.
posts.keywords: same chance contentment happiness spirituality karma comfort conscience truth pain unselfish action nature nurture equality

sections.text: You throw a piece of trash at a garbage can and miss. Nobody's looking. Do you go back and pick it up? I believe everyone gets exactly the same chance at contentment and happiness, including folks whose lives end too early. By contentment I mean feeling connected to other people and less restless inside. Life shows each of us the truth about the harm we're doing. Then it's our choice: do the uncomfortable thing we know is right, or keep doing the comfortable thing we know is wrong. I think pain is usually what finally turns us around. The trash is a small version of that choice. You know it's yours, and you know what you should do. Walking away is easier. Most chances are this small, and they come all day long. Pleasure is getting what I want. It feels good for a while, and it can leave me cut off from people. What's actually made me content is unselfish action, doing something that helps somebody besides me. I want to be comfortable, and I chase it like it's the only thing that matters. I did that until I hurt so badly that my choices were death or doing the uncomfortable things I knew were right. Even then, I didn't believe being less selfish would make me feel better. So I tested it, for a long time. I'd act less selfishly and feel more connected. Then I'd get some of my comforts back, get selfish again, and watch the restlessness and disconnection come back. That happened over and over. I kept growing by learning more and, more importantly, by doing more constructive, unselfish things. I call this karma: the harm I do to other people also harms me. The opposite is just as real. Unselfish action brings connection and contentment back, and I call that reverse karma. I believe both happen because we're all part of one spiritual world. Nobody has to catch me for it to count. It isn't permanent. What I have is a daily reprieve, relief that lasts as long as I keep living this way. I can go back to the old way any day. I can pick up the trash today and walk right past it tomorrow. I believe there's a spiritual compass, a sense of right and wrong, in all life, including us. We know right from wrong, and I don't think there's any denying it. Someone can sincerely believe something harmful is right. That's natural. It's part of their journey, and anyone could be on that part of it, me included. I think arguing about right and wrong just separates us. When somebody tells me I hurt them, I want to argue. I'm better off shutting up and listening, because part of it is usually true. Genes and upbringing are part of the journey. Nobody picks their family or the brain they're born with. Some of the best people in the world had the worst upbringings, and some of the worst people had some of the worst upbringings too. If you were raised wrong or born with bad genes, I think you're kind of innocent for a while. At some point, though, life shows you the truth: you're hurting other people, and it's hurting you. However different our lives look, I believe we're all exactly the same underneath, the way every wave in the ocean is the same. And I believe the chance is exactly equal. I can't explain how it comes out even for a kid with every advantage and a kid with none. I think it's infinitely complex in the way it's spread out, and nobody will ever prove it with math. How it works out is beyond us.

The strongest evidence against me is a housing lottery. In the 1990s, a federal experiment called Moving to Opportunity let 4,604 low-income families in public housing sign up for a chance to move to a less poor neighborhood. Ten to fifteen years later, Jens Ludwig and colleagues found that the adults whose families won were happier on average, even though winning hadn't raised their incomes. Happiness is the exact thing I'm saying everyone has the same chance at, and a lottery changed it. Emmy Werner's study is closer to what I believe. She followed all 698 children born on the Hawaiian island of Kauai in 1955 , from birth to age 40. Some had four or more serious risks by age two, such as poverty, a hard birth or a family in constant conflict. Two-thirds of those kids had problems with school, the law or their mental health by 18. The other third grew into what Werner called "competent, confident and caring" adults. Most of the teenagers who'd had serious problems had recovered by midlife. Their turning points included going back to school as adults, the military, a stable marriage, a religion that asked something of them, and surviving a life-threatening illness or accident. Those were mostly help or a second chance, and you have to live long enough to get one. The study can't tell me how much of it was choice, or what was possible for the ones who died. Pain shows up in the drinking research too. Helen Matzger and colleagues followed 659 problem drinkers in Northern California who had started cutting back. Three reasons for cutting back predicted who would stay out of problem drinking over the next five years: hitting rock bottom, going through something traumatic and having a spiritual awakening. Those were reasons people gave after they'd already cut back, so it doesn't prove the pain did it. Pain doesn't simply make people more ready to change, though. Carlo DiClemente and colleagues studied about 1,400 people starting treatment for alcohol dependence. The ones who said drinking had cost them more were a little more ready to change. The ones under more stress were a little less ready. It's one snapshot, so it can't show what caused what. I still think pain is usually what turns people around. It's what turned me. I can't show it's true for most people, and these are only drinking studies. I'm not saying anybody has to hurt like I did. Viktor Frankl survived Auschwitz and wrote a famous book about finding meaning in suffering. Even he said that if suffering can be avoided, you remove its cause: " To suffer unnecessarily is masochistic rather than heroic. " I'd never tell someone to wait for their life to get worse before they accept help. If I can help someone's pain stop, that can be the right thing for me to do, whatever they might have learned from it. I don't get to look at somebody who's hurting and decide it's their karma. I can't see their life from the inside. Good people suffer. When they do, I can't explain it, and I'm not going to blame them for it. If somebody's hurting people, that may be part of their journey, and you still stop them. Punishing them isn't my job. Karma takes care of that. I suspect the connection between us goes all the way down to the quantum level, the physics of atoms and particles. That's a hunch. Experiments with entangled particles, pairs that share one state however far apart they are, won the 2022 Nobel Prize in physics . They don't test right and wrong or happiness, and I have nothing that links the two.

I can't test the equality either. It's a spiritual commitment, and I'd keep it without proof. I might explain it differently someday. I'll never decide some people didn't get the chance. The hardest case is a baby who dies before they're old enough to know right from wrong, or a person who never develops the ability. I believe they got exactly the same chance too. I can't tell you what their chance looked like or how it could be equal to mine. I still won't make an exception. If I made one, I'd be saying I'm different from them, and we're all exactly the same.

posts.title: What You Get Used To
posts.desc: Do we get used to everything? No. Some feelings fade, some get stronger, and feeling something less doesn't mean it's doing less to you.
posts.keywords: repetition familiarity habituation sensitization pleasure pain sleep exercise food abuse luxury tolerance alcohol practice expertise perceptual learning service happiness

sections.text: Sleep in a really expensive hotel bed for a month and it stops feeling special. It's still a better bed, though. So do we get used to everything? No. Here's where the line is. A lot of things lose their kick, like a nice bed or a drug's high. Some hit harder the more they repeat, like some people's pain and a problem drinker's craving. And feeling something less doesn't mean it's doing less to you. Drugs really can end up feeling like decaf. That's tolerance: the same dose does less. But tolerance doesn't hit every effect equally. With opioids like morphine , the body builds a lot of tolerance to the high and the pain relief, and less to the slowed breathing. Slowed breathing is what kills people in an overdose. So someone chasing the old high takes more, and their breathing hasn't built up the same tolerance. Alcohol didn't turn into decaf for everyone. A Chicago study gave 190 young drinkers alcohol in a lab, then did it again five and ten years later . About one in five ended up with a drinking problem. For them, alcohol got more stimulating over the decade, they wanted it more, and they liked it as much as ever. Pain can go the other way too. In one set of heat-pulse experiments , 312 adults got short pulses of heat on the palm or foot, three seconds apart, each peaking at the same temperature, about 124 F. For some of them, the pain got worse as the pulses went on. Others felt about the same, or less. The whole test took about twelve seconds. Plenty of things do fade. A loud noise makes you jump, and if it keeps coming, you jump less . Take a break and the jump comes back, at least partly. Pleasure can do something similar. In one experiment , people enjoyed a three-minute massage more when 20 seconds in the middle were a break, even though that meant less massage. Repeat something and you might jump less , hurt more , or get better at it . Then there's no sleep from having kids. I'd have said you get used to it. The closest test I found didn't involve kids. In a lab, people were allowed four or six hours in bed a night for two weeks . Their sleepiness went up at first and then mostly leveled off. Their attention didn't. By day 14, the six-hour group was doing about as badly on alertness tests as someone who'd been up all night, and the four-hour group as badly as someone up two nights straight. At their worst, they said they felt only slightly sleepy. One reason exercise gets easier is that your body changes. In a twelve-week cycling study , the most oxygen the men's bodies could use went up 18 percent in the young ones and 31 percent in the older ones. It's like carrying the same box up the same stairs once you're in better shape. Practice is a separate thing. It makes you notice more. A coffee roaster can see the exact shade the beans should be. A chef eyeballs ingredients. A race car driver hits the right line without thinking about it. Researchers call this perceptual learning , and they point to it in radiologists, chess masters and air traffic controllers. The experts often can't say what they're seeing, which is part of why it's so hard to teach. Food goes both ways. You can get used to eating shitty, and you can get used to eating healthy. In one trial , parents gave their three-year-olds a taste of a vegetable the kid disliked every day for two weeks, with a sticker for trying it. Afterward, the parents said those kids liked it more and ate more of it than kids who skipped the program.

I think people really do get used to abuse. Nobody I found measured whether it actually hurts less over time. A study that followed about a thousand people in New Zealand from birth found that the ones who'd been maltreated as kids were more likely to have raised markers of inflammation in their blood at 32. That doesn't prove the abuse caused it, and it isn't something you'd feel. For luxury, the best evidence I found is about money. In Sweden, researchers compared lottery players who won big prizes with players who won small prizes or nothing. Surveyed five to twenty-two years later , the big winners rated their lives higher, and the gap was no smaller for people who'd won longer ago. Asked how happy they were, all things considered, the two groups weren't clearly different. Here's how I think about what lasts. Pleasure is what you get from doing what you want. Happiness is what you get from doing what's right. Pleasure fades, and you can't keep going back for more. Happiness fades too, but it never gets old, and you can always go back for more. Some of the evidence above pushes back on the pleasure half. A break brought the massage back, and the problem drinkers liked alcohol as much after ten years as at the start. The happiness half has one small test behind it. In two experiments , people got a little money over and over to spend on themselves or give away: $5 a day for five days in one, a nickel a round over ten rounds of a quick online game in the other. The good feeling from giving faded more slowly than the good feeling from getting, about half as fast in the game. It still faded some, and nobody followed it past five days. The best objection to my answer is the word "eventually." Maybe every feeling fades at least a little if you wait long enough. The heat test lasted about twelve seconds, but the drinking study ran ten years, and for the people who developed a problem, the wanting was stronger at the end than at the start. If a longer study watched that wanting fade, I'd change my answer. Without a deadline, though, "eventually" can never be proven wrong, because you can always wait another year.

posts.title: Negative temperature
posts.desc: Two paddles stir a live superfluid. Dark vortex cores move through the luminous field and collect into groups with matching circulation.
posts.keywords: superfluid negative temperature condensate Gross Pitaevskii vortex circulation clustering quantum WebGPU simulation physics

sections.text: A superfluid study

sections.head: Negative temperature
sections.text: A field of tiny whirlpools, left to find its own order. Preparing the field Preparing a condensate with imaginary-time evolution. 10 model units Pause Instruments Restart Fullscreen View Surface lighting Density contours Cyclic phase Density and velocity Show vortex signs Replay seed Save diagnostics Fixed offline seed. Apply it with Restart. Opens during the first paddle sweep, after 12,000 computed steps. Floating-point replay can diverge across GPUs. Model configuration Energy includes the moving paddles, which do work on the field. Real-time evolution has no damping or norm correction. Candidate annihilations are estimates between samples. Surface lighting follows density slopes; its highlights are illustrative. The contour view marks equal density. Warm circles mark positive winding; blue circles mark negative winding. Phase hue is a smooth, constant-lightness OKLab color wheel, an encoding rather than emitted light. Each dark core carries one turn of the condensate’s phase. Two repulsive paddles move through the field, shed vortices, and withdraw. The wave equation then decides what survives. Same-sign cores can organize into persistent groups; Instruments measures their circulation and organization. “Negative temperature” refers to the statistical temperature of the vortex subsystem. This prototype does not estimate that temperature or establish thermodynamic equilibrium. The condensate is a two-dimensional mean-field model, with dimensionless lengths and time. Sources and numerical notes Gauthier and collaborators, Giant vortex clusters in a two-dimensional quantum fluid . Preprint 2018; Science , 2019. The double-paddle protocol is the starting point for this smaller, smooth trap. Johnstone and collaborators, Order from chaos . Preprint 2018; Science , 2019. Signed nearest-neighbor correlations measure organization. Implementation, validation and measured limitations . The live solver uses a 512 by 512 grid and symmetric split-step Fourier evolution.

posts.title: How Long Can You Live?
posts.desc: One verified person has lived past 120. How unlikely another birthday becomes at 110, and what a calorie-restriction trial actually measured.
posts.keywords: longevity lifespan aging Jeanne Calment calorie restriction mortality survival health

sections.head: How Long Can You Live?
sections.text: Only one person has been verified to live past 120. 3 min read / Updated 2 Oct 2026 Jeanne Calment died in France in 1997 at 122 years and 164 days . Her record still stands. The next-longest verified life , Kane Tanaka's, ended at 119 years and 107 days. At 90, Calment sold her apartment under an agreement that let her stay for life. The buyer paid her each month and would get possession when she died. He died first, at 77. His family kept paying until her death .

sections.head: Is 122 the limit?
sections.text: Researchers haven't established a biological cutoff at 122. A 2016 Nature paper argued for a natural lifespan limit. A reanalysis found that its apparent decline in maximum ages depended heavily on Calment's exceptional result. One model fitted to validated records puts the chance of surviving another year after 110 at roughly one half. Whether that risk really stays flat is still disputed . But even a flat risk makes another decade very unlikely. Pearce and Raftery, 2021 If you've reached 110, and each year's survival chance is 50%: Reach age Chance from 110 115 1 in 32 120 1 in 1,024 122 1 in 4,096 130 1 in 1,048,576 Calculated as 0.5 raised to the number of additional years. A simplified model, conditional on reaching 110, not your odds from birth. That model has no fixed upper age, yet almost everyone dies long before 130. A constant death rate wouldn't mean the surviving bodies had stopped aging.

sections.head: The calorie-restriction experiment
sections.text: The CALERIE trial assigned healthy adults without obesity to cut calories or keep eating normally for two years. The target cut was 25%; the restriction group achieved about 12%. They lost weight and improved several measures of heart and metabolic health. Ravussin and colleagues, 2015 A later analysis found a 2 to 3% slowdown on DunedinPACE, a blood test that estimates the pace of aging from chemical marks on DNA. Two other aging measures, PhenoAge and GrimAge, showed no significant change. The study didn't establish that participants lived longer. Waziry and colleagues, 2023

sections.head: Smoking costs a decade
sections.text: In a large US study, current smokers lost more than a decade of life expectancy compared with people who'd never smoked. Those who quit between 45 and 54 gained about six years compared with those who continued. These are group averages, not a promise to an individual. Jha and colleagues, 2013 How high the record might go remains a separate question. Pearce and Raftery's model gave a 13% chance that someone reaches 130 this century. That forecast depends on its survival and population assumptions. We still don't know whether a human body can last that long. The forecast Sources and evidence Verified ages: Guinness World Records and LongeviQuest's validated list . Calment's apartment agreement: Guinness, 2025 . Contested limit: Dong, Milholland and Vijg, 2016 ; Brown, Albers and Ritchie, 2017 . Survival model and forecast: Pearce and Raftery, 2021 . Evidence against a flat late-life death rate: Dang and colleagues, 2023 . The table uses a rounded assumption, not observed counts. Randomized calorie-restriction trial: Ravussin and colleagues, 2015 ; subsequent blood-test analysis: Waziry and colleagues, 2023 . Neither result establishes a gain in human lifespan. Smoking: Jha and colleagues, 2013 . A national observational cohort, with comparisons adjusted for age, education, alcohol use and body fat.
