posts.title: Five Hundred Children, No Books
posts.desc: Would children raised without inherited religion invent a faith? An island thought experiment, child psychology and historical cases, with their limits kept visible.

sections.text: What is inside The island is a thought experiment. The studies test particular intuitions; the historical cases show what people made from traditions they already had. 01 An island with no inherited religion the question 02 What would count as religion? definitions 03 What the children actually tell us psychology 04 The Americas were never a blank slate history 05 Three cases with three different limits comparisons 06 The Gathas ask for a choice differences 07 Similar forms, several possible causes the analogy 08 Ritual can survive without belief secular life 09 A temple built for grief the memorial 10 What AA kept from its inheritance the program 11 What the island leaves open the close The question

sections.head: An island with no inherited religion
sections.text: Nobody has tested whether five hundred children, raised without an inherited religion, would invent one. I expect they would develop some religious beliefs and practices. The evidence gives reasons for that expectation, but it cannot tell us what they would believe or how long it would take. Imagine an island where the children have language, food, shelter, care and one another. They grow up, have children of their own, and remain there for two hundred years. No scripture arrives. Nobody teaches them about gods or an afterlife. Would their descendants have a religion? This is an imagined community, not a proposal for an experiment. Even its premises need help: language, child care and rules for living together already carry culture. We can subtract familiar religious teaching on paper. We cannot assume we have subtracted everything that might shape a faith. Henderson Island, photographed from space. The island in this essay is imaginary; this photograph is an illustration. Uninhabited Henderson Island, South Pacific , from the International Space Station. NASA, public domain. Alcoholics Anonymous offers a useful contrast. It began in Akron in 1935 after Bill Wilson met Dr. Bob Smith. Both had been involved with the Oxford Group, a Christian fellowship. Their new recovery program adapted an inheritance rather than starting without one. AA history Dr. Bob's House in Akron, where early AA members met. The fellowship grew out of an existing Christian movement. Dr. Bob's House, Akron . Photo by Nyttend, released to the public domain, via Wikimedia Commons. AA adapts an inheritance. The island removes one. They ask different questions. Definitions

sections.head: What would count as religion?
sections.text: If a funeral, a shared song or a coming-of-age ceremony is enough to count, the island prediction becomes easy. Those practices need no supernatural belief. I mean something more specific: shared beliefs about gods, spirits or other sacred realities, expressed in practices that a community passes on. That working definition still has awkward edges. A community may treat its ancestors as present in daily life without dividing the world into a religious part and a secular one. A humanist funeral can mark a death without making any claim about a surviving soul. Resemblance is a reason to compare them, not to give them the same name. One cross-cultural study coded seven religious traits in thirty-three hunter-gatherer societies, using ethnographic accounts. All were coded as having animism, belief that natural beings or phenomena have intentions or a vital force. Other traits, including afterlife beliefs, ritual specialists and creator gods, varied. The authors then used genetic and linguistic relationships to model earlier states of these traditions. forager study That is evidence of a widespread pattern in a defined sample. It does not show how unexposed children would begin, and present-day hunter-gatherers are not living copies of the distant past. Even here, the proposed universal bundle comes apart. Psychology

sections.head: What the children actually tell us
sections.text: Children can find a purpose where an adult sees a physical cause. In Deborah Kelemen's 1999 study, forty-eight elementary-school children and sixteen undergraduates chose explanations for properties of unfamiliar animals and natural objects. Younger children more often accepted purpose-based accounts of nonliving things, such as pointy rocks existing so animals would not sit on them. This is teleology, explaining something by what it is for. pointy rocks Those children were already growing up in a culture. The task compared explanations supplied by a researcher; it did not observe children inventing a creator god. A separate experiment with eighty physical scientists found more acceptance of inaccurate purpose-based explanations under time pressure. That measures a reasoning tendency, not a hidden religious commitment. scientists Afterlife reasoning is more complicated than the idea that young children believe and schooling gradually removes it. Bering and Bjorklund's 2004 abstract reports that children could distinguish biological death from continued mental activity, with different patterns across ages and types of question. Older children and adults still attributed some knowledge, emotions and desires to the dead. That is the result available in the abstract; I could not inspect the full paper's methods. afterlife study A conceptual distinction used in afterlife research. There is no single curve showing belief fading as children get older. Diagram for this essay. See Bering and Bjorklund (2004) and Watson-Jones and colleagues (2017) in the sources. A later study interviewed children, adolescents and adults in Texas and Vanuatu after a death story framed in either medical or religious terms. It found cultural and framing differences, including continued bodily functions in some Vanuatu responses. The questions people have heard, and the way an interviewer asks, can affect their answers. cultural comparison Children also copy unnecessary actions. In one experiment, sixty-three children aged three to five watched an adult open unfamiliar objects after training to spot pointless steps. Many still copied those steps. This overimitation can help explain how a precise procedure gets passed on. The experiment used objects and demonstrations, not worship, and it does not establish that faithful copying has only one cause. overimitation These findings give religion some plausible raw material: purpose-seeking, thoughts about minds after death, and careful social learning. They leave the decisive step untested. A tendency that makes a belief easy to learn is not the same as a tendency that generates a whole religion without teaching. History

sections.head: The Americas were never a blank slate
sections.text: The Americas make the island question tempting. The monuments are there to compare: a pyramid in Mexico, a temple in Greece. People separated by an ocean built places for communal worship. The Pyramid of the Sun at Teotihuacan and the Parthenon at Athens. Similar public monuments do not establish independent origins for the beliefs behind them. Left: Pyramid of the Sun, Teotihuacan by Mario Roberto Durán Ortiz, CC BY-SA 4.0 . Right: the Parthenon, Athens , public domain. Both via Wikimedia Commons. But the people who settled the Americas arrived with cultures. Their descendants inherited, changed and exchanged traditions. Shared human ancestry includes cultural ancestry; it is not just a shared kind of brain. Calling the Americas a second blank-slate experiment erases the very inheritance we need to understand. Nor was 1492 the first contact across the Atlantic. Researchers dated wood worked with metal tools at the Norse site of L'Anse aux Meadows to 1021, using a known radiocarbon event and tree rings. Genetic research also supports pre-European contact between Polynesian and Native American populations. Neither result tells us how a particular religious practice originated. Norse evidence Pacific evidence The comparison cannot supply two independent groups starting with no religious history and reaching the same result. Comparisons

sections.head: Three cases with three different limits
sections.text: The Tongan castaways had Christian schooling. Their survival cannot tell us what children raised without religion would believe. reported recollections John Frum on Tanna developed among people already living with local traditions, missionaries and colonial rule. Jean Guiart's field study cites reports of the movement from 1941, before wartime American military bases reshaped the region. A new movement grew out of a complicated history. Tanna field study A John Frum ceremonial cross on Tanna, photographed in 1967. The movement developed among people with local traditions and a history of contact. John Frum ceremonial cross, Tanna by Tim Ross, 1967, CC BY 3.0 , via Wikimedia Commons. Nicaraguan Sign Language shows something else. A 2004 study compared thirty deaf signers from successive school cohorts with ten hearing Spanish speakers. Later cohorts more often separated a movement's manner and path into successive signs. Children helped develop the structure of an emerging language within a communicating community. sign-language study The castaways retained a faith, Tanna transformed traditions, and deaf Nicaraguans developed a language. Putting them in a row does not turn them into three replications of the island. Differences

sections.head: The Gathas ask for a choice
sections.text: The Gathas, hymns central to Zoroastrian worship, ask people to choose between truth and falsehood. Yasna 30 links that choice to thought, words and actions. It gives moral choice a prominent place. But the hymns also contain prayers for divine help: Yasna 28 opens with a petition to Mazda. Reducing this tradition to a refusal to surrender would miss those prayers. Yasna 30 and 28 A winged figure at Persepolis, commonly called the Faravahar. The Gathas ask people to choose truth over falsehood. Faravahar relief, Persepolis by Napishtim, CC BY-SA 3.0 , via Wikimedia Commons. A confession, a prayer and a moral demand can mean different things in different traditions. Their visible similarities do not settle whether the self is corrupt, whether there is a creator, or what salvation would mean. The analogy

sections.head: Similar forms, several possible causes
sections.text: Convergent evolution offers an analogy for similar forms arising along different histories. Vertebrate and cephalopod camera eyes both focus light onto a retina, although those retinas are arranged differently. An octopus's photoreceptors face the incoming light; ours face the other way. octopus eye review Vertebrate and octopus eyes. Both focus light, but their retinas are arranged differently. The comparison is an analogy, not evidence about the origin of religion. Vertebrate (left) and octopus (right) eye by Caerbannog, CC BY-SA 3.0 , via Wikimedia Commons. Religion adds a problem the eye diagram cannot solve: people teach, travel, translate and borrow. To distinguish independent invention from inheritance, we need evidence about those routes. Similarity alone will not do it. Nor can we count broad labels such as Indian, Chinese and Native American as independent witnesses with no shared roots. Each label covers many histories and communities. Related scriptures also carry earlier teachings forward. A count of matching ideas has to account for that transmission before it can tell us anything about convergence. A claim that every society has the same religious skeleton needs a stable definition. If we keep expanding the skeleton whenever a counterexample appears, we make it impossible to test. A secular ceremony must be allowed to count as secular. Secular life

sections.head: Ritual can survive without belief
sections.text: The Soviet state restricted religious institutions and promoted atheism. After its collapse, Orthodox identification in Russian surveys rose from 31 percent in 1991 to 72 percent in 2008. Monthly attendance was still only 7 percent in 2008. Identification, belief and practice are different measures; a rise in one does not mean all three returned together. survey and methods Visitors waiting to enter Lenin's Mausoleum in Moscow, 1969. Calling this a religious scene is an interpretation of the photograph. The queue at Lenin's Mausoleum, Moscow, 1969 . Fortepan / Pohl Pálma, CC BY-SA 3.0 , via Wikimedia Commons. The same automatic-return story fails in former East Germany. In the 2008 International Social Survey Programme, about 52 percent of respondents there said they did not believe in God. That was the highest proportion among the thirty countries and territories compared in Tom Smith's report. It was a dated comparison of belief in God, not a measurement of every form of spirituality. ISSP report The Jugendweihe, a secular coming-of-age ceremony, continued after German reunification. Its history reaches back before the East German state, which later tied it to a socialist pledge. A present-day organizer describes participation as voluntary and open across worldviews. organizer's history That survival tells us a ceremony can remain useful after the political setting changes. It does not demonstrate that religion secretly returned. People can want a public way to mark adulthood while continuing to disbelieve in God. The memorial

sections.head: A temple built for grief
sections.text: The Temple at Burning Man began with a death. In 2000, David Best and Jack Haye brought the Temple of the Mind to the event. When fellow builder Michael Hefflin died in a motorcycle accident, it became a memorial to him. Other participants began leaving remembrances of their own dead. Temple history Memorial messages at the Burning Man Temple, 2011. The event's Temple tradition began with a memorial to a builder who died. Messages at the Burning Man Temple by Victor Grigas, 2011, CC BY-SA 3.0 , via Wikimedia Commons. The Burning Man Project describes the Temple as a space for people of any religion or none. Participants leave photographs, inscriptions and mementos; the Temple is then burned in silence. This is an intentionally maintained memorial practice, with its own history. It matters to the island question because it shows that a shared creed is not required for a shared response to grief. It also makes the definition problem unavoidable. A rite for the dead can carry religious meaning for one participant and no supernatural claim for another. The program

sections.head: What AA kept from its inheritance
sections.text: AA's practices make the inheritance visible. In a later account of the program before the Twelve Steps, Bill Wilson recalled admitting defeat, taking a moral inventory, confessing shortcomings, making restitution, helping others and praying for help. This was his retrospective summary, not a fixed six-step text used from the first meeting. Wilson's account Saying grace before a meal in Pie Town, New Mexico, 1940. Shared prayer can accompany ordinary meals as well as formal worship. Saying grace before the barbecue dinner, Pie Town, New Mexico . Russell Lee, Farm Security Administration, 1940, Library of Congress, public domain. The published Twelve Steps retain God, prayer and a spiritual awakening, alongside inventory and amends. They qualify God with the words "as we understood Him." That leaves room for differing understandings; it does not make the text free of theology. the Twelve Steps A program's survival cannot prove that only its effective elements survived. That would require comparing the effects of those elements, not reading their history backward from success. AA shows an inherited religious practice adapted for recovery. It gives us no controlled test of which parts of religion humans need. The close

sections.head: What the island leaves open
sections.text: Religious texts have their own accounts of what people bring into the world. Romans 2:14 and 2:15 describes people without the law doing what it requires, with its work written on their hearts. Quran 30:30 speaks of the natural disposition in which God created people. These are claims inside traditions, not results from developmental psychology. Romans Quran A believer may understand human capacities as part of creation. A nonbeliever may understand them through natural history. Finding a psychological route to a belief does not, by itself, decide whether the belief is true. I do not think the island can settle whether God is real. My expectation is that the descendants would develop repeated ceremonies, ways to mourn, and perhaps beliefs about spirits or continued life after death. I would not put a probability on the last part. The research does not supply one. An island in the Mekong at dusk. The thought experiment ends with a prediction we cannot check. Dusk over an island in the Mekong, Don Det, Laos by Basile Morin, CC BY-SA 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons. Two hundred years gives the imaginary community time to change. It gives us no evidence of what the descendants would actually say when asked about their dead. Sources

sections.head: Evidence and limits
sections.text: The sources support different kinds of statements: laboratory findings, historical accounts, models and religious teachings. None observes the island community imagined here. The prediction is my judgment; it is not a measured probability. Evidence and access limits, grouped by claim

sections.head: History and practice
sections.text: Alcoholics Anonymous. The Start and Growth of A.A. . The fellowship's own history of its beginnings and Oxford Group connection. Bill Wilson, via AA Cleveland. Origin of the Twelve Steps . A retrospective account of the earlier oral program. Alcoholics Anonymous. How It Works . The published Twelve Steps. This is a program text, not an effectiveness study.

sections.head: Psychology and comparison
sections.text: Kelemen (1999). Why Are Rocks Pointy? . Methods and relevant results inspected in full text. Supplied explanation choices test reasoning in culturally situated children. Kelemen, Rottman and Seston (2013). Professional physical scientists display tenacious teleological tendencies . Methods and relevant results inspected in full text. A speeded judgment task, not a test of religious belief. Bering and Bjorklund (2004). The natural emergence of reasoning about the afterlife . Abstract only. The full-paper link was inaccessible. No numerical curve or claim of unexposed children rests on it. Watson-Jones and colleagues (2017). Does the Body Survive Death? . Methods and relevant results inspected in full text. Death narratives and interviews in the United States and Vanuatu; responses depended on context. Lyons, Young and Keil (2007). The hidden structure of overimitation . Methods and relevant results inspected in full text. Copying object-use demonstrations is relevant to transmission, not proof of religious origins. Peoples, Duda and Marlowe (2016). Hunter-Gatherers and the Origins of Religion . Methods and relevant results inspected in full text. Ethnographic coding and a model of population relationships, rather than an experiment with religion removed. Senghas, Kita and Ozyurek (2004). Children Creating Core Properties of Language . Methods and relevant results inspected in full text. Compares motion expressions across cohorts, not the emergence of an entire grammar in a fixed decade.

sections.text: Kuitems and colleagues (2021). Evidence for European presence in the Americas in 1021 . Methods and relevant results inspected in full text. Dates worked wood at one Norse site. Ioannidis and colleagues (2020). Native American gene flow into Polynesia . Article findings read; full methods were not accessible. Genetic evidence of contact does not identify transmitted beliefs. Rutger Bregman (2020). The Tongan castaways . Reported recollections. Jean Guiart (1956). Un siecle et demi de contacts culturels a Tanna . Selected introductory and historical pages inspected in full text, especially printed pages 151 and 152. Field research and colonial records, with their perspectives and limits. Paul Raffaele (2006). In John They Trust . Reporting from Tanna, with interviews and historical context. The movement did not begin without traditions. Yasna 28 and 30. The Gathas . The edition attributes its Gathas translation to Christian Bartholomae. Read alongside the prayers in Yasna 28. Hanke and Kelber (2020). The Eye of the Common Octopus . Anatomical review accessed in full text. Used for the eye comparison, not as a model of cultural history.

sections.head: Secular rites and religious claims
sections.text: Pew Research Center (2014). Russians Return to Religion, But Not to Church . Analysis and methods read. Repeated representative adult samples distinguish identity from attendance. Tom W. Smith (2012). Beliefs about God across Time and Countries . Report, question wording and tables read. Its 2008 comparison is not a current ranking of all societies. Jugendweihe Berlin/Brandenburg. History of the Jugendweihe . The organizer's history and description of its present ceremony. No national participation rate is claimed. Burning Man Project. Temple History and Meaning . The project's account of the memorial origin and continuing burn. Romans 2:14 and 2:15; Quran 30:30. Religious accounts of human nature . Romans read in NRSVUE; Quran read in Mustafa Khattab's translation. These passages describe beliefs within their traditions.

posts.title: Forty, Not a Hundred
posts.desc: The first edition of the Big Book claimed more than one hundred recovered members. The real roll was about forty. A field guide to the exact, buried particulars of how Alcoholics Anonymous actually began, in forty-seven sourced deep cuts.

sections.text: The count

sections.head: The roll, and the real start
sections.text: Start with the number on the cover, because it was not true. No. 01

sections.head: The book said a hundred. There were about forty.
sections.text: When Alcoholics Anonymous went to press in April 1939, its foreword announced "more than one hundred men and women who have recovered." The best reconstruction of the actual roll: 74 people had ever passed through the two groups, and roughly 41 were sober. Bill Wilson, years later, dropped the salesmanship and just said "about 40." the roll No. 02

sections.head: The forty were almost all Akron's.
sections.text: The two cities were not close. New York, where Bill himself got sober and started first, had produced almost nobody: of roughly thirty-five or forty men who passed through his Brooklyn house, only three had come clear in nearly two years, Bill, Hank Parkhurst, and Fitz Mayo. Akron, under Dr. Bob, had quietly made almost all the rest. When the two founders counted heads in Dr. Bob's living room in November 1937 and found "upwards of 40 alcoholics staying bone dry," they bowed their heads and wept. It was the first time the thing looked real. No. 03

sections.head: "One Hundred Men" was the title, until a woman wrote a chapter.
sections.text: The working title for the book was One Hundred Men . It had to be thrown out for a simple reason: one of the personal stories was a woman's. The runner-up, The Way Out , lost too, after a check at the Library of Congress found at least a dozen books already using it and none at all called Alcoholics Anonymous. No. 04

sections.head: AA exists because a hostile takeover failed.
sections.text: Bill Wilson was in Akron in May 1935 to win a proxy fight for a rubber-machinery company. He lost, and found himself broke and alone in the lobby of the Mayflower Hotel, one end of the corridor leading to the bar and the other to a church directory and a payphone. He worked the phone instead, looking for another drunk to talk to, and reached Dr. Bob through it. The whole fellowship turns on which way he walked. The Mayflower lobby in Akron, where Bill Wilson chose the church directory over the bar in May 1935. Main lobby, Mayflower Hotel, Akron by Warren LeMay, CC BY-SA 2.0 , via Wikimedia Commons. No. 05

sections.head: The founding vision arrived during a belladonna delirium.
sections.text: Bill's famous white-light experience, the spiritual jolt the whole program traces back to, came in December 1934 at Towns Hospital, while he was being dosed around the clock with belladonna and henbane, two deadly nightshades. Whether the light was God or the pharmacology is still openly argued, including by AA's own historians. Bill always insisted it was real. The former Towns Hospital on Central Park West, where the vision happened in a belladonna ward. 293 Central Park West, the former Towns Hospital by Eden, Janine and Jim, CC BY 2.0 , via Flickr. No. 06

sections.head: Its official birthday is probably a week wrong.
sections.text: June 10, 1935, the date of Dr. Bob's last drink, is the fellowship's birthday. But the medical convention Dr. Bob drank his way through that week did not even open until June 10, which puts his real final beer closer to June 17. The most celebrated date in AA is a best guess. No. 07

sections.head: Four years made the first hundred. Two more made six thousand.
sections.text: It took from 1935 to 1939 to produce about a hundred sober members across three cities. Then a single Saturday Evening Post article ran in March 1941, and the fellowship roughly quadrupled in ten months, to six or eight thousand by the end of that year. One magazine piece did more than the first four years. growth The opening of one AA convention, San Antonio, 2010. Forty people once. More than fifty thousand in this room alone. Opening ceremony, A.A. International Convention, San Antonio, 2010 by Tony Kent, CC BY-SA 2.0 , via Wikimedia Commons. No. 08

sections.head: The membership table still opens with "1935: two members."
sections.text: AA's headquarters keeps a running census, and the very first row reads "1935: 2 members, 0 groups," backdated to Bill and Bob themselves. The same table peaks at 2,138,201 members in 129,790 groups in 2020. It is the only census on earth that begins with two named men. The big book

sections.head: The book itself
sections.text: Nine decades, and the whole approved library fits on one short shelf. No. 09

sections.head: In ninety years, AA has approved exactly eleven books.
sections.text: The General Service Conference has put its stamp on eleven full-length books, from the Big Book in 1939 to a volume of Bill's talks in 2019. Everything else AA publishes, the great bulk of its paper, is pamphlets, around sixty of them. The "Conference-approved" label itself only goes back to 1951. approved No. 10

sections.head: Bill Wilson wrote three of them.
sections.text: Three of the eleven are genuinely his: the Big Book, the Twelve Steps and Twelve Traditions (1953), and Alcoholics Anonymous Comes of Age (1957). Three more are anthologies of his own words, assembled by other hands. The rest, including both official biographies and the daily meditation book, were written by other members or by anonymous committee. Even the Twelve and Twelve was not a solo act: Bill wrote it with two paid editors at his elbow. Of the three, only Comes of Age is his start to finish; the Big Book's front is his, but its back third is the members' own stories, coming up next. the 12 and 12 No. 11

sections.head: He wrote all of the first 164 pages but two chapters.
sections.text: The famous front half of the Big Book is Bill's, with two exceptions. "The Doctor's Opinion" was a letter from Dr. William Silkworth, and "To Employers" was written by Hank Parkhurst. The personal stories filling the back third were written by the members themselves. The copyright names Bill as sole author, but he admitted he had become "much more of an umpire than an author." who wrote what Dr. William Silkworth, whose letter of support became "The Doctor's Opinion," one of the two front chapters Bill did not write. Portrait via storiesofrecovery.org . No. 12

sections.head: Lois wanted to write the chapter to the wives. Bill took it.
sections.text: The chapter addressed to the wives of alcoholics was offered first to Dr. Bob's wife Anne, who declined, and then claimed by Bill, over the wishes of his own wife, who had lived every line of it. Asked about it decades later, Lois answered without softening it: "Bill wrote it, and I was mad." to wives No. 13

sections.head: The hundred drunks fighting over every word never happened.
sections.text: The romantic image is the whole membership battling over the text in meetings. The archival historian William Schaberg checked the record and put it flatly: "blood on the floor... it didn't happen in meetings; it did happen in a New Jersey office." The real editing was a handful of men in Hank Parkhurst's Newark office. A wider circle of about four hundred did get to weigh in, by mail: mimeographed loan copies went out to members, doctors, clergy, and judges for comment before the book was set. Schaberg The mail was the nervous system of early AA: draft chapters, loan copies, and later the floods of pleas for help all moved by post. Sorting the mail, 1938 . Arthur Rothstein, Farm Security Administration, Library of Congress, public domain. No. 14

sections.head: "God as we understood Him" was the unbelievers' victory.
sections.text: The phrase that lets an atheist stay in the room was the price of peace with the New York agnostics, usually credited to a former salesman named Jim Burwell. In the same compromise, the Seventh Step lost the words "on our knees." The book's most famous opening to non-believers was won by its non-believers. No. 15

sections.head: It is called the Big Book because of the paper.
sections.text: Nothing about its length earned the nickname. The first printer ran it on the thickest stock in the shop, so that a $3.50 book in 1939 would feel hefty enough to be worth the money. The first run was 4,730 copies. The name is a printing decision, not a compliment. No. 16

sections.head: AA forgot to renew the copyright.
sections.text: Through a clerical lapse, the first edition's United States copyright was never renewed, and the original text has been in the public domain since 1967. AA still maintains it controls the book everywhere else on earth, and has fought to keep doing so. No. 17

sections.head: The marked-up 1939 manuscript sold for $2.4 million.
sections.text: The typed printer's copy of the Big Book, the handwritten edits still on its pages, sold at auction in 2018 to the owner of the Indianapolis Colts. AA's publishing arm sued to stop the sale, then settled by signing away any and all claims to it. No. 18

sections.head: The book now exists in more than seventy languages.
sections.text: From a first run of under five thousand, the basic text has been carried into seventy-plus languages. One of them, Navajo, has no written form for it: the translation took four years and was issued as a spoken fourteen-disc recording, sold out of its first run of eight hundred sets. The Big Book in Hebrew. The cover is the same plain promise in every alphabet it reaches. The Big Book in Hebrew . Released under CC0 , via Wikimedia Commons. The rooms

sections.head: The rooms before the book
sections.text: Before there was a book, there was a house, a hospital bed, and a set of rules nobody wrote down. No. 19

sections.head: The whole meeting format was borrowed from a church movement.
sections.text: AA did not invent its meetings. Those early gatherings were meetings of the Oxford Group, a popular evangelical Christian movement founded by a Lutheran minister, Frank Buchman, in the 1920s, years before Bill ever got sober. It had no clergy and no buildings; it ran on house meetings, open confession, making amends, a morning "quiet time" of listening for guidance, and a yardstick called the Four Absolutes (honesty, purity, unselfishness, love). When Bill later wrote the Twelve Steps, he was reworking that material. The alcoholics only became their own thing when they walked out, New York in 1937 and Akron in late 1939, because the Group's hunger for publicity, its all-or-nothing standards, and its hard Protestant edge all worked against drunks just trying to get through one day. the Oxford Group The first six years. Akron and New York both began as Oxford Group meetings (brass) and only became A.A. once they broke off (green): New York in 1937, Akron in late 1939. The counts are sober membership; the roughly 6,000 of 1941 is a looser figure, since it counts people reached after the Saturday Evening Post article. The five-day hospital stay and the surrender on your knees were Akron's rule under Dr. Bob, never New York's. No. 20

sections.head: When it was forty people, Akron met in a living room on Wednesday nights.
sections.text: There was no clubhouse and no book. From 1935 to 1939 the Akron group met every Wednesday in the living room of T. Henry and Clarace Williams, at 676 Palisades Drive, inside an Oxford Group meeting where the alcoholics were a minority bloc. When that grew impossible the meeting moved to Dr. Bob's own house, which once held 74 people in one night. the sites Dr. Bob's house at 855 Ardmore Avenue. For a stretch in early 1940 the whole Akron meeting crammed inside it. Dr. Bob's House, Akron . Photo by Nyttend, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons. No. 21

sections.head: There was a meeting about the meeting.
sections.text: Every Monday the most surrendered members held a "set-up meeting," sitting in silence with pads and pencils to write down the name God gave them for who should lead on Wednesday. One member marveled that they nearly always wrote the same name. No. 22

sections.head: You could not attend until you had knelt.
sections.text: This was Akron's rule, and Akron's alone. Usually it happened at the hospital, where a man who had shown he was serious knelt by the bed and admitted out loud, to God, that he was licked. If he somehow got out without doing it, he had to make the surrender in an upstairs bedroom at the Williams house before his first meeting, the wives waiting downstairs, and "down would come the new man, shaking, white, serious, and grim." New York, looser and far less scriptural, ran no such ritual. No. 23

sections.head: The weekly meeting was rated "important, but not vital."
sections.text: A 1938 fact-finding memo, the only contemporary written description of the program, ranked the meeting itself as merely important. The truly mandatory part was a daily morning quiet time, skipped at "grave danger of backsliding." The thing AA is now built around was once the optional part. No. 24

sections.head: New York met on Tuesdays, in the Wilsons' front room.
sections.text: The other founding group met at 182 Clinton Street in Brooklyn, about fifteen people counting families, looser and far less scriptural than Akron. Drunks boarded in the house and were sometimes drunk in it; Bill called it a boiler factory, "from which practically no one issued sober, but we had a pile of experience." No. 25

sections.head: The front door was a hospital bed.
sections.text: In Akron, getting in meant five to eight days in a hospital room with nothing to read but a Bible, visited two or three at a time by recovered drinkers a sponsor had summoned with twenty or thirty phone calls. The visits, a manual explained, were the medicine. Akron City Hospital, where Bill Dotson, AA number three, sobered up in a bed in June 1935. City Hospital, Akron, Ohio . Tichnor Brothers Collection, Boston Public Library, public domain. No. 26

sections.head: The sobriety chip began as a deal with a nun.
sections.text: Sister Ignatia gave every alcoholic leaving St. Thomas Hospital in Akron a Sacred Heart badge, on one condition: if he ever decided to drink, he had to come back and hand it to her first. The chip handed out for years of sobriety descends directly from that small contract. Ignatia No. 27

sections.head: "Hi, I'm an alcoholic" has no early paper trail.
sections.text: Nobody can document the ritual greeting at any meeting before the mid-1940s; AA's own archives say the earliest member memory of hearing it dates to about 1945. The Akron old-timers found the later custom of reciting your drinking history strange. As one put it, they did not think it was anybody's business. the phrase No. 28

sections.head: The Serenity Prayer came out of a newspaper obituary.
sections.text: A member spotted the lines in a June 1941 death notice in the New York Herald Tribune. Within weeks the office had them printed on wallet cards, known at first simply as the "God Grant Me" cards. The most quoted prayer in recovery entered AA off the obituary page. the prayer A modern sobriety medallion, the prayer engraved on the back. Two customs, the chip and the prayer, both improvised in the early years, fused onto one coin. Sobriety medallion by Yolanda, CC BY 2.0 , via Flickr. The cast

posts.title: Do You Get Used to Everything?
posts.desc: A visual experiment and a close look at repetition: why sensations fade, skills improve, and life satisfaction does not always return to where it began.

sections.text: Different kinds of change

sections.head: Time doesn't erase everything
sections.text: Lottery winnings can leave people more satisfied with life years later. The claim that everyone returns to the same happiness baseline goes beyond the evidence. Lindqvist et al., 2018 "Getting used to it" can mean that a sensation fades, a repeated noise stops making you jump, a drug has less effect, or a difficult task becomes easy. Those changes have different causes. A smaller response doesn't tell us much until we know what was measured. "You'll get used to it" may describe the feel of a new shirt. It gives a person living with pain, bereavement or an exhausting job little to go on. Familiarity and relief can come apart. Perception

sections.head: A dot can fade without moving
sections.text: Fix your gaze on a small point and a faint shape off to the side may disappear from awareness. This is Troxler fading. The shape remains on the screen; its visibility changes while you look elsewhere. Try steady fixation perception demo Press Start fixation, then look at the center cross for up to 30 seconds. Let the soft dots stay in your peripheral vision. Some may seem fainter or disappear; the result varies with your gaze, screen and viewing distance. Move your eyes to a dot to check that it is still there. Start fixation Refresh pattern ready Start runs a timer. It never changes the dots' opacity or measures what you see. Refresh pattern stops the timer and shifts the dots slightly. Mouse movement has no effect. If nothing fades, that is a possible result. In a 2006 experiment, eight people watched a peripheral target while an eye tracker recorded their movements and they reported when it faded or returned. Tiny involuntary eye movements called microsaccades became less frequent before fading and more frequent before renewed visibility. That relationship helps explain why steady fixation can produce fading, even though our eyes are never completely still. Martinez-Conde et al., 2006 Sensory adaptation is a change in responsiveness during sustained stimulation. Habituation is a learned reduction in a response to repetition, such as a shrinking startle. Researchers distinguish it from sensory adaptation and from a muscle becoming tired. A response that recovers after a rest, or remains strong to a different stimulus, gives them clues about which process they are studying. Rankin et al., 2009 Repetition

sections.head: A response can shrink or grow
sections.text: A sea slug supplied an unusually clear view of habituation. In Aplysia , a touch can trigger a defensive gill-withdrawal reflex. Castellucci and Kandel isolated nerve tissue and repeatedly stimulated sensory neurons while recording the response in motor neurons. The signal weakened. Their analysis traced the change to less chemical transmitter being released by the sensory cell, while the receiving cell's sensitivity remained unchanged. Castellucci and Kandel, 1974 Sensitization is an increased response, and it can coexist with habituation. In some pain conditions, increased responsiveness in pathways carrying pain signals contributes to pain from ordinarily harmless touch. Clifford Woolf's review calls this central sensitization. It contributes to some forms of chronic pain, with different degrees and durations. Woolf, 2011 Tolerance has another definition: the same dose of a drug produces less of a particular effect. Richard Solomon's opponent-process theory offered a model in which a pleasant response evokes an opposing reaction that strengthens with repetition. The stronger opposition reduces pleasure during exposure and leaves a worse state afterward. That pattern can help describe aspects of drug tolerance and withdrawal. Solomon, 1980 Solomon's opponent-process model Schematic responses during and after a stimulus. Repetition strengthens the opposing reaction in Solomon's model. The axes show no measured doses, durations or ratings. The model connects reduced pleasure during exposure with a stronger negative after-reaction. It is one account of tolerance and withdrawal. Addiction also involves processes that this picture leaves out. In Berridge and Robinson's incentive-sensitization account, cues associated with a drug can acquire an increased power to provoke wanting, even as the pleasure from taking it declines. Wanting and liking needn't move together. The account concerns addiction, rather than a general mechanism for enjoyable habits. Berridge and Robinson, 2016 Life satisfaction

sections.head: The lottery story left things out
sections.text: The famous 1978 lottery study interviewed 22 winners, 29 people paralyzed in accidents, and 22 controls. It didn't follow them from before the event to after it. Winners weren't significantly happier than controls at that one interview; the injured group was significantly less happy. The often repeated story that both groups returned to the same baseline goes beyond the experiment. Brickman et al., 1978 The fading impact of changed circumstances is often called hedonic adaptation. Lucas and colleagues used 15 annual waves of a German household survey to follow changes within the same people. Their marriage analysis followed 1,761 people who married and stayed married: average life satisfaction rose around marriage and then moved back toward its earlier level. Individual changes varied substantially. Widowhood showed a more persistent average loss during follow-up. Neither finding gives a newly married or bereaved person a two-year deadline. Lucas et al., 2003 Recovery can take different forms Two possible average paths after an event: return toward an earlier level, or partial recovery during the period observed. The shapes are illustrative, with no numerical scale or fixed recovery deadline. Marital-status and disability studies find different patterns, and people within each group differ too. A line ending below its starting point says nothing about the rest of a person's life. In a British panel, Oswald and Powdthavee found partial recovery in life satisfaction following the onset of work-limiting disability, while average satisfaction remained lower, especially with severe limitations. Their paper explicitly disagrees with earlier estimates of very little recovery. These are statistical averages, with no prediction for an individual's recovery. Oswald and Powdthavee, 2008 Lindqvist, Östling and Cesarini surveyed 3,362 Swedish lottery players 5 to 22 years after prizes were awarded. Comparing players whose prize amounts had been randomly determined, they found lasting gains in overall life satisfaction. Effects on reported happiness and mental health were smaller and weren't statistically significant. The follow-up was a single survey, not a record of each winner's mood over those years. Lindqvist, Östling and Cesarini, 2018 A prize may improve someone's judgment of their finances long after the initial excitement passes. A question about life as a whole and a question about feelings right now measure different things. Stutzer and Frey's German panel analysis found that longer commutes were associated with lower life satisfaction, including in comparisons within the same people over time. It didn't establish that nobody adapts to commuting, or identify an income increase that would causally compensate a commuter. Stutzer and Frey, 2008 A route that takes an hour each way still consumes two hours after you learn every turn. Familiarity can change how the journey feels without returning the time. Before relying on future adaptation, it helps to ask which part of a problem would actually have to change. Small pleasures

sections.head: A break can restore some enjoyment
sections.text: Quoidbach and Dunn had 55 students taste chocolate at two sessions a week apart. Between sessions, one group abstained, another received a large supply, and a control group received no instruction about consumption. At the second tasting, the abstaining group reported more savoring and positive feeling than the other groups. Quoidbach and Dunn, 2013 That is a small experiment about one food over one week. It suggests a way to keep a favorite treat enjoyable; it doesn't establish a general reset for pleasure. Taking a break from chocolate is also quite different from depriving yourself of company, rest or security. Another experiment changed attention rather than consumption. Koo and colleagues asked participants to write about how a positive event might never have happened. Thinking through the near-miss produced more positive feeling immediately afterward than simply describing the event's presence. In a relationship experiment, they selected people who were already relatively happy in relationships lasting at least five years. The result doesn't promise lasting affection or repair a troubled relationship. Koo et al., 2008 The exercise can be quite ordinary. How did you end up knowing a particular friend? Which chance meeting made that possible? Looking at the route by which something arrived may make it easier to notice. Imagining catastrophe isn't required. These experiments concern noticing an existing pleasure. Accepting continuing harm is a different proposition. Expectations

sections.head: Surprise affects a moment's happiness
sections.text: In Rutledge and colleagues' gambling experiments, people repeatedly reported how happy they felt while receiving certain rewards and taking risks. A model using recent rewards, expectations and the difference between expected and actual outcomes predicted those ratings. Cumulative winnings alone didn't account for the fluctuations. A smartphone version tested the model in 18,420 players earning points. Rutledge et al., 2014 A welcome surprise can therefore matter even when it barely changes a total. But the model also gave positive expectations a role before the outcome arrived. Setting expectations low isn't a free way to increase happiness: you give up some anticipation along the way. Direction and level are different Two invented trajectories of circumstances. One begins higher and declines; the other begins lower and improves. A graph of circumstances alone cannot tell us which person feels better. The gambling study modeled expectations and recent outcomes. It did not compare lives like these, and these lines contain no happiness measurements. The measurements were brief ratings in a reward task. Extending them into "you feel the slope, not the height" skips the rest of a person's life. Improving circumstances can still leave someone in pain or short of money. Familiar warnings

sections.head: An alarm can become routine
sections.text: A warning that has accompanied several uneventful days can start to seem less urgent. That reassurance may affect a decision even when the danger hasn't changed. Challenger: an organizational comparison The Rogers Commission's account of the 1986 Challenger launch describes earlier damage to the seals between solid rocket booster segments, incomplete communication of concerns, and a launch decision made without key managers knowing that contractor engineers had initially opposed launch in the cold conditions. The history includes active warnings, not just people ceasing to notice. Rogers Commission, 1986 Calling this habituation would imply a psychological mechanism that the commission did not measure. The narrower comparison is useful: repeated survival and an acceptable engineering margin are different kinds of evidence. Learning

sections.head: Practice can make more visible
sections.text: Repetition can also improve recognition. Chase and Simon showed chess positions briefly to a master, a class A player and a beginner, then asked them to reconstruct the boards. The master's advantage was much greater for positions from real games than for randomly arranged pieces. Their explanation was learned groups of pieces, or chunks. The master had encountered arrangements that made the board easier to remember. Chase and Simon, 1973 This classic study had three participants. It illustrates memory supported by knowledge of chess, with no claim that the master possessed a generally superior memory. Some practiced responses become less demanding of deliberate attention. In Shiffrin and Schneider's visual-search experiments, people learned to find target characters among distractors. With a consistent distinction between targets and distractors, detection became easier. When the roles were reversed, the old learning interfered: characters people had learned to ignore now needed a response. Repeating a task and practicing flexible responses aren't automatically the same thing. Shiffrin and Schneider, 1977 Practice can make a task less demanding A schematic of improving performance and decreasing deliberate checking. The lines represent different quantities, so their intersection has no scientific meaning. There is no universal practice schedule. Automatic responses develop under some training conditions. They can also make a changed task harder: an old response may keep interfering with the new one. Habit and attention

sections.head: Making the familiar strange
sections.text: William James described one benefit of habit in 1890: it "diminishes the conscious attention with which our acts are performed." A familiar action can leave us freer to think about something else. That was his account of everyday conduct, long before the visual-search experiments. James, 1890 The critic Viktor Shklovsky was interested in what habitual recognition leaves out. In his 1917 essay on art, he argued that an unfamiliar description can slow perception and let us experience something we ordinarily pass over. His phrase was "to make the stone stony." This is a claim about what art can do, not a laboratory demonstration of dishabituation. Shklovsky, 1917 A painting of a familiar street might draw a viewer's attention to window shapes they ordinarily pass by. That is the attention Shklovsky describes, without requiring a return to a first impression. We can sometimes change where we look, how we practice, or how often we take a pleasure for granted. What that changes, and how long the change lasts, remains much harder to predict. References

sections.head: Studies and primary texts
sections.text: Links beside the claims identify the evidence used. The list distinguishes experiments, observational panels, theories and literary interpretation. The four charts are conceptual illustrations, not plots of the studies' data. 19 references, with their limits Rankin et al., 2009 . Habituation revisited: an updated and revised description of the behavioral characteristics of habituation. Definition review; distinguishes reduced responding from adaptation and fatigue. Martinez-Conde et al., 2006 . Microsaccades counteract visual fading during fixation. Eye tracking and visibility reports from eight participants. Castellucci and Kandel, 1974 . A quantal analysis of the synaptic depression underlying habituation of the gill-withdrawal reflex in Aplysia. Cellular experiment in isolated nerve tissue; full original paper. Woolf, 2011 . Central sensitization: implications for the diagnosis and treatment of pain. Clinical and experimental review, not a single cause of all chronic pain. Solomon, 1980 . The opponent-process theory of acquired motivation: the costs of pleasure and the benefits of pain. Theory and evidence review. The figure here is schematic. Berridge and Robinson, 2016 . Liking, wanting, and the incentive-sensitization theory of addiction. Theory review; drug-related wanting and pleasure can diverge. Brickman et al., 1978 . Lottery winners and accident victims: is happiness relative? Small comparison at one interview, without measured pre-event baselines. Lucas et al., 2003 . Reexamining adaptation and the set-point model of happiness: reactions to changes in marital status. Longitudinal household survey; group averages conceal individual variation. Oswald and Powdthavee, 2008 . Does happiness adapt? A longitudinal study of disability with implications for economists and judges. Observational British panel; estimated partial recovery depends on the analysis. Lindqvist, Östling and Cesarini, 2018 . Long-run effects of lottery wealth on psychological well-being. 2018 working paper; published in 2020. Random prizes, one later survey. Stutzer and Frey, 2008 . Stress that doesn't pay: the commuting paradox. Panel association; compensation estimates are not experimental income effects. Quoidbach and Dunn, 2013 . Give it up: a strategy for combating hedonic adaptation. One-week randomized experiment; 55 students completed both visits. Koo et al., 2008 . It's a wonderful life: mentally subtracting positive events improves people's affective states. Writing experiments measuring feelings immediately afterward. Rutledge et al., 2014 . A computational and neural model of momentary subjective well-being. Gambling tasks and a smartphone study, not a comparison of whole lives. Rogers Commission, 1986 . Report of the Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident, chapter V. Official investigation of the launch decision; an organizational comparison. Chase and Simon, 1973 . Perception in chess. Original manuscript; three participants at different skill levels. Shiffrin and Schneider, 1977 . Controlled and automatic human information processing: II. Perceptual learning, automatic attending, and a general theory. Search experiments with consistent and changing target categories. James, 1890 . The Principles of Psychology, chapter IV: Habit. Primary text; historical account of conduct and attention. Shklovsky, 1917 . Art as Technique. Primary critical essay, translated by Lemon and Reis in 1965.

posts.title: From the Machine to the Atom
posts.desc: Chipmaking in photographs and micrographs, from a High-NA EUV scanner through wafers, the Apple M1, metal wiring, a research transistor, and silicon atom columns.

sections.text: Click or tap an image to enlarge it. In the viewer, scroll or pinch to zoom and drag to pan. The scanner · ASML High-NA EUV, EXE:5000 This scanner projects a circuit pattern onto a light-sensitive coating. High-NA means a larger numerical aperture, an optical property that improves resolution. ASML's first EXE:5000 modules shipped in December 2023 ; the joint ASML-imec development lab opened in 2024 . It's a newer tool than the one used to make the M1 below. It also performs one stage of fabrication: exposure. The Apple M1 contains 16 billion transistors , tiny devices that control electric current. Making them takes a factory full of tools. Lithography uses light to define a pattern; etching removes material; deposition adds it. The images here move through that work and then into smaller structures. They come from different factories, devices, and years. The two M1 images show the same processor design. The cleanroom · Intel, High-NA installation The suits help keep particles shed by people away from the machinery and wafers. A particle that interrupts a fine pattern can spoil a device. Cleanliness is controlled throughout the factory and within the tools. This is an Intel cleanroom photograph , a different site from the ASML-imec scanner image. The light source · schematic, not a photograph · 13.5 nm A weak laser pulse reshapes a tin droplet; a stronger pulse turns it into plasma, a hot gas of charged particles. A collector mirror gathers radiation near 13.5 nm, the wavelength used for EUV exposure. The plasma emits other wavelengths too. ASML describes 50,000 droplet cycles per second . EUV is absorbed by air and ordinary lens materials, so mirrors guide it through a vacuum . Versolato's diagram shows the source, not the whole scanner. purification and crystal growth

sections.head: A single crystal
sections.text: Silicon for chips starts with purification. In the Siemens process , silicon metal is converted into trichlorosilane, a compound that can be distilled to separate unwanted substances. In a reactor, silicon is deposited from the gas onto heated rods. Those rods contain many crystals; the wafer needs one. A seed crystal is dipped into molten silicon and slowly pulled upward while rotating. The solid growing beneath it takes the seed's crystal orientation. This Czochralski process produces a single-crystal ingot, also called a boule. Wafer makers can deliberately add small amounts of boron or phosphorus to set its electrical properties. High purity means controlling unwanted impurities, not banning every atom of another element. The crystal · a silicon boule The tapered neck records where the crystal was pulled from its seed. The wider body supplies material for wafers. Single crystal describes the repeating atomic orientation through the material; it doesn't promise a perfectly defect-free lattice. Photograph by Don DeBold. For scale · Intel headquarters, 2011 Federico Faggin beside a displayed silicon ingot during a visit marking the Intel 4004's anniversary. He led that processor's chip design. The photo record identifies the visit, but doesn't give this ingot's weight, length, or wafer yield. The ingot's usable length, slice thickness, and material lost to sawing determine the number of wafers. sawing and polishing

sections.head: Into a wafer
sections.text: Sawing turns the ingot into discs. SUMCO describes slices about 0.04 inches thick, cut with a wire saw or an inner-diameter saw. Lapping brings them to the required thickness, chemical etching removes surface damage, and polishing gives them a mirror finish. Large production wafers are about 12 inches across . Smoothness and flatness describe different things. Local surface roughness measures tiny irregularities over a small patch. Flatness concerns the shape over a larger area; thickness variation compares the two faces. A mirror finish doesn't mean the entire wafer is flat to a fraction of a nanometer. A 2007 NIST experiment , for example, achieved about 40 nm of total thickness variation on a full wafer. That's an experimental result, not a specification for every wafer sold today. The wafer · Lawrence Livermore research, 2013 A Lawrence Livermore researcher holds a wafer for neural-interface fabrication. The Department of Energy caption calls it a finished wafer. Its polished face illustrates the working surface, but the photograph doesn't establish its diameter or show a blank starting wafer. light defines the pattern

sections.head: Building the chip
sections.text: A wafer travels repeatedly between tools. A representative patterning sequence adds a film, coats it with photoresist, exposes the resist to a pattern projected from a mask, and develops it to leave protected and exposed regions. An etch can then transfer the pattern into material beneath the resist. Other steps add insulating films or metal, introduce dopants, and polish surfaces before the next pattern. Each step has its own equipment . The scanner must place each new pattern over the structures already there. Misalignment can break a connection or short neighboring features. Different layers need different feature sizes, so EUV and longer-wavelength deep-ultraviolet tools can work on the same advanced chip. The number of patterned steps isn't the number of metal wiring layers. Coating · photoresist during spin coating Spinning spreads liquid photoresist across the wafer and sheds the excess. Exposure and development will turn the coating into a temporary pattern. Resist thickness depends on the material and process; the red photograph doesn't measure it. The resist is later removed, while the transferred structure remains. The pattern · a wafer photographed in 2019 Repeated die layouts share one wafer. Fine patterns on a wafer can diffract reflected light , separating colors by angle. The rainbow doesn't show which circuits work. This 2019 photograph records a patterned wafer, without identifying its chips or processing stage. Dicing · a six-inch wafer of dies The straight gaps between dies provide paths for separating them. Testing on the wafer identifies which devices meet their requirements before packaging; testing can continue afterward. This six-inch example is a different wafer from the one above. A wafer's die count depends on die size as well as wafer diameter. one chip

sections.head: Into the Apple M1
sections.text: The next photographs show an Apple M1, introduced in 2020 using a 5 nm process . It predates the High-NA machine above. A die is the piece of silicon inside a chip package. From above, its large blocks are visible, but individual transistors aren't. The regular arrays and less regular logic regions reflect different circuit layouts. One die · Apple M1, 2020 generation · 16 billion transistors Fritzchens Fritz's optical die image shows the M1 after its package has been opened. Apple reports 16 billion transistors and eight CPU cores . The large blocks combine logic, memory, and the wiring between them. A die image can reveal their arrangement even when its smallest components remain unresolved. Closer view · Apple M1 detail This detail retains the repeating arrays and irregular circuit regions visible in the whole-die view. Memory needs many copies of the same storage cell, which produces regular layouts. Logic follows the connections a particular computation needs. The crop shows those differences in texture without identifying every block. electron microscopy

sections.head: Wires and switches
sections.text: To see the buried wiring, the specimen and the imaging method change. The cross-section below is from Intel's 14 nm process, published in 2014. It's an electron micrograph of a different chip. Metal lines connect devices within each layer; vertical connections called vias join layers. A slice cuts some lines along their length and others across it, which is why a connected network can appear as bars and separate dots. Nanometer process names don't give every transistor or wire the same size. Intel's 14 nm paper reports a 20 nm gate length and a 52 nm minimum interconnect pitch, the distance between corresponding points on neighboring lines. The M1's 5 nm label also names a manufacturing generation. Use a measured dimension or a scale bar when comparing sizes. Influenza virus · separate magnification Intel interconnect · 14 nm process Buried wiring · Intel 14 nm process, 2014 Intel's original paper identifies this view as ten of its thirteen copper wiring layers and reports a minimum pitch of 52 nm. Beside it is a CDC transmission-electron image of influenza. Roughly spherical influenza particles are typically 80 to 120 nm across , comparable to a few minimum wiring pitches. These two displayed pictures have different magnifications. Their on-screen widths are not a common-scale measurement. A research switch · Si/SiGe superlattice FinFET, 2023 A FinFET controls current through a raised semiconductor fin. Voltage on the gate, which covers the fin's top and sides, controls that current. This Yao et al. experiment uses alternating silicon and silicon-germanium layers, visible inside the fin; TiN labels the titanium-nitride gate. The authors report a 30 nm fin width and 200 nm gate length. Each black scale bar represents 20 nm. It's a research device imaged in transmission, not an M1 transistor or a 20 nm-long switch. Another layout · ring gates in radiation-hardened memory These gates enclose a region of each transistor. NASA shows annular layouts among the design techniques used to improve radiation tolerance. Cumulative radiation damage and single-particle errors need different protections. This image illustrates a memory design made for a different purpose from the M1; a round gate alone doesn't establish how much radiation a chip can tolerate. projected atomic columns

sections.head: The silicon lattice
sections.text: The final image changes specimens again. It's silicon viewed along a crystal direction called [110], reconstructed from electron diffraction measurements. The technique, ptychography , records how electrons scatter at overlapping probe positions and calculates an image from those measurements. The colors map the reconstructed signal; they aren't the visible color of silicon. The crystal lattice · silicon along [110] · 1 nm scale bar Each bright spot represents an atomic column projected through the specimen, with atoms lying behind one another along the electron beam. The paired spots resolve the structure of the silicon lattice. This is a crop of Suh et al., Figure 1b , published in Applied Microscopy in 2025. Resolving separate columns does not mean each spot is one isolated atom.

posts.title: What's Actually on an MRI Disc
posts.desc: I asked for my MRI on a disc and got 1,189 image files. Browse 515 selected slices from my brain, neck and lower back, plus two illustrative 3D models.

sections.text: I asked the hospital for my MRI on a disc and got 1,189 image files. The scan was for numbness down one side, and covered my brain, neck and lower back in one sitting, including a contrast injection. The files were in DICOM (Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine), the medical-imaging standard that stores images alongside scan settings and patient information. The viewer here contains 515 selected slices in 16 series . These are grayscale JPEG exports with a fixed contrast window, the range of signal values mapped to black through white. They don’t preserve the full signal range of the DICOM files. Pick a region and series, then scroll, drag or scrub the slider. Play runs through the stack. The slices Loading slices scroll, drag, or use the slider Loading slices Play Loading

sections.head: Why the same tissue looks different
sections.text: MRI detects radio signals from hydrogen nuclei, mainly in water and fat. Magnetic-field gradients encode where those signals came from, and a computer reconstructs the image. It doesn’t measure one little box of tissue at a time. Brightness depends on the pulse sequence, its timing and the tissue’s magnetic properties, rather than simply its density. NIH’s MRI introduction and Siemens’ sequence guide explain the signal and encoding. A sequence is a programmed pattern of radio pulses and gradients. T1 and T2 refer to two ways the signal relaxes after excitation. In ordinary T1-weighted images, fat is usually bright and spinal fluid dark. In T2-weighted images, fluid is usually bright; fat can still be bright unless suppressed. T2 is not a reversal of every shade in T1. Lauder and Driscoll’s sequence table compares them. FLAIR suppresses spinal fluid; STIR and the labels marked FS suppress fat. SWI emphasizes differences in how tissues affect the local magnetic field, useful for seeing veins and iron-rich tissue. DWI is sensitive to the motion of water molecules , and MEDIC combines several signal echoes. Post-contrast means images taken after the injection. Axial slices cut across the body; sagittal slices divide left from right; coronal slices divide front from back. These are different acquisitions, so slice 12 in one series needn’t match slice 12 in another. Sequence guide ; original SWI paper .

sections.head: What the models can show
sections.text: The brain below is a processed surface made from T1 images. Its build used neural-network estimates between slices, removed the surrounding skull and scalp, filled the ventricles and closed deep grooves before smoothing the surface. Those edits make it easier to display as a solid object, but alter its shape. It isn’t an untouched cortical surface. The second model is a rough torso envelope from a localizer, a scan used to plan the examination. It doesn’t trace individual vertebrae. MRI can show marrow and abnormalities in bone, as well as discs, nerves and the cord; the limits of this model aren’t the limits of spine MRI . Drag to rotate and scroll to zoom. This viewer draws two finished triangle meshes, not a volume you can cut through to expose the original signal. Illustrative surfaces WebGL2 drag to rotate · scroll to zoom Loading 3D viewer Region Brain Spine / torso Auto-rotate Download: brain.glb · torso.glb Brain: processed T1-derived surface. Filled spaces and smoothing alter the anatomy. How the web version was made Keep compatible slices together. DICOM records image position, orientation and pixel spacing . These locate a slice in the body. Slice thickness and the distance between slice centers are separate measurements. A volume needs a consistent acquisition and geometry; stacking different planes or contrasts together would mix different measurements of the same tissue. Export the slice sheets. Each selected series is packed into a JPEG sprite sheet, a grid of slice images. The JavaScript crops one tile onto the canvas. Most tiles are 448 by 448 pixels; the SWI tiles are 240 by 256. These are display dimensions, not measurements of anatomical resolution. The exports contain no physical slice-spacing fields. Estimate between slices. For the brain build, I trained a small network on degraded versions of the scan’s sharper slices, then used it to estimate detail in the thicker direction on a roughly 0.9 mm grid. That is output spacing, not proof of 0.9 mm anatomical resolution. Self-super-resolution research makes the distinction: resampling adds grid points, while missing detail has to be estimated. Correct coordinates allow a 3D display even when the original voxels aren’t cubes. Make the surface. HD-BET estimated a brain mask, separating brain tissue from its surroundings. I filled the ventricles and closed deep grooves, then used marching cubes to turn the mask boundary into triangles. Smoothing and simplification left 120,000 triangles in the brain mesh. The NiiVue WebGL2 library draws it in the browser. The original images and training logs aren’t included in these web assets, so the finished mesh alone can’t establish the accuracy of the reconstruction.

sections.head: What 1.5 tesla tells us
sections.text: My scan used a Siemens MAGNETOM Sola, a 1.5-tesla system . The number is the magnet’s field strength. Field strength affects the available signal, but scan time, motion, coils and sequence settings also matter. Clinical MRI uses both 2D and 3D acquisitions. A JPEG export or a smooth model isn’t enough to rank this examination against a 3-tesla scan, or to explain why a particular protocol was ordered. What was removed before sharing I left out the DICOM headers containing my name, birth date and record number. The published slice sheets have no patient text burned into them, and the meshes contain geometry rather than patient identity fields. Removing those fields doesn’t guarantee anonymity : anatomy can itself carry identifying information. This is my own scan, published under my own name. I haven’t tried to diagnose anything from these images. The JPEGs have fixed contrast and compression, and the models include estimated and edited detail. A clinical reading belongs to the original study and the radiologist’s report.

posts.title: The DSM: What a Diagnosis Can Tell You
posts.desc: How the DSM diagnoses common mental disorders, what biological tests can establish, and what field-trial reliability can tell us about diagnostic confidence.

sections.text: Andre Brouillet, Une lecon clinique a la Salpetriere , 1887. Public domain. Seven parts What tests establish Attention and mood Psychosis Physical symptoms Personality and identity Addiction Diagnostic confidence The manual

sections.head: What a test can establish
sections.text: There is no blood test that diagnoses depression. Doctors can order blood tests to look for conditions such as thyroid disease or anemia that may explain the symptoms, but those results cannot confirm major depression. MedlinePlus ADHD and autism also rely on clinical assessment rather than a single biological marker. That means a history of symptoms, information about development and daily functioning, and often observations from other people. A test can contribute information without being able to make the diagnosis. APA: ADHD CDC: autism The DSM, the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders , organizes these assessments. Published by the American Psychiatric Association, its current edition is DSM-5-TR, the fifth edition's 2022 text revision, with subsequent updates. It gives criteria, descriptions and other conditions to consider. The APA explicitly says the criteria require trained clinical judgment. APA: about DSM-5-TR But the manual does include disorders with identifiable biological causes. Narcolepsy appears in its sleep chapter. The neurocognitive chapter includes conditions due to Alzheimer's disease, Huntington's disease and prion disease. Other entries describe psychiatric symptoms caused by substances, medications or another medical condition. A disease doesn't automatically leave psychiatry when someone finds a test for it. APA: contents APA: narcolepsy Even a biological test has a specific job. In 2025 the FDA cleared a blood test that helps detect amyloid pathology associated with Alzheimer's in adults aged 55 and older who have cognitive symptoms. The FDA says it is neither a screening test nor a stand-alone diagnosis. A positive result still needs a clinical interpretation. FDA, 2025 Different kinds of diagnostic evidence Some tests identify a cause or pathology. Many common psychiatric diagnoses depend primarily on the course of symptoms and their effects on a person's life. Both columns need clinical judgment. A biological cause and a DSM diagnosis can describe different aspects of the same illness. The harder question is how well a diagnosis explains a person's difficulties. Does it distinguish their condition from similar ones? Does it predict the course, identify a useful treatment or justify an accommodation? Those questions require evidence beyond whether a checklist fits. These are short sketches, not diagnostic criteria. They omit exclusions and many differences between people with the same diagnosis. Recognizing a symptom can start a conversation with a clinician; it cannot complete an assessment. Attention and mood

sections.head: Where ordinary traits become disabling
sections.text: Everyone gets distracted or worried. Diagnosis asks about a persistent pattern: how it developed, how severe it is and what it prevents someone from doing. A familiar symptom is only one part of that account. ADHD Persistent difficulty with attention, organization or impulse control that interferes with daily life. A person can concentrate well on some activities and struggle badly with others. Some symptoms must have been present before age 12, with difficulties in more than one setting. APA Major depression Depressed mood or loss of interest, accompanied by changes such as fatigue, sleep disturbance, impaired concentration or thoughts of death. An episode lasts at least two weeks. Duration alone is insufficient: the symptom pattern, impairment and alternative explanations matter. APA Generalized anxiety Persistent, excessive worry about several areas of life, difficult to control and often accompanied by tension, fatigue or disturbed sleep. The concern may have a real subject. The difficulty is its persistence, intensity and cost. APA Bipolar disorders Episodes of mania or hypomania, changes in mood and activity that can include unusually little need for sleep, racing thoughts and risky behavior. Bipolar I requires mania; bipolar II involves hypomania and major depression. Everyday mood swings are insufficient. APA A cutoff creates a difficult boundary. Two people just above and below it may resemble each other more than two people who both qualify. Yet a shared label helps clinicians communicate, compare treatments and arrange support. Its usefulness and the uncertainty around its boundary can coexist. Biological evidence also comes in forms that aren't diagnostic tests. A review of ADHD twin studies reported an average heritability estimate of 74 percent. Heritability describes variation in a population under a model; it isn't the percentage of an individual's condition caused by genes, or a DNA result that confirms ADHD. Faraone and Larsson, 2019 A gene test with substantial predictive power Huntington disease involves an expanded CAG sequence in the HTT gene. Penetrance means the likelihood that a genetic variant produces the disease. These are categories, not a proportionally spaced number line. An intermediate allele generally does not cause disease in the carrier, but can expand when passed to a child. With 36 to 39 repeats, some carriers never develop symptoms. Full penetrance assumes survival through a normal life span. GeneReviews A specific biological cause Huntington disease Genetic testing identifies an expanded HTT repeat Huntington disease progressively affects movement, cognition and mental health. A gene test can identify the expansion before symptoms begin. Higher repeat counts generally mean earlier onset, but they do not determine the year an individual will become ill. Predictive testing requires genetic counseling. GeneReviews That is a much stronger prediction than a symptom inventory usually permits. It still distinguishes a genetic finding from a person's current clinical state. The DSM includes neurocognitive disorder due to Huntington disease. APA: contents Psychosis

sections.head: A symptom with several possible causes
sections.text: Psychosis includes hallucinations, such as hearing voices others don't hear, and delusions, beliefs held despite compelling contrary evidence. It is a set of symptoms with several possible causes. APA Schizophrenia A disorder involving symptoms such as hallucinations, delusions, disorganized thinking and reduced motivation. Diagnosis considers the course over time and effects on functioning. APA Schizoaffective disorder Psychosis and major mood episodes over the course of an illness. Mood episodes occupy most of that course, but at least two weeks of hallucinations or delusions occur outside them. clinical reference Delusional disorder Delusions lasting at least a month, without the full symptom pattern of schizophrenia. Functioning outside their effects is relatively preserved, although their consequences can be serious. Merck Manual Brief psychotic disorder Psychotic symptoms lasting at least a day and less than a month, followed by a return to the previous level of functioning. Stress may precede the episode, but is not required. clinical reference The last three sketches concern the timing and pattern of psychosis.
