Bell tests do not prove that every physical property is created by looking, nor exclude nonlocal hidden-variable theories. Entanglement still cannot send a message faster than light. Either station's own list looks random. Choosing a different measurement at the other station does not change that local outcome distribution into readable information. The correlations emerge when the two lists are compared through an ordinary communication channel. Relativistic quantum information and no-signaling The unfinished part

sections.head: Gravity still needs a quantum account
sections.text: Special relativity and quantum mechanics already work together in quantum field theory. Researchers can also study quantum fields on an approximately classical curved spacetime. Neither achievement supplies a complete theory in which spacetime's geometry is itself quantum. Proposed approaches to that problem have not yielded an experimentally established successor to general relativity. Quantum gravity Hawking's calculation is an example of what the intermediate approach can do. Quantum fields on a black-hole background predict thermal radiation reaching distant observers. That prediction has not been directly observed from an astronomical black hole . Large black holes would be colder than today's cosmic microwave background, so they absorb more energy from that background than they emit through this process. Hawking's 1975 paper Extrapolating the radiation calculation suggests eventual evaporation in a sufficiently cold environment. The final stage is precisely where its approximation stops being dependable. We don't yet have an established answer for that endpoint. Webb's First Deep Field. Galaxies fill the image, with some distant galaxies stretched into arcs by the gravity of the foreground cluster. Bright objects with diffraction spikes are foreground stars. Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, and STScI (public domain). Image and observing details . What spacetime does when its own quantum effects become unavoidable remains an open experimental question. Sources

sections.head: Experiments, calculations and illustrations
sections.text: The diagrams are explanatory drawings, not measurements. Links beside the claims lead to the relevant experiments or explanations. The notes below identify the calculations behind the rounded numbers and the assumptions that matter for interpreting them. Source notes and calculations

sections.head: Light and clocks
sections.text: Vacuum light speed. NIST's exact value is 299,792,458 meters per second, about 670.6 million mph. Feynman, volume I, chapter 15 , develops frame comparisons, light clocks and time dilation. The light-clock SVG is schematic and has no specified velocity. Look-back times. Rounded NASA distances for the Moon , Sun and Proxima Centauri , and Andromeda supply the figure's estimates. Two feet divided by light speed gives about 2 nanoseconds for the hand example. The diagram uses an approximate logarithmic scale. GPS. Neil Ashby's 2003 review distinguishes proper time from the system's coordinate time and derives the nominal clock offset. The gain from gravity and loss from motion are rounded in Richard Pogge's university explanation . The post does not turn the clock offset into a universal daily position error. Muon lifetime. The 2024 Particle Data Group listing gives a mean rest lifetime of approximately 2.197 microseconds. Multiplying by light speed gives about 659 meters, or 720 yards. This is a characteristic length calculated from the mean, not a maximum range or a fixed decay deadline. Expansion. Davis and Lineweaver (2004) distinguish cosmological recession speeds, locally measured speeds and horizons. Superluminal recession does not by itself imply that a galaxy is unobservable. A measured height difference. Chou and colleagues (2010), Science 329, 1630 , compared aluminum-ion optical clocks over a noise-canceled fiber link. Raising one clock by 33 centimeters gave a fractional rate change consistent with g Δh / c 2 . Applying that approximation for 79 years gives about 90 nanoseconds, with the height difference held constant and Earth's near-surface conditions assumed. The lifetime extrapolation is also explained in the NIST release .

sections.head: Energy and gravity
sections.text: Energy accounting. Feynman, volume I, chapter 16 , gives the energy-momentum relation. For one gram, mc 2 is about 8.99 × 10 13 joules. Princeton's stellar-fusion notes describe the reaction chain and the tunneling barrier. The Sun's radiated mass-equivalent. The IAU's 2015 nominal solar luminosity , 3.828 × 10 26 watts, is a standard conversion value. Dividing by c 2 gives about 4.26 × 10 9 kilograms per second, or 4.7 million US short tons. It is an estimate of the mass-equivalent carried by sunlight, not an exact measurement of the Sun's changing luminosity or all of its mass loss. Proton mass. Yang and colleagues (2018) use lattice quantum chromodynamics and state their renormalization scheme and uncertainties for the mass decomposition. The post retains the qualitative result without presenting scheme-dependent fractions as universal pieces. Free fall. Einstein Online's equivalence-principle explanation distinguishes supported observers from freely falling ones. The globe SVG illustrates geodesics on a surface, not the equations of motion in spacetime. The 1919 eclipse. The Max Planck Society's historical account gives the expeditions, the 1.75-arcsecond prediction and the measurement uncertainties. ESA / Hubble identifies the Cosmic Horseshoe's lens and background galaxy. M87. The ESO / Event Horizon Telescope release explains the 2017 radio observations, 2019 publication, shadow, estimated mass and independent reconstruction checks. The displayed image is false-color radio imaging. GW150914. The original LIGO / Virgo paper defines strain as the differential arm-length change divided by the 4-kilometer arm length. Thus hL at a strain of 10 −21 is approximately 4 × 10 −18 meters. Its black-hole masses are waveform-based estimates, not exact counts. Calibration, environmental checks and time-shifted noise estimates enter the detection analysis.

sections.head: Quantum experiments and their interpretation
sections.text: Interference. Feynman, volume III, chapter 1 , distinguishes adding amplitudes from adding probabilities. Bach and colleagues (2013) used a low-intensity electron source, nanometer slits, a movable mask and individual detections to compare one- and two-slit patterns. Their experiment is not the source of this post's drawn dots, nor a which-path detector experiment. Large-molecule interference. Fein and colleagues (2019), full manuscript , studied molecules up to about 2,000 atoms with a three-grating interferometer. They scanned a grating and measured molecular flux, comparing fringe behavior with quantum and classical predictions. This is an example from 2019, not a claim about today's size record. Measurement and decoherence. The Stanford Encyclopedia's measurement entry describes the problem and alternative accounts. Schlosshauer's review distinguishes suppression of local interference from a physical collapse or selection of one outcome. Uncertainty and atoms. The Stanford Encyclopedia's uncertainty entry distinguishes the position-momentum standard-deviation relation from disturbance relations. Feynman, volume III, chapter 2 , estimates hydrogen's finite size from competing kinetic and potential energies. The sound SVG is a schematic Fourier analogy, with no measured sound data. Bell's theorem. The Stanford Encyclopedia entry lays out locality and measurement-independence assumptions. The singlet example in the main text is a pure state. More generally, a mixed state is entangled if it cannot be expressed as a mixture of product states . For the convention used here, S = E 00 + E 01 + E 10 − E 11 , where each E is the average product of the two ±1 outcomes at that setting pair. Equivalent sign conventions give the same bound. The Hensen experiment. Hensen and colleagues (2015) separated stations by 1,280 meters and used heralded entanglement, fast random setting choices and spin readout. The figure distinguishes the theoretical bounds from their measured S = 2.42 ± 0.20 . The paper's conservative null-model probability bound is 0.039; its assumptions and treatment of memory and imperfect randomness matter to that statement. No faster-than-light message. Peres and Terno (2004) explain why local quantum operations, with distant outcomes unread, leave the other station's marginal statistics unchanged under the stated relativistic locality conditions.

sections.head: The open problem
sections.text: Quantum gravity. The Stanford Encyclopedia overview distinguishes quantum fields on classical spacetime from a theory of quantum geometry and discusses the limits of current evidence. Hawking radiation. Hawking's full 1975 paper, Particle Creation by Black Holes , treats quantum fields on an approximately classical black-hole background. The linked copy is a mirror of the original paper. Its derivation is not evidence of radiation detected from an astronomical black hole, and its approximation does not establish the final evaporation stage. CERN's current experiment overview identifies black-hole Hawking radiation as still undetected. Cover image: the M87 black-hole image , Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration, CC BY 4.0 . Photographs and illustrations retain their individual credits. The seven SVG diagrams were drawn in code for this post.

posts.title: Star Signs, X-Rayed
posts.desc: Try an approximate birth chart, compare signs and house systems, and see what a generic personality reading and a blinded astrology test can actually establish.

sections.head: Star Signs, X-Rayed
sections.text: A birth chart can locate Jupiter without telling you whether you're lucky. Try the calculations, compare their conventions, and see what happens when a reading ignores your birthday. 3 min main read / Optional chart and source details When were you born? Read me How accurate is that about you? This custom paragraph illustrates the Forer, or Barnum, effect. In Forer's 1949 paper , 39 students completed a test and then received identical, individually named sketches containing 13 statements, drawn largely from an astrology book. Their sketch ratings averaged 4.26 on a scale from 0 to 5. That demonstrates the weakness of personal recognition as a test of accuracy; it doesn't by itself test natal astrology. See the birth chart The chart

sections.head: Positions, then interpretations
sections.text: Enter a Gregorian date from 1900 through 2099. The wheel estimates positions as seen from Earth's center. Open a body row for sample astrological keywords and a historical note. House comparison Houses divide the chart relative to the horizon. Whole sign uses the entire rising sign as house one; Equal starts at the rising degree. Both have ancient precedents . Placidus divides daily motion by time and was popularized in the seventeenth century . Highlighted entries change house when the rule changes. What this calculator assumes An ephemeris gives celestial positions over time. This one uses Paul Schlyter's simplified formulae . They omit corrections such as the travel time of light and small changes in Earth's orientation. Whole-degree readouts suit a demonstration; they don't certify which side of a boundary a planet occupies. All body positions here are geocentric , viewed from Earth's center. In particular, the Moon's position from a specific place on Earth's surface can differ. The rising sign, or Ascendant, is the point of the ecliptic on the eastern horizon. An incorrect birth time or UTC offset can substantially change it. City presets supply rounded coordinates and modern standard-time offsets. They don't look up daylight saving or historical time zones. Check the offset in force at birth. Unknown-time mode uses local noon, samples positions across that calendar date, and hides the Ascendant and houses. Sampling can flag changing signs; it cannot recover the birth instant. Placidus becomes problematic near the polar circles. This implementation uses Equal above 66 degrees north or south, or if its iterative calculation fails to converge, and labels that substitution. Its house assignments use ecliptic longitude alone. They are an illustration of the conventions, not a full astrological house-position calculation. The Swiss Ephemeris manual describes the more complete calculations. Signs and the sky

sections.head: Three labels for the Sun
sections.text: In the tropical zodiac, Aries begins at the March equinox and each sign spans 30 degrees of the ecliptic , the Sun's apparent annual path. Sidereal zodiacs also use equal signs, with a starting point tied to the stars. Their chosen offsets differ. The panel uses an approximate Fagan-Bradley offset, about 25 degrees today, rather than treating one sidereal convention as the uniquely correct sky. Astronomical constellations are unequal regions. Under the IAU boundaries , the Sun's path crosses thirteen, including Ophiuchus . The panel's constellation label is only a fixed modern month-and-day guide. It ignores the entered year and time, so it cannot establish your birth constellation near an entry date. Precession, the slow change in Earth's axis direction, shifts the equinox against the stars. That doesn't make a tropical astrologer's chart an accidentally outdated star map: the seasonal starting point is deliberate, and Ptolemy explicitly favored it . The fair question is whether the chosen coordinates predict something about a person. The interpretations changed too. Ptolemy's Tetrabiblos , written in the second century CE, records planetary rulerships and qualities such as heat and moisture. It isn't the source of every modern description of an Aries or a Gemini. The panel labels its personality words as sample modern shorthand and keeps the historical records separate. How the chart acquired its layers Late fifth century BCE Equal signs in Babylonia The uniform zodiac made calculation easier by dividing the celestial band into twelve equal parts. Its structure parallels a schematic year of twelve 30-day months. Historian John Steele traces it through astronomical and astrological tablets. Earlier constellation lists were a different system; the equal zodiac didn't simply shrink them to twelve. Second century CE An influential Greek synthesis Ptolemy, Book I , presents the Sun as heating and drying, Mars as excessively drying, and Jupiter as temperate. His explanations belong to an ancient physical theory. He also records inherited rulerships, rather than supplying a date when each present-day personality trait was invented. 1781 / 1846 / 1930 New bodies enter the chart The discoveries of Uranus , Neptune , and Pluto gave later astrologers new objects to interpret. Their assigned meanings developed after discovery. Those dates are astronomical milestones, not moments when astrologers unanimously settled a meaning. 1930s Horoscopes become a mass-market column R. H. Naylor's feature on Princess Margaret appeared in the Sunday Express on August 24, 1930. Historian Nicholas Campion describes the move from birth-date forecasts toward familiar Sun-sign profiles. Astrology and published forecasts already existed; this was a change in audience and format. 1928 / 1930 Astronomers standardize constellation boundaries The IAU approved Eugène Delporte's boundaries in 1928; they were published in 1930. They formalized regions for naming astronomical objects. They didn't move the Sun, add a new star pattern, or suddenly make tropical signs stop matching constellations. Testing the prediction

sections.head: Can a chart identify its person?
sections.text: A full natal chart uses more information than a newspaper Sun sign. Testing only twelve birthday labels wouldn't fairly test that stronger claim. A useful experiment gives astrologers complete charts, hides identifying clues, and asks them to distinguish the people those charts describe. In Shawn Carlson's 1985 experiment , astrologers helped design a blinded matching task. Each chart came with three California Personality Inventory profiles, one belonging to its subject. They expected at least 50 percent correct first choices. The result was 40 of 116, about 34 percent, close to the one-third chance rate. That result counts against their claim under those conditions. It doesn't test every kind of astrology, and a personality inventory doesn't capture an entire life. Carlson also declined to draw a negative conclusion from the study's separate self-recognition test: participants had trouble identifying their own inventory profiles, which undermined that method. The opening reading demonstrates another problem. A description can feel accurate while failing to distinguish you from anyone else. A conversation prompted by a horoscope may still be useful to its reader, but that usefulness doesn't establish that the planets supplied the information. How did the matching test hide clues? blinded Names were replaced with codes. Charts omitted explicit birth dates and places, and competing inventory profiles were matched by sex. Advising astrologers approved the inventory as covering relevant traits. See the original paper's experimental design and double-blind procedures, pages 420 to 423. What limits remain? scope The task used selected practitioners, a specific questionnaire, and the charts that were returned. Fewer participants completed the work than planned. It tests chart-to-profile matching without a consultation, so a claim about a different practice needs its own test. The limit doesn't turn this result into evidence that the matching claim worked.

sections.head: Keep the calculation with its limits
sections.text: The copied summary includes the date, time assumption, and approximate signs you entered here. It makes no personality forecast. A more accurate ephemeris could improve those positions; showing that they predict your character would still require a separate experiment. Copy chart summary Sources and calculation notes Forer (1949) , pages 120 to 121 and Table 1. The displayed paragraph is a custom example, not his original sketch. Carlson (1985) , Nature 318, pages 419 to 425, especially Table 2 and the conclusions separating the two tests. Steele (2018) , sections 2 to 5, on Babylonian constellations, equal signs, and their changing names. Ptolemy, Tetrabiblos , Book I , translated by F. E. Robbins: chapters 4 to 5 on planetary qualities, 17 on rulerships, and 22 on the seasonal zodiac. Campion (2004) , chapter 7, pages 142 to 145, on the development of newspaper forecasts. IAU constellation history and charts ; NASA/JPL's constellation guide , page 71. The calendar guide here is approximate and isn't a boundary calculation. Schlyter's formulae ; Swiss Ephemeris manual ; Fagan-Bradley reference epoch . The panel's linear sidereal offset uses about 24.7403 degrees at J2000. James Holden on ancient house division , pages 21 to 22; Deborah Houlding on Placidus . Historical interpretations are contested, particularly when reconstructing ancient practice.

posts.title: Sure Things, Open Questions
posts.desc: Eighteen questions, from dark matter and quantum measurement to bicycles and machine learning, with the evidence, mechanisms and limits beside each image.

sections.text: A riderless bicycle can recover from a lean. Equations predict which designs will do it; finding a short physical rule that covers every stable design is harder. Other questions are different. Dark matter's identity is unresolved. Gödel's incompleteness is a proved limit within specified formal systems. These eighteen entries put each question beside what the evidence supports. The captions identify telescope reconstructions, scans, paintings and photographs. I

sections.head: The cosmos
sections.text: Mass, expansion and the early universe. Radio image of M87* reconstructed from 2017 observations and released in 2019. The bright ring surrounds a dark shadow, not a directly photographed event horizon. Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration, CC BY 4.0 . No. 01 · Gravity

sections.head: How does gravity fit with quantum mechanics?
sections.text: General relativity describes gravity through the curvature of spacetime. It predicts how light travels around a black hole, and the reconstructed M87 image agrees within the observations' limits. This black hole is about 55 million light-years away. The unfinished work is a theory reliable when gravity and quantum effects both become strong, as they may near a black hole's center. The image tests gravity in one regime; it doesn't settle every regime. Sources: EHT analysis (2019) ; Quantum gravity at low energies (2022) . Bullet Cluster composite: pink is hot gas detected in X-rays; orange and white are galaxies; blue is mass inferred from gravitational lensing. NASA/CXC, NASA/STScI, ESO and Magellan, public domain . No. 02 · Dark Matter

sections.head: What is dark matter made of?
sections.text: The Bullet Cluster's hot gas slowed during a collision. The galaxies largely passed through. Astronomers used distortions in more distant galaxies to map the gravitational mass, which stayed mostly with the galaxies. Since the gas holds most of the ordinary matter, that separation is strong evidence for another mass component. The blue patches show an inference from lensing. The measurement constrains dark matter's behavior without identifying what it is. Sources: Bullet Cluster analysis (2006) . Hubble eXtreme Deep Field, assembled from many exposures. Nearly every speck is a galaxy. This is a deep view of the sky, not a map of dark energy. NASA, ESA and the HUDF09 team, public domain . No. 03 · Dark Energy

sections.head: What is accelerating the expansion?
sections.text: In the late 1990s, teams compared the brightness and redshift of distant exploding stars. The results indicated accelerating expansion. A cosmological constant, an energy density of empty space that stays constant as space expands, fits a broad range of observations. In the standard cosmological model, dark energy accounts for roughly two-thirds of the total energy density. Its physical origin remains unsettled. Galaxies held together by gravity aren't being blown apart. Sources: Supernova measurements (1999) ; Planck cosmological parameters (2018) . WMAP's nine-year map of microwave-background temperature variations. Colors show small departures from the average after foreground emission was removed. NASA/WMAP Science Team, public domain . No. 04 · The Big Bang

sections.head: What happened before the hot Big Bang?
sections.text: The microwave background reached us from an era when the expanding universe cooled enough to become transparent. Its temperature variations help reconstruct a hot, dense early history. Combining WMAP with other observations gave an age of about 13.8 billion years within the fitted cosmological model. That history doesn't establish an absolute first instant. A theory of the early universe still has to explain whether there was an earlier stage, and whether asking what came before has a physical meaning. Sources: WMAP cosmological analysis (2013) . Aurora australis photographed from the International Space Station in 2010. An illustration of atmospheric light from charged particles, not the 1991 cosmic-ray event. NASA, public domain . No. 05 · Cosmic Rays

sections.head: Where do the highest-energy cosmic rays come from?
sections.text: On October 15, 1991, the Fly's Eye detector recorded an air shower produced by a cosmic ray. Researchers reconstructed an energy of about 51 joules, roughly a thrown baseball's kinetic energy, in one incoming particle. The uncertainty was about 15 joules; the particle wasn't identified as a proton. Its source was unresolved. Magnetic fields can deflect charged particles, while interactions during their journey limit how far they can travel. Sources: Fly's Eye event analysis (1995) . II

sections.head: The physical world
sections.text: Clocks, materials and moving air. A strontium atomic clock photographed in 2017. The 2025 aluminum-ion result discussed here came from a different instrument. G.E. Marti/JILA (NIST), public domain . No. 06 · Time

sections.head: Why does time have a direction?
sections.text: A 2025 aluminum-ion clock reported a fractional systematic uncertainty of 5.5 × 10 -19 . That is an uncertainty in its rate, not evidence that the instrument will run for billions of years. Relativity predicts how clock rates change with gravity. The thermodynamic arrow of time concerns entropy, which tends to increase in isolated systems. Why the early universe had the special low-entropy condition that makes this direction possible remains an open cosmological question. Sources: Aluminum-ion clock measurements (2025) ; The low-entropy problem (2004) . Colors from interference in a soap film, a classical wave effect used here as an illustration. Dietmar Rabich, CC BY-SA 4.0 . No. 07 · Quantum Mechanics

sections.head: Why does a quantum measurement give one outcome?
sections.text: Quantum theory predicts measurement probabilities with extraordinary success. When a system interacts with a detector and its surroundings, their states become entangled. This suppresses observable interference between alternatives, helping explain everyday classical behavior. It is called decoherence. How that account relates to the single outcome recorded in an experiment is the measurement problem. Interpretations and proposed modifications answer it differently. A person consciously looking at the apparatus isn't required for decoherence. Sources: Decoherence and the measurement problem (2005) . The Starry Night (1889), oil on canvas. The swirls have invited comparisons with fluid turbulence. Vincent van Gogh, public domain . No. 08 · Turbulence

sections.head: Can a smooth fluid flow become singular?
sections.text: The Navier-Stokes equations describe velocity and pressure in a fluid with viscosity. They support useful calculations of turbulence, although resolving every small eddy can be prohibitively expensive. A mathematical problem remains open: in a three-dimensional incompressible fluid, do smooth initial conditions always yield a smooth solution, or can a singularity develop? Researchers have compared brightness patterns in The Starry Night with turbulent scaling laws. Those patterns provide no measurement of an actual fluid's velocity. Sources: The mathematical problem ; Painting luminance analysis (2024) . The north rose window of Notre-Dame, photographed in 2010. This image is a panorama stitched from two frames. Julie Anne Workman, CC BY-SA 3.0 . No. 09 · Glass

sections.head: What makes a liquid slow down into glass?
sections.text: Glass is an amorphous solid: its atoms lack a crystal's repeating order, yet it resists deformation on ordinary timescales. As a glass-forming liquid cools, rearrangements become so slow that the structure falls out of equilibrium. That accounts for its solidity. The harder question is what drives the enormous slowdown, and whether a hidden equilibrium transition underlies it. Competing accounts emphasize different features of the structure and motion. Sources: The glass-transition problem (2013) . A magnet levitating above a cooled copper-oxide superconductor. Magnetic screening and flux pinning help support it. Julien Bobroff and Frédéric Bouquet, LPS Orsay, CC BY-SA 3.0 . No. 10 · Superconductivity

sections.head: What pairs electrons in warmer superconductors?
sections.text: In conventional superconductors, crystal-lattice vibrations produce an effective attraction between electrons. Their pairs form a collective state with zero electrical resistance. The 1957 BCS theory explains this mechanism. Copper-oxide superconductors also form pairs, but their detailed pairing mechanism remains debated. A 2025 calculation reproduced important pressure and layer trends using electronic interactions. It used approximations and omitted lattice vibrations, so it doesn't close the question for every material. Sources: BCS theory (1957) ; Cuprate calculations (2025) . Cloud-to-cloud lightning over Albury, Australia. Thennicke, CC BY-SA 4.0 . No. 11 · Lightning

sections.head: What starts the first discharge inside a cloud?
sections.text: A thunderstorm separates electric charge. Lightning discharges some of it through conducting channels in the air. Radio observations have traced rapid positive electrical breakdown at the start of some flashes. Connecting that first activity to cloud conditions is difficult: measured large-scale fields often seem too weak to start ordinary air breakdown. Models involve local field enhancement, ice and water particles, or energetic electrons. Researchers are testing how these processes work together. Sources: Lightning initiation observations (2016) ; Lightning modeling roadmap (2025) . III

sections.head: The living world
sections.text: Experience, navigation and relief. Ramón y Cajal's drawing of a rabbit hippocampal neuron, published in 1904. Wellcome Collection, CC BY 4.0 . No. 12 · Consciousness

sections.head: Why does brain activity feel like anything?
sections.text: In 2011, researchers reconstructed rough versions of movies watched by three participants. They trained a separate model for each person, measured brain activity with fMRI, and built reconstructions using an outside video library. This was constrained visual decoding. Whether explaining perceptual functions also explains subjective experience is disputed. Chalmers's hard problem names that philosophical challenge; it isn't an experimentally established limit on neuroscience. Sources: Movie reconstruction methods (2011) ; Chalmers's argument (1995) . European robin, photographed in Switzerland in 2022. C-M, CC BY-SA 4.0 . No. 13 · Animal Compass

sections.head: How does a bird's magnetic compass send a signal?
sections.text: Migrating robins can orient using Earth's magnetic field. A candidate sensor is cryptochrome, a light-sensitive protein whose reactions involve electron pairs. In 2021, purified robin Cry4 showed magnetic effects on those reactions. The laboratory fields were much stronger than Earth's; simulations explored the requirements at natural field strengths. Establishing how the protein functions in a living bird, including how it sends a signal to nerves, requires further evidence. Sources: Cryptochrome experiments (2021) . Pills used as an illustration. These are not the placebo pills from the IBS trial. Hal Gatewood/Unsplash . No. 14 · The Placebo Effect

sections.head: How much relief can a treatment ritual produce?
sections.text: In a trial, 80 people with irritable bowel syndrome received openly labeled placebo pills or no pills, with similar clinician contact. After three weeks, 59% of the placebo group reported adequate relief over the preceding week, compared with 35% of controls. Patients knew their assignment and reported their symptoms; this small, short trial didn't establish a cure. Some placebo analgesia has known mechanisms involving the brain's opioid system. Open questions include how expectations, prior learning and clinical care contribute to particular outcomes. Sources: Open-label IBS trial (2010) ; Opioid-system measurements (2005) . IV

sections.head: The edge of reason
sections.text: Balance, evidence, proof and learned computation. A high-wheel bicycle in a 1920 press photograph, not the experimental vehicle in the 2011 study. Agence Meurisse/BnF, public domain . No. 15 · The Bicycle

sections.head: What makes a bicycle self-stable?
sections.text: A leaning bicycle can steer into its fall and recover. Models predict stability from its mass distribution and geometry. In 2011, researchers built a riderless bicycle that recovered after they canceled the wheels' gyroscopic effects and gave it negative trail, reversing the usual caster geometry. The experiment ruled out two popular ingredients as necessary for self-stability. The remaining difficulty was a simple physical criterion covering all stable designs. The bicycle's mechanics were understood well enough to design the experiment. Sources: Self-stability model and experiment (2011) . An unknown artist's wood engraving, published in Camille Flammarion's L'atmosphère in 1888. Public domain . No. 16 · Reality

sections.head: Can observation rule out a perfect deception?
sections.text: Descartes imagined a deceiver supplying false impressions of an external world. A modern version could be a simulation stipulated to reproduce every possible observation. If the alternative gives exactly the same evidence, observation cannot distinguish it. That limit is built into the thought experiment. Particular simulation proposals can be tested if they predict detectable differences. Radical skepticism questions absolute certainty; it supplies no positive evidence that the ordinary world is a deception. Sources: Descartes, First Meditation (1641) . An ouroboros engraving by Lucas Jennis (1625), used here to illustrate self-reference. Public domain . No. 17 · The Limits of Proof

sections.head: Can one formal system prove every arithmetic truth?
sections.text: A consistent formal system that includes basic whole-number arithmetic and whose axioms a computer program can list cannot settle every arithmetic statement. The incompleteness theorems establish that some statements can be neither proved nor disproved within that system. This is a demonstrated limit under specified conditions. A statement may become provable in a stronger system, which has its own limits if it meets the same conditions. Gödel didn't show that particular truths must remain beyond every possible proof. Sources: Gödel's original paper in translation ; Gödel-Rosser proof and conditions . Brain fiber tracts inferred from diffusion MRI. This rendering illustrates biological anatomy, not the workings of an artificial neural network. Thomas Schultz, CC BY-SA 3.0 . No. 18 · The Machine

sections.head: How does a trained network reach a particular answer?
sections.text: People choose a neural network's architecture, training data and objectives, and write its training code. Training adjusts its numerical weights through optimization. Those operations are understood; explaining a large trained network's individual answers is harder. Researchers have extracted interpretable features from a language model and changed its behavior by manipulating some of them. The work examined activations at one middle layer, with substantial reconstruction error and incomplete coverage. An AI helped draft this page and gather its images. Its fluency supplied no guarantee that its claims were right. Sources: Training and backpropagation ; Interpretable features and their limits (2024) . For the AI that helped write this page, one question is especially practical: can we trace an answer through the trained network well enough to explain why it produced a confident mistake?
