sections.head: Water machines: progress
sections.text: Updated October 9, 2026. Air pressure now appears inside the sealed pockets. Gold means pressure above the room, rose means below; the small labels show the difference in psi. Room air and water stay clear. Use Air pressure beside the flow readout to hide or restore it. Water pressure remains available in Instruments. Slow motion now keeps the water moving. At low speeds, the engine was discarding the partial steps it needed to advance. The fix restores movement in all three machines and turns off when you return to an ordinary scene. Normal-speed particle and render comparisons match exactly across three speeds and three seeds; smoke also matches. Slow-motion checks and comparison records. The performance revision remains private. It shortens the GPU queue and keeps the simulation advancing while you drag a slime, but a full cup run drains 94.47% of its estimated drainable water, below the existing 95% target. It averages about 56 updates per second in that run. Better responsiveness alone does not pass the cup test, and steady 60 FPS and phone performance remain unproved. A private water-step revision passes all nine cup drainage and hold tests. On three seeds, it delivers 100.5%, 100.4% and 96.8% of the initially estimated drainable amount, with no rim spills and no lost particles. The first two also drain some water below that estimate. A version that reduces the work in crowded water matches the short tests, but its longer trials deliver 100.7%, 99.6% and 93.7%. The last misses the 95% target. Its two playback trials average 45.4 and 53 FPS. Both revisions remain experimental. The released timing fix changes slow motion; these particle revisions have not shipped. Cup checks, ordering tests and frame measurements. One six-second Retina browser check records 59 to 60 FPS for the fountain and siphon, and 35 to 60 for the cup. These short runs do not establish steady 60 FPS or phone performance. The default particle and pressure buffer hashes match the prior release in three scenes, on three seeds, at three checkpoints. Air-view checks and native comparisons. The pressure image and apparatus labels are reused between measurement samples. Paused scenes get an initial sample, and pressure controls update the picture while paused. A further boundary cache reduced CPU work, but paired browser runs did not get faster, so that change stays out of the release. A trial gas equation and vapor boundary pass 90 behavior and accounting checks across fifteen fountain runs, with no negative-volume events. Small pockets still lose stored gas, and pressure and air-boundary errors remain. A smaller GPU test now reproduces one cause: relabeling a cell as water can discard its gas while more than half its accessible space remains empty. Cavity trial and remaining limits. A private fix retains that gas in eighteen small-pocket tests. In 96 further checks, its pressure, water flow and gas volume agree with an independent calculation. These tests prescribe the water entering one pocket; they do not establish natural bubble motion. Larger pockets, the reverse classification change and the shape of the water/air boundary still need work, so the fix stays out of the published scenes. Small-pocket checks and limits. A second test gives the same water and air volumes two different cell labels. The old rule changed the calculated water inertia with the label. A private revision uses the known shape of that water instead; all 96 paired GPU comparisons give identical pressure, motion and gas volume. The test still prescribes the water's shape. Pressure…

sections.head: Three engines, one box
sections.text: The water flows around the same walls that hold the gel and deflect the smoke. Draw a wall and all three simulations see it. These are the engines from Sluice , my mining game, with the slime creatures reduced to their squishy material.

sections.head: Pipes and trapped air
sections.text: The cup uses the existing water particles. Drop the slime into the upper vessel and watch the lower tank fill. Instruments shows measured head, flow and sample age; pressure readings remain diagnostic. Greedy cup The low inlet leads up over a bend and down through the cup’s base. Below the bend, the cup holds its water. A rising level can flood that route and start a siphon, which drains until the inlet admits air. The University of Maryland’s apparatus shows the tube inside the central shaft. How the simulation works Water Particles carry the liquid. A temporary grid exchanges their momentum and applies pressure, then sends them on their way. The MLS-MPM solver runs on WebGPU, adapted from saharan’s water demo . Air Machine mode adds a pressure solve while keeping the water particles. Room air sets zero gauge pressure. Each connected sealed pocket has one pressure at a fixed temperature, and compresses as water takes its space. Aanjaneya, Patkar and Fedkiw’s bubble model describes this uniform, isothermal approximation. Room pressure and sound speed are scaled for this toy; Instruments lists their current values. A pressure floor limits the modeled drop below room pressure, and column separation is still being tested. Airflow within a pocket, heat transfer and dissolved gas are omitted. Smoke A WebGL fluid solver moves velocity and dye through a grid, following Pavel Dobryakov’s work . The visible smoke is dye in that flow. Slime A mesh of elastic connections holds its volume while stretching and compressing. Sluice’s current material, skin contacts, and spring grip use XPBD on the CPU. Highlights attach to the deforming mesh. There are no creature brains or eyes here. The instrument scale makes the box 30 inches wide and 1 inch deep. Its clock converts simulation time to seconds using Earth gravity. The energy display includes sampled water motion, height, pressure compression and available air work; its remainder includes numerical losses and sample error. Work done by a slime is not yet measured. This is a game simulation tuned for interaction. The water, smoke, and gel exchange approximate boundary motion; they aren’t one unified physical solver. Water needs WebGPU. Smoke needs WebGL. If either is unavailable, the other materials still work. The simulation pauses when you leave the tab or scroll it out of view. posts.title: The Zhuangzi
posts.desc: A cook finds room for his knife; a useless tree survives the axe. The Zhuangzi asks how to live without making your judgments the measure of everything.

sections.text: 01 Summary

sections.head: The Zhuangzi, in plain English
sections.text: A tree survives because nobody can make anything out of it. Its wood is crooked, so the carpenters leave it alone. In the Zhuangzi, something everyone calls a failure turns out to have a life of its own. The book keeps asking who gets to decide what a thing is for, and what happens to it once they do. It asks the same question about people. A ruler wants useful subjects. A teacher wants good students. You want to be a certain kind of person, and you judge each day by whether you’re becoming one. Those expectations can help you live, or make you spend your life defending a picture of yourself. Zhuangzi is especially interested in the moment when a useful judgment hardens into a demand that everything obey it. Chapter 2 describes a mind wearing itself out over what to accept and what to reject. We learn distinctions and use them to settle new questions. The way things look to us begins to feel like the way things simply are. Winning an argument may convince the people who already share your standards; the chapter asks who could settle it for everyone else. The book gives this problem to animals as well as philosophers. A small bird laughs at the enormous Peng, which needs a vast wind to carry it south. The small bird can reach the next branch. Its experience cannot account for Peng’s life. Peng has limits too: without enough wind, it cannot fly. Seeing farther doesn’t make it independent of the world. The chapter keeps looking for a freedom that won’t collapse when praise, success, or favorable conditions disappear. Dao , also spelled Tao, means a way or course. Here it can name a way of doing something and the larger course of things happening and changing. Zhuangzi turns disputes over which way to follow toward the question of how well someone can respond to what is in front of them. Cook Ding has learned an ox’s structure so thoroughly that his knife moves through its openings. When he reaches a difficult place, he becomes cautious. His skill includes knowing when ease has ended. In chapter 4, Yan Hui wants to advise a violent ruler. The imagined Confucius warns that arriving full of righteous plans could get him killed. He tells Yan Hui to fast his mind: loosen the judgments that make him hear only what he already expects. Yan Hui still has to notice whether the ruler will listen, whether speech is possible, and when to stop. Good intentions do not give him control over the other person. The freedom the book calls wandering involves moving through such situations without fastening your whole life to one outcome. Its people still cook, talk, teach, and care for others. What changes is their dependence on being recognized as right, useful, successful, or complete. Chapter 5 gives authority to people with amputated feet and appearances others despise. Those who meet them discover a steadiness their judgments about bodies had hidden. A person’s capacity to sustain a life need not match their rank or appearance. The hardest case is your own body. It changes, gets sick, and dies. In chapter 6, an ill man imagines his arm becoming a rooster: then he could use it to announce the dawn. If the process that gave you this body changes it, can you meet the change without insisting that you must always remain this particular person? Elsewhere Zhuangzi sings after his wife’s death. He says he grieved at first, then considered her death within the changes that had brought her into life. It offers no evidence that she is still conscious somewhere. The butterfly dream brings the uncertainty home. While dreaming, Zhuang Zhou is a butterfly and knows…

sections.head: Where the ideas come from
sections.text: Open a story to follow its argument. Chapter links lead to the text.

sections.head: 01 The bird that needs the wind Chapter 1
sections.text: Kun, an immense fish, becomes Peng, an immense bird. Smaller creatures laugh at its journey because they can’t imagine needing to go so far. Peng still needs deep enough air, just as a large boat needs deep water. The chapter then considers people who seem freer than most. One is unmoved by public praise and blame. Another can ride the wind. Even the wind-rider still needs something to ride. The question becomes how to live when those conditions change. Read chapter 1.

sections.head: 02 Useful to whom? Chapters 1, 4, and 20
sections.text: Hui Shi complains that a huge, crooked tree is useless. Zhuangzi suggests resting beneath it. Its failure as timber makes that possible. In chapter 4, another tree explains the fate of its useful neighbors: their fruit and wood invite people to damage them. Calling something useful usually means useful to someone who wants to take something from it. Chapter 20 complicates the lesson. A useless tree survives, but a goose that cannot sound an alarm is chosen for dinner. A disciple asks which example they should follow. The reply warns against occupying a fixed position between usefulness and uselessness, too. No label reliably tells you how to survive the next situation. Read the tree and goose together.

sections.head: 03 The mind that has to be right Chapter 2
sections.text: The chapter first shows judgment as a form of strain. The mind shoots out like a weapon to decide a question, then clings to its decision. The description makes certainty feel costly before the argument asks whether it is justified. Shi and fei can distinguish this from not-this, affirmation from denial, and right from wrong. A thing is “this” from here and “that” from there. In disputes, each party likewise treats its own starting point as decisive. The image of the pivot of the Dao offers a way to respond without being trapped on one side of that opposition. How far this goes is disputed: it can suggest openness to changing perspectives, or a deeper unity behind them. Neither reading makes every decision disappear. Read chapter 2.

sections.head: 04 The butterfly and the waking man Chapter 2, the ending
sections.text: In the dream, the butterfly is content. It has no thought of being Zhou. Waking replaces that certainty with another one, but Zhou can now ask a question the butterfly never asked: which experience gives him the final account of who he is? Between a man and a butterfly there is necessarily a barrier. The transition is called Metempsychosis. Herbert Giles, 1889, chapter 2 That last word imports the idea of a soul passing between bodies. Robert Eno instead ends: “this is what we call the transformation of things!” Both versions preserve a distinction between Zhou and the butterfly. A reading that says everything is an illusion has to explain why the passage insists on that distinction. Lu Zhi, Zhuangzi Dreaming of a Butterfly , Ming dynasty. Asian Art Museum, San Francisco. Public domain.

sections.head: 05 Cook Ding knows when to slow down Chapter 3
sections.text: Cook Ding’s knife has lasted nineteen years. He follows the spaces in the ox rather than hacking through bones. The lord watching him hears advice about caring for life in those movements. What I love is the Course, going beyond mere skill. Brook Ziporyn, The Complete Writings , chapter 3 The difficult joint matters as much as the graceful cutting. He attends closely and slows down. Watson’s version makes the change explicit: “whenever I come to a complicated place” he will “work very slowly.” Experience lets him respond to resistance, including resistance that interrupts his usual ease. Read Watson’s complete story.

sections.head: 06 Empty enough to hear someone Chapters 4 and 6
sections.text: Yan Hui wants to reform a ruler whose violence is killing his subjects. Confucius warns that displaying his own goodness against the ruler’s wickedness may inflame the danger. Yan Hui keeps proposing approaches; Confucius keeps finding what they assume in advance. Fasting the mind asks him to receive the encounter without making those assumptions its conditions. The Chinese xin , often translated “heart-mind,” includes feeling, judgment, and the direction of action. Emptying it need not mean ceasing to think. On Chris Fraser’s reading, fixed aims and expectations give way to attention that can respond to the situation. Chapter 6 goes further with “sitting in forgetfulness,” where Yan Hui describes letting go of bodily and intellectual distinctions. These passages do not supply a step-by-step meditation method. Read Yan Hui’s dangerous assignment.

sections.head: 07 The people others dismiss Chapter 5
sections.text: Wang Tai has lost a foot, yet attracts followers to rival Confucius. Another amputee, Shentu Jia, challenges an official who carries his rank into the place where they study. The official sees a punishment and assumes it tells him who the person is. The chapter also describes Ai Tai Tuo, whose appearance initially repels people. Those who remain with him come to trust him. The term de , translated as virtue, power, or potency, concerns the capacity these people have despite the marks others judge them by. Their bodies aren’t repaired to earn them a place in the story. Read chapter 5.

sections.head: 08 A life that cannot keep its shape Chapters 6 and 18
sections.text: Chapter 6 describes friends who can face bodily change without treating it as an insult. One imagines his arm becoming a rooster or a crossbow. Another dying man compares himself to metal in a great foundry. Metal that insisted on becoming one particular sword would be troublesome material; why insist that transformation must keep producing him as a human? In chapter 18, Hui Shi finds Zhuangzi singing and beating a vessel after his wife dies. He objects on behalf of their shared life. Zhuangzi answers that he did feel grief, then thought back through the changes preceding her birth and forward into death. The account redirects his mourning; it cannot establish what happens after death. It also leaves Hui Shi’s objection worth hearing: does this response give enough weight to the particular person who has been lost? Read their exchange.

sections.head: 09 Hui Shi has a point about the fish Chapter 17
sections.text: On a bridge, Zhuangzi remarks on the fishes’ enjoyment. Hui Shi asks how someone who isn’t a fish can know it. Zhuangzi asks how Hui Shi, who isn’t Zhuangzi, can know what Zhuangzi knows. Hui Shi accepts the symmetry and presses his argument: their difference is exactly why Zhuangzi cannot know the fish. Zhuangzi’s final reply turns the question toward the place he knows it from: here, above the river. It can be read as wordplay, an evasion, or an appeal to knowledge available through a shared situation. It does not logically dispose of Hui Shi’s objection. The scene lets the reader feel the difference between enjoying what is happening and demanding a justification for that enjoyment. Read the end of chapter 17.

sections.head: 10 The help that kills its recipient Chapter 7, the ending
sections.text: Hundun, whose name evokes undivided chaos, is a generous host. Two rulers decide to repay him. People have seven openings for seeing, hearing, eating, and breathing. Hundun has none, so they set about correcting him. ... but on the seventh day Hun Tun died. Herbert Giles, 1889, chapter 7 The preceding passage compares the mind to a mirror, responding to what arrives without holding on to it. Hundun’s friends do the opposite: they bring a settled idea of what he should be. Their kindness makes the story more troubling. They have no wish to hurt him, and still cannot recognize that their improvement is destroying their host. 03 Context

sections.head: A name, several authors
sections.text: Zhuangzi means Master Zhuang. Zhuang Zhou probably lived in the late fourth century BCE, during China’s Warring States period. Almost no biographical details can be independently confirmed. Stories in which he refuses office or faces death are literary scenes, rather than verified episodes from his life. The received work has seven Inner, fifteen Outer, and eleven Miscellaneous chapters. The Inner Chapters are traditionally associated with Zhuang Zhou, but even their authorship and unity remain disputed.

sections.head: An edited inheritance
sections.text: The surviving edition comes through Guo Xiang, a commentator who died in 312 CE. He reports reducing a 52-chapter collection to 33. The whole collection he worked from is lost, so his editorial decisions cannot all be checked. Zhuangzi and the Tao Te Ching later became foundational works of Daoism. That pairing does not establish that Zhuang Zhou was Laozi’s student. This page focuses on the Inner Chapters, with later stories identified by chapter.

sections.head: What remains difficult
sections.text: Recognizing the limits of your judgments can make you less cruel and more attentive. It does not automatically tell you when to resist someone. Yan Hui’s ruler is harming people. Advice that helps Yan Hui survive the encounter may leave those people unprotected. The Zhuangzi offers searching accounts of personal freedom; it gives a reader less guidance on building institutions that restrain violent power. Its treatment of death creates another tension. Cook Ding teaches how to preserve a life. The dying figures ask how to accept losing one. Care for life might include recognizing its limits, but these are different demands. Singing after a death may express acceptance; for someone still mourning, it may sound like a refusal to acknowledge the loss. Nor is every extraordinary person in these pages an attainable model. Some are described as immune to fire or able to ride clouds. Whether those figures depict spiritual realization, provoke us to imagine another way of living, or parody claims to perfect wisdom remains part of the disagreement over how to read it. Sources, translations, and the limits of this reading The received text. The Chinese Text Project provides the Chinese with James Legge’s translation. References here use received chapter numbers. Stories are paraphrased unless marked as quotations. The Inner Chapters. Robert Eno’s translation and notes , Indiana University, 2019. The butterfly’s closing sentence quoted here comes from chapter 2. Cook Ding. Brook Ziporyn, Zhuangzi: The Complete Writings , 2020, chapter 3, supplies the short Course quotation. The caution and slowing are checked against Burton Watson’s translation , reproduced by Columbia’s Asia for Educators. The older wording. Herbert Giles, Chuang Tzŭ , 1889, chapters 2 and 7. Giles’s explanatory commentary, including his claims about souls and God, is not treated as the Chinese text. History and rival readings. Chad Hansen’s Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry explains the uncertain authorship, Guo Xiang’s edition, and disputes about knowledge and perspective. Its philosophical account is one interpretation. Attention and forgetting. Chris Fraser, “Heart-Fasting, Forgetting, and Using the Heart Like a Mirror” . The account of responsive attention draws on his interpretation. Scope. This is a reading of selected connected themes, rather than a translation or an account of every chapter. The criticisms in the final section are this page’s judgments. Painting. The illustration shows Lu Zhi’s Zhuangzi Dreaming of a Butterfly , in the Asian Art Museum, San Francisco.
